  • According to recent reports, whisk together 1 cup/115 g mayonnaise, ⅓ cup/80 ml buttermilk or kefir, 1 tsp.
  • In a recent development, lay 6 chicken thighs, skin on and bones removed (about 1¾ lb./800 g), out flat on a parchment-lined baking sheet and season with ½ tsp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is pretty clever, if we do say so ourselves—using roasted chicken thighs to create a Caesar salad, all in the same sheet pan. The wedges of lettuce, tossed in the leftover juices, soften and then everything melds in a comforting way. It’s a family favorite, with kids finding the dressing to be the closest possible thing to a “ranch” that hasn’t come premade in a bottle.

More sheet-pan dinner favorites this way.

According to recent reports, whisk together 1 cup/115 g mayonnaise, ⅓ cup/80 ml buttermilk or kefir, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, 2 green onions, finely chopped, ½ tsp. ground onion, ½ tsp. ground garlic, ½ oz./15 g parmesan, finely grated (2 Tbsp.), and ¾ cup/15 g dill, finely chopped, in a small bowl, along with 1 tsp. fine sea salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Set aside.

In a recent development, lay 6 chicken thighs, skin on and bones removed (about 1¾ lb./800 g), out flat on a parchment-lined baking sheet and season with ½ tsp. salt and a good grind of pepper. Add 1 lemon, very thinly sliced (about 12 slices), drizzle with 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and bake for 30–35 minutes, until the chicken is crispy and the lemon slices have started to caramelize.

Transfer the chicken and lemon to a shallow bowl and let rest for 10 minutes. Keep the baking sheet and parchment paper with all the pan juices. Finely chop half the lemon slices and add them to the dressing. Cut the chicken into ½"-/1-cm-thick slices and toss in the bowl with the rest of the lemon slices.

Add 2–3 heads of romaine lettuce, quartered lengthwise (14 oz./400 g), to the baking sheet, season with a pinch of fine sea salt and some black pepper, and turn them a couple of times in the pan juices. Spoon half the dressing over the lettuce and scatter the chicken on top. Finish with the rest of the dressing, a handful of croutons, store-bought or homemade, the extra parmesan, and a few sprigs of dill.

#391. The Future of Techno Is Being Forged in Monterrey

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1388 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Atlasobscura ↗ Open Full Page

The Future of Techno Is Being Forged in Monterrey

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1388 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Atlasobscura

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on a mild November evening in Monterrey, Mexico, the city’s largest urban park flashed from green to pink to blue, pulsating with the rhythmic beats resounding from a 360-degree sound system.
  • Recent findings suggest that for one weekend in 2026, Monterrey, a city best known for its international corporations and industrial history, became a glowing metropolis of the future — more specifically, the new second home of FuturFestival.
  • According to recent reports, within the park’s open-air steel and concrete structures, the Turin festival became a singular addition to Europe’s house and techno scene: a celebration not only of electronic music but also of the technological progress it represents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on a mild November evening in Monterrey, Mexico, the city’s largest urban park flashed from green to pink to blue, pulsating with the rhythmic beats resounding from a 360-degree sound system. Beneath a steel walkway, in a concrete depression once used for piling steel, thousands of people swayed, trancelike, to DJs’ ethereal mixes. As the sun set over a giant steel furnace, crowds continued to spill through the gates, leaving glitter in their wake as they flocked to the stages.

Recent findings suggest that for one weekend in 2026, Monterrey, a city best known for its international corporations and industrial history, became a glowing metropolis of the future — more specifically, the new second home of FuturFestival. Established in Turin, Italy, in 2006, Futur began as an arts association honoring the tenets of Italian Futurism: namely, youth, urban industrialism, and modernization. By 2012, it had become a full-fledged house and techno music (EDM) festival and found its permanent home in Parco Dora, a former Fiat factory turned 110-acre urban park.

According to recent reports, within the park’s open-air steel and concrete structures, the Turin festival became a singular addition to Europe’s house and techno scene: a celebration not only of electronic music but also of the technological progress it represents. By 2025, Kappa FuturFestival (named for its sponsor, the Italian sportswear brand Kappa) was welcoming more than 120,000 attendees from more than 150 countries; the same year, it was ranked the sixth-best festival in the world by DJ Mag. As the event grew year by year, it put Turin on the global map, marking it as a hub for innovative, avant-garde art.

When Futur chief innovation officer and co-founder Gianluca Brignonen floated bringing the event to his adopted country, Mexico, Carlos López — CEO of the event firm Lostnights — immediately knew the festival would thrive at Parque Fundidora. The massive Monterrey park was a site remarkably similar to Parco Dora, from its historical significance down to its very name.

Now Mexico’s eighth-largest city, Monterrey developed into a major business hub shortly after the Mexican War of Independence and, with the establishment of the Monterrey Foundry in 1900, emerged as the country’s primary industrial center. The first of its kind in Latin America, the foundry took advantage of the city’s easy access to iron and coal deposits to become the backbone of the entire region’s economy.

From structural steel to railways, wire rods, and train wheels, the foundry contributed to some of Mexico’s most notable 20th-century engineering projects and counted the country’s wealthiest families among its investors. However, shortly after it was nationalized in 1977, its fortunes reversed, and it was forced to shut down in 1986.

The people of Monterrey refused to let the foundry’s towers and furnaces simply sit in obscurity, and only two years after it ceased operations, the government unveiled aims to repurpose the site into a public park and recreation space.

In a recent development, as construction began and stretched into the 1990s, Parque Fundidora evolved into much more than just green space. Additions included a convention center, children’s museum, steel museum (inside the former blast furnace), contemporary art center, and restaurant. A “Plaza of the Visionaries” was also added, paying tribute to those who helped establish the foundry over a century ago.

According to recent reports, “All the premises, all the areas are unique. Just to feel and to dance in this place with a lot of heritage — there’s a feeling of greatness,” López indicates. Whether Parque Fundidora would feel right never concerned him because it so clearly had everything: the same industrial spectacle and local reverence as Parco Dora transposed into a new cultural setting.

Getting the 360-acre park festival-ready was a years-long process. (“You could spend days in there doing different things,” Lostnights COO Yalia Bailleres observes.) The team at Lostnights needed to determine not only which sections of the massive space to use but how to let it shine — with lighting, stages, and layouts that would make its mechanical remains as compelling as the artists headlining.

After putting out an open call to audiovisual artists around the world, the Lostnights team selected a handful of moving digital artworks to play on giant LED screens throughout the park and even on one of its stages, “Voyager.” The open call’s theme, “Envision the FUTUR,” encouraged exploration at the intersection of art, technology, and electronica, reflecting Futur’s message that any festival is only as memorable as its environment.

Industry observers note that lópez, Bailleres, and their colleagues also took advantage of the park’s inconspicuous nooks and crannies, turning an area between old towers into a midsize stage for techno funk and a small brick building into a “secret” stage that nevertheless attracted a long line out the door. The festival’s premier stage, “Nova,” sat underneath a long steel bridge, the peaks of the Sierra Madre Oriental just visible behind its beatmakers and record-spinners.

“We wanted to find the perfect location that could give the same atmosphere as [Parco Dora], but at the same time, something a little different,” says Gabriella Botte, project manager of Kappa FuturFestival. “The park has such a strong identity. People know it from how the venue looks in pictures and in videos.”.

The Turin festival’s steampunk setting had become inextricable from Futur itself, making it recognizable even to non-techno fans. Incorporating Parque Fundidora’s architecture into the event as much as possible meant keeping Futur’s brand alive while, at the same time, honoring Monterrey’s cultural and economic history.

Recent findings suggest that “Monterrey is really like [Turin],” Futur CEO and co-founder Maurizio Vitale observed on opening night, Nov. 13, from inside one of the old furnace rooms. “The mountains around, the industry that we see here, and the smiles of people on the welcoming day. There’s a special energy. The people, the venue, the nation itself.”.

It has been revealed that when choosing the event’s lineup, Futur’s organizers sought to maintain its international variety while also spotlighting Mexican techno artists. As Botte explains, “The festival has to be connected with the territory in order to grow. It’s important to represent the locals.”.

Among the Mexican artists who took the stage were betterxfly (Daniela de la Garza), LABIBE (Labibe Bujaidar), and Opuntia (Camila de Laborde), as well as Monterrey up-and-comer SADA, whose unique blend of EDM and cumbia (a dance genre that originated in Colombia) has made him a rising star of the city’s growing music scene.

Recent findings suggest that it was thanks in part to this scene that more than 24,000 people revealed up for FuturFestival Mexico — a turnout that Bailleres views as a huge achievement. Past festivals held in Parque Fundidora, while attracting larger crowds, have centered on traditional Mexican music or more general arts-and-culture fare; FuturFestival is the first to introduce techno music to the mix.

“For us, having electronic music this big — for locals, it’s like ‘What is that?’ because it’s something latest,” Bailleres says. “But then we’ve started getting all this engagement, and people love this space.”.

Recent findings suggest that the team now looks ahead to the 2027 festival, with intends to increase the number of stages and take over even more areas of the park. Botte is already dreaming of a DJ atop the 230-foot-tall blast furnace, while Bailleres has her eyes set on the small river that runs through the park, imagining boats floating, lazy-river-style, past a colorful stage.

In a recent development, A place where thousands of workers once poured and molded molten steel is now a testing ground for what’s possible in electronic music exhibition and, just as importantly, a symbol of what’s next for Monterrey. “Everybody states a long-term plan, but this is more than long. This is a lifetime plan. We are here to stay,” Vitale says.

Once night set in, spotlights illuminated the foundry itself, bathing its pipes and winding staircases in neon against the dark sky. Artists mingled over drinks next to old machinery in the green room, while audience members swarmed past mill halls, cranes, and smokestacks to get to the front row for their favorite artists’ sets. Even far beyond Parque Fundidora’s gates, music echoed through the city. The future had come to Monterrey, and there was no going back.

7 Things You'd Find in a 1950s Grocery Store That Have Disappeared

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shoppers from the 1950s would probably be in awe of all the modern conveniences we have to get groceries.
  • According to recent reports, grocery stores still market products that promise convenience for busy lives, but the whole experience has become impersonal.
  • Here are a few things that were common in '50s grocery stores but have vanished today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shoppers from the 1950s would probably be in awe of all the modern conveniences we have to get groceries. The internet and Instacart would be completely mind-blowing. Convenience and saving time were a key focus for grocery stores in the '50s, so products and store features all catered to making shopping an easy and pleasant experience.

According to recent reports, grocery stores still market products that promise convenience for busy lives, but the whole experience has become impersonal. You might not even speak to another person at all if you grab what you need and head to the self-checkout. Some of the features and items of the 1950s disappeared to make way for more profit and technology, and the old ways of grocery shopping disappeared with them.

Here are a few things that were common in '50s grocery stores but have vanished today.

Beginning in 1950, "self-service" meats, pre-packaged in cellophane, became quite the trend, but enough people still preferred ordering custom cuts from the butcher that the meat counter at the grocery store kept its line of patrons. You used to order specific cuts of meat, including how fatty you wanted it, and then the butcher would measure, cut, and weigh your meat. Then, they would wrap it carefully in paper before handing it to you.

Recent findings suggest that at an A&P grocery store in the 1950s, you could grind your own coffee beans in the coffee aisle. The coffee beans were in barrels or containers, and you could scoop out the amount you wanted. Then, the grinder was right there, ready for customers to use. If you loved the smell of coffee, this aisle was heavenly, and you would walk down it even when you didn't need to buy any beans.

Industry observers note that do you ever wish, as an adult, that you could find a fun surprise like the toys that came in cereal boxes? Well, in the 1950s, you could. Duz brand laundry detergent gave a free dish with each box purchased, and families bought laundry soap weekly to collect an entire dining set. There were even gravy boats and platters! If your parents or grandparents have a set of dishes with pictures of golden wheat on them, they likely collected them from laundry soap boxes.

Recent findings suggest that another collection people got from the grocery store were stamps, though not postal stamps. These "Green Stamps" were part of a rewards program, and if you collected enough stamps, you could trade them in for a prize. S&H was not the only company to feature a loyalty stamp program, but it was the most popular. By the end of the 1950s, S&H gave out more stamps than the United States Postal Service. And the prizes weren't cheap either; you could get a bicycle, luggage, or even furniture with enough stamps.

According to recent reports, TV dinners can still be found in the frozen section of the grocery store, but they have changed a lot from the originals. Before microwaves, people heated their frozen meals in the oven, so TV dinners came in aluminum trays. They were so convenient and allowed the family to watch their new televisions together while eating. And housewives loved not having to prepare and cook a full meal every night.

According to recent reports, franco-American brand of canned pastas operated under Campbell's Soup Organization, and while they had several meals that people miss, the most famous was the macaroni and cheese. It was technically long macaroni-type noodles in a cheese sauce, but it was a popular canned meal in the 1950s. It was so popular that Campbell's didn't discontinue it until 2004, and there have been petitions to bring it back.

You can still find boxes of hair dye at the grocery store, but the at-home perms have, thankfully, faded from popularity and store shelves. In the 1950s, though, the Toni Home Permanent for women and the Tonette Home Permanent for girls were all the rage. Not needing to go to a salon for a perm was a massive plus for many women and their pocketbooks. But after many perms that just came out wrong and a lawsuit involving a little girl losing all her hair, the perm in a box lost its status as peak beauty care.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Caviar from an all-inclusive might sound like an oxymoron. With an ounce of mid-tier caviar running about $200âroughly the cost of a night at a resort of the same caliber in the Caribbeanâyou wouldn't expect to find it on a menu. But the kind I dared to try at Secrets MoxchÃ© Playa del Carmenâ"Mexican caviar," which isn't actually fish eggs at allâmost definitely changed my mind on the matter.

Sources indicate that buttery, slightly nutty, and a perfect match for toasted pumpkin seeds, escamoles are the edible larvae and pupae of ants. Unlike sturgeon roe, acquiring these delicate orbs requires conquering colonies of venomous ants rather than the belly of the beast. The name comes from the Indigenous Nahuatl words azcatl, meaning "ant," and molli, meaning "stew," which gives surprisingly accurate insight into how escamol is still prepared all these years later.

Sources indicate that while the caviar you now eat with a mother-of-pearl spoon started off as peasant food in 12th-century Russia, the "caviar of the desert" (another moniker for escamoles) was once a celebrated delicacy among Aztec emperors. From the protein's prestigious history to its current place on high-end tasting menus, its value all comes down to how the food is foraged.

In a recent development, as its upwards of $100-per-pound price tag suggests, harvesting escamoles can be tricky. The process leads straight into the underground tunnels of the velvety tree ants of Central Mexico, Liometopum apiculatum. Although these nests sit surrounded by the roots of agave and maguey plants, getting your hands on escamol is a lot more challenging than harvesting tequila or mezcal. When done sustainably, the ants and nest are preserved while the larvae are carefully scraped out by traditional escamoleros in the springtime.

While this wasn't my first dance with ants on the dinner plate, trying the escamol taco in Playa del Carmen made it much harder to ignore the reality of eating insects than the ground-up chicatana ants blended into the chile mayo on the famous baby corn dish at Pujol, a Michelin-starred institution in Mexico City. Back at the resort, sautÃ©ed and paired with epazoteâa pungent Mexican herbâand pepitas on a warm corn tortilla, it was just one bite of the seven-course taco tasting at its Mexican restaurant, Dos Almas. Yet getting past the anthill my mind had turned into a mountain to taste a centuries-old traditionâway outside my usual taco orderâstuck with me.

The rest of the tasting menu leaned just as heavily into local Mexican flavors without playing it safe. Alongside the ant eggs, the meal moved through a crisp taco dorado stuffed with pork and potato and topped with hamachi tartare and green onion oil, a smoky taco brasero piled with lobster and chipotle mayo, rich pork belly under an Oaxaca-style manchamantel mole, and my favorite, a steak taco on a queso-encrusted flour tortilla topped with charred avocadoâeach paired with regional spirits from mezcal to licor de elote (corn liqueur).

Industry observers note that it was the kind of meal I usually associate with "traveling" over "vacationing"âhunting down hard-to-get reservations and street food instead of settling for whatever is on the hotel buffet. Over a decade ago, my first trip to a Cancun-area all-inclusive cemented the idea that subpar food was just part of the deal. So when I found Secrets MoxchÃ© through Apple Vacations, I expected the usual perks of an easy beach tripâbundled flights, airport transfers, zero legworkânot food I'd actually write home about.

Aside from the few pounds I gained over the long weekend, what actually surprised me was how much Indigenous history and culture made it onto the property, rather than getting watered down for an American palate. Beyond the upgraded tasting dinners, the resort runs a year-round program called "Roads Through Mexico" that brings regional folk art, live music, and local bites onto the immaculately manicured grounds. Catching it during DÃ­a de los Muertos drove the point home: you don't always have to leave the resort gates to get a real taste of where you are.

Indianola, Texas a coastal town that was once the second largest port in Texas next to at the time Galveston.In 1956 the port received a shipment of camels as part of the United States Camel Corps experiment to replace horses and mules as the primary work animal for southwestern America.

Sources indicate that during the Civil War, it was occupied by the Union army, once in 1862, then again a year later. Part of that regiment later drowned moving from Indianola to Matagorda island.

The island was later hit twice again, this time by hurricanes, in 1876 and 1886. The second hurricane was accompanied by a major fire and also submerged most of the town, killing hundreds.

Now basically no sign of the town is left other than a few plaques (one being a marker of where the courthouse used to be). It is however valued as a great spot for fishing for local trout, redfish and flounder.

The first Thanksgiving took place in the fall of 1621. It honored the harvest and gathered the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag people in Plymouth County for three days of food and togetherness. Their relationship was not entirely conflict-free, more like temporarily cordial, and peace did not last.Â.

54 years later, King Philip's War ended with the Wampanoag tribe losing their land and freedoms to the colonists.

The tradition all but disappeared (give or take a few gatherings) until President Abraham Lincoln issued a proclamation in 1863 making Thanksgiving a national holiday on the last Thursday in November. In 1939, President Franklin D. Roosevelt declared it the third Thursday, but that only lasted two years. In 1941, Congress permanently made Thanksgiving the fourth Thursday in November. And thatâs how weâve celebrated it ever since!Â.

You need, expectedly, Original capsules for Original machines and Vertuo capsules for Vertuo machines. I've broken down the differences between the lines below, and the defining details about specific models in each line that are on sale right now. And be sure to bookmark this story because we’ll update it with more Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals on Nespresso coffee makers and espresso machines as they happen.

Introduced in 2014, Nespresso’s Vertuoline modernized the brand’s original pressure brew method and marked the true beginning of Nespresso espresso and coffee machines. Most Vertuo machines feature just one button and brew both coffee and espresso-style shots using a centrifugal method. Once you choose your preferred pod based on style, roast, and cup size, the machine takes care of the rest. That’s because the rim of every dome-shaped Vertuo capsule features a barcode that tells the Nespresso Vertuo machine how much water and what extraction speed to use for each pod—and can brew everything from a single and double espresso shot to a 14-ounce cup of coffee. Some Vertuo machines can even fill an 18-ounce carafe from a single coffee pod.

The very first Vertuo machine released more than a decade ago is still kicking, and it's one of the best values you can get.

It has been revealed that enabled with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi connectivity, the Nespresso Vertuo Next can brew 18 ounces of coffee from a single pod. If you’re intrigued by the tech or pod yield, it’s worth a try—especially considering Nespresso’s 30-day return policy, warranty, and reputation for maintenance and machine repairs.

Vertuo Next Coffee with Aeroccino Milk Frother.

The Pop Plus machines have slightly bigger water reservoirs than the Pop models, and they can hold more used capsules, but all of the machines have small-kitchen-friendly footprints.

Nespresso Vertuo Pop + Aeroccino Milk Frother.

Industry observers note that released earlier this year, the Vertuo Up is Nespresso's newest machine, and brews the one-touch Vertuo pods. This compact machine heats up in just three seconds (which, is really, really, ridiculously fast for any coffee maker to heat water) and depending on the specific model you get, it can brew six or seven different cup sizes, ranging from a single shot of espresso to a full carafe from a single Vertuo pod. Like the Next and Pop machines, the Vertuo Up is Wi-Fi enabled and you can use the companion app for maintenance alerts and to customize how the machine brews your favorite pods, if you'd like tweaks to the pod-specific presets.

The Vertuo Creatista is the first machine in the Vertuo line with a built-in steam wand. It’s not quite a one-touch cappuccino machine because brewing espresso from a pod and steaming the milk are two separate processes. But if you want the look of a real espresso machine (well, if you don’t look too closely) with the convenience of Nespresso Vertuo capsules, the Vertuo Creatista is a great option. This is the machine that I’ve been using at home for years and it works sort of like a super-automatic espresso machine.

The newest Vertuo machine, the Vertuo Lattissima is a one-touch machine that makes coffee, espresso, cappuccinos, and latte macchiatos at the push of a button.

Until the Vertuoline was introduced in 2014, the OriginalLine machines were simply known as Nespresso machines. These models brew either single or lungo (Italian for "long") espresso-style shots from any compatible pod using a pressure-driven method. The Original Line features a collection of compact pod-only machines (Nespresso CitiZ, Nespresso Essenza Mini, and Nespresso Pixie) as well as a variety of pricier Creatista and Lattissima models, with built-in steam wands or other automatic milk frothers. Airports are places of departures and arrivals, but what happens to those who never seem to leave? At Terminal 1 of Madrid-Barajas Airport, a bronze man sits quietly, apparently waiting for a flight that may never come. Known as El Vagamundos (The Wanderer), this 1996 sculpture by Spanish artist Casto Solano captures the peculiar feeling of being suspended between destinations.

Sources indicate that the seated figure has acquired a life of its own through local folklore. Some people believe it commemorates those who have turned airport terminals into temporary homes, stranded by immigration bureaucracy or personal circumstances. One popular story connects the sculpture to a Cuban traveller who allegedly spent 18 months wandering around Barajas in 1992 while trying to secure permission to return to his homeland.

Whether or not the legend is true, El Vagamundos perfectly embodies the strange limbo of airport life: the endless waiting, the transient encounters, and the feeling of belonging nowhere and everywhere at once. Among hurried passengers dragging their suitcases, this traveller has nowhere else to be.

You can find the statue of El Vagamundos on the corridor that links Terminal 1 of the airport with the metro station.

  • Sant Pere dels Arquells lies right next to the motorway, just over an hour’s drive from Barcelona.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in a village of just sixty inhabitants in the heart of rural Catalonia, you’d expect to find stone buildings, farmland and perhaps a church. And sure enough, that’s exactly what you get. What you wouldn’t expect, though, is to stumble upon three Soviet fighter jets in someone’s garden. But there they are. And alongside them, an American fighter jet, completing what must be the strangest aviation museum in the entire country.

Sant Pere dels Arquells lies right next to the motorway, just over an hour’s drive from Barcelona. Like many other places in the area, it is an old walled village, dating back to the time when Muslims and Christians were fighting over the region, a thousand years ago. There isn’t much to see here, really, apart from its bizarre collection of aircraft, clearly visible from above and on Google Maps.

Sources indicate that the four aircraft on display are three Mikoyan-Gurevich (MiG) fighters, models 15, 21 and 23, and a Lockheed F-104 Starfighter. According to the local press, their owner, Xavier M., is a military history enthusiast who bought them as scrap after the dissolution of the Soviet Union and the fall of the Iron Curtain. Despite being left outdoors, exposed to rain and sunshine, they are in surprisingly good condition. The Starfighter, in fact, was recently repainted and restored, and looks as though it could take off at any moment.

The aircraft are clearly visible from the village’s main street, as well as from behind the 15th-century church. Amateur pilots taking off from and landing at the two nearby airfields use them as a landmark. Over the years, they have become so well known in the area that the village is now popularly known as Sant Pere dels Avions (Saint Peter of the Airplanes).

Public transport to the village is virtually non-existent. The easiest way to get there is by car; under normal traffic conditions, the drive from Barcelona takes around an hour and ten minutes. Alternatively, you can take a taxi from Cervera. Access to the grounds is not permitted, and you cannot get up close to the aircraft, but they are clearly visible from the street.

Industry News: Summit House/Prospect House in Hadley, Massachusetts

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Atlasobscura

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the 400-plus-acre Skinner State Park adjoins the 3,000-acre Mount Holyoke Range State Park, where visitors can enjoy scenic vistas, picnic areas, and more than 40 miles of trails open year-round.
  • During its heyday, the hotel welcomed an impressive array of notable guests.
  • Sources indicate that one of the Prospect House’s most remarkable features was its mountain railway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the 400-plus-acre Skinner State Park adjoins the 3,000-acre Mount Holyoke Range State Park, where visitors can enjoy scenic vistas, picnic areas, and more than 40 miles of trails open year-round. At the heart of Skinner State Park stands the Prospect House, better known as the Summit House, a hotel that opened in 1851 and rapidly became a fashionable destination for wealthy travelers from eastern Massachusetts and New York City.

During its heyday, the hotel welcomed an impressive array of notable guests. Jenny Lind, the celebrated opera singer known as the “Swedish Nightingale,” visited in the year the hotel opened, and Alexander Graham Bell was a regular guest. Ralph Waldo Emerson, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, and Emily Dickinson were also among the writers associated with visits to the summit.

Sources indicate that one of the Prospect House’s most remarkable features was its mountain railway. In 1854, the hotel installed what is often described as Fresh England’s first tramway, initially to transport supplies up the mountainside and soon afterward to carry guests. At a time when train travel itself was still a relatively novel experience, a mechanical railway climbing a steep mountainside was an extraordinary attraction. The tramway operated until 1942, and visitors driving past the sign for Track 6 may still catch a glimpse of the cut through the mountainside where the tracks once ran.

In a recent development, reaching the hotel was an adventure in its own right. Guests arriving by train at Smiths Ferry, on the western bank of the Connecticut River, crossed the river by steamboat ferry. A stagecoach then carried them to the tramway, which transported them partway up the mountain before they continued to the summit. The journey offered a memorable combination of river travel, carriage rides, and pioneering mountain engineering.

In a recent development, the hotel’s story is also one of ambition and perseverance. John and Fanny French were instrumental in establishing and expanding the Prospect House. Fanny was only 19 when she and John began building their lives on the mountain. They spent their first winter in the original 1851 house, but the conditions proved so harsh that they built the Half Way House as a more practical winter residence.

The hotel expanded substantially under their proprietorship. An addition in 1861 was followed by a much larger annex in 1894, bringing the hotel to 44 guest chambers and a dining room that seated 200 people.

Industry observers note that by the early 20th century, however, the Prospect House faced mounting challenges. In 1908, following the deaths of the hotel’s owners, local industrialist and philanthropist Joseph Allen Skinner and a group of like-minded businessmen formed the Mount Holyoke Firm. Their interest increasingly centered on preserving the property rather than operating it as a commercial venture. Skinner eventually took sole ownership in the 1910s and introduced modern conveniences, including indoor plumbing, electricity, and a upcoming road for automobiles.Despite these improvements, the hotel’s popularity declined. Automobiles gave vacationers more destinations to choose from, while the economic hardships of the 1930s put a stay at the hotel beyond the reach of many travelers.

The final blow came with the devastating hurricane of 1938. Although the original 1851 and 1861 sections survived, the storm severely damaged the 1894 annex, which Skinner subsequently had demolished.

Recent findings suggest that in 1940, Skinner donated the hotel, its associated outbuildings, and 375 surrounding acres to the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. He asked for nothing in return except that the park bear his name. At the dedication ceremony, he expressed his hope that the property would become a “thing of beauty and a source of joy to the people of the Commonwealth.”.

Recent findings suggest that skinner’s legacy extends beyond the mountain. Visitors can learn more about his life and interests at the Joseph Allen Skinner Museum in South Hadley, which displays his extraordinary collection of nearly 7,000 objects.

Recent findings suggest that mount Holyoke’s appeal predates the hotel itself. In 1836, landscape painter Thomas Cole sketched the Connecticut River valley from the summit, inspiring his celebrated painting The Oxbow. Ralph Waldo Emerson also visited, according to the hotel guest book. It is intriguing to imagine these figures making the arduous climb when the only structure at the summit was a simple shack.

The mountain continues to inspire visitors today. Since 1838, Mount Holyoke College has celebrated its annual Mountain Day, when the ringing of the bells at Abbey Chapel unexpectedly cancels classes and sends students hiking to the summit.

Even the deteriorating Summit House has acquired a folklore of its own. During the 1970s and 1980s, visitors reportedly spotted the ghosts of John and Fanny French: John standing on the porch and Fanny appearing in the windows.

Sources indicate that from its pioneering railway and celebrated guests to the people who built their lives on the mountain, Mount Holyoke’s Summit House offers a fascinating glimpse into an era when reaching a mountaintop could be an adventure in itself. Today, the park preserves not only a remarkable historic building but also a landscape that has drawn travelers, artists, and nature lovers for nearly two centuries.

Belgium’s airline and travel sector is demanding stronger safeguards against strike-related disruption after air traffic controllers helped bring the country’s airports to a standstill on Monday.

The Board of Airline Representatives in Belgium (BAR Belgium) described it as the 11th strike affecting Belgian airspace in 11 months and accused public-sector workers of repeatedly undermining the country’s international connectivity.

Air navigation provider Skeyes said it could not safely provide regular air traffic control from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. local time after some of its staff joined a nationwide demonstration against government austerity measures. #373. Industry News: A colossal oscillation

Industry News: A colossal oscillation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4224 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As I write these words, surface water temperatures across a great swath of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have been rising for months.
  • Industry observers note that it’s still uncertain how the warming ocean will reshape global weather in the months to come, let alone how ecosystems – and human populations – will respond.
  • Global sea-surface temperature anomalies in November 2015, at the peak of the 2014-16 El Niño event, one of the strongest recorded by meteorological instruments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As I write these words, surface water temperatures across a great swath of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have been rising for months. El Niño is the name for the recurring and sustained warming of this part of the Pacific. And temperatures are soaring to such highs, relative to their long-term averages, that the El Niño of 2026 may be the strongest in 1,000 years.

Industry observers note that it’s still uncertain how the warming ocean will reshape global weather in the months to come, let alone how ecosystems – and human populations – will respond. The future is always murky. Still, when it comes to El Niño, the past could teach us what to expect. And not just the recent past, but also the deep past recently recovered by scientists, historians and archaeologists.

Global sea-surface temperature anomalies in November 2015, at the peak of the 2014-16 El Niño event, one of the strongest recorded by meteorological instruments. Courtesy NOAA.

According to recent reports, I’m an environmental historian. I work with climatologists to understand how climates have changed in the past. I study how communities understood and adapted to the climate’s changes. And my research suggests that history can help us understand even the most extreme events in today’s rapidly warming climate.

Industry observers note that the past can help us see why El Niño is so hard to forecast, for example, or even define. It can show us that, while El Niño has contributed to the deaths of millions of people in the past, it has also enabled others to amass wealth and power.

El Niño indisputably scrambles worldwide weather patterns, but history teaches us that it’s as much a human creation as a natural reality. And this context may help us weather not only the effects of the 2026-27 El Niño in the months to come, but also El Niño’s future on a warming planet.

According to recent reports, A vast current of cold water snakes up the western coast of South America. In December each year, that current breaks down for about a month. An influx of warm water delivers tropical fish and – because warm water evaporates more readily than cold water – abundant rainfall.

According to recent reports, it’s impossible to know when people first noticed this annual reversal of water temperatures and precipitation. We do know that, sometime after the 16th-century Spanish conquest of the Inka Empire, fishermen named it El Niño, meaning literally ‘the boy’ or, when capitalised, ‘The Christ Child’. At least the reason for the name seems clear: the reversal of current happens around Christmas.

The colonised heartland of the Inka Empire, now known as Peru, won its independence in the 19th century. Towards the end of that century, Peru’s government joined many of its counterparts by establishing a society of geographers to describe the country’s environment and to catalogue its resources. In 1892, the society’s vice president, Camilo Carrillo, introduced the annual switch in water temperatures – and the term El Niño – to the scientific community.

When it entered scientific nomenclature, El Niño was therefore a cycle that was small in time (involving just one month every year), space (affecting only the Peruvian coast), and perceived importance (interesting only to a handful of local scientists).

El Niño is actually the oceanic expression of a colossal seesaw of atmospheric pressure over the Pacific.

Only gradually did researchers detect a much bigger oscillation in Pacific Ocean temperatures, one that happened every two to seven years. This oscillation was eventually branded as El Niño. By the end of the 20th century, the effort to forecast its onset and worldwide impacts became a quintessential example of big, state-supported science.

The modern version of El Niño seems easy to define. It’s a dramatic warming of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean – a warming that’s confined to the tropics, lasts for many months, and tends to peak around the end of the year. It transfers a stupendous quantity of heat and moisture into the atmosphere, which the tropical jet stream redistributes, reshuffling weather patterns from one region to another.

According to recent reports, but what causes these recurring warmings of Pacific Ocean water? And how, exactly, do they affect regional weather patterns?

It has been revealed that only recently have scientists been able to answer those questions. It turns out that El Niño is actually the oceanic expression of a colossal seesaw of atmospheric pressure over the Pacific Ocean, known as the Southern Oscillation. When air is tightly packed together over the eastern Pacific – when atmospheric pressure there is high, in other words – and when it’s low over the western Pacific, the pressure difference reinforces persistent winds that blow west along the equator.

These trade winds, as they’re called, can push so much warm surface water into the tropics of the western Pacific that they allow deeper, colder water to reach the top of the eastern Pacific. This is called La Niña. But when the difference in Pacific Ocean pressure dips, the trade winds falter, and the warm water of the western Pacific surges east. This we call El Niño.

Recent findings suggest that scientists have learned that the Southern Oscillation involves reinforcing relationships, known as feedbacks, between the air and sea. Usually, hot water in the western Pacific evaporates in towering storms, releasing heat. The air flows east, cools down, grows denser, falls, then surges back to the west, warming up.

Industry observers note that this pattern, known as the Walker Circulation, strengthens the pressure differences of the Southern Oscillation and fuels the trade winds. But during an El Niño, warm water, evaporation and rains shift to the eastern Pacific, weakening transpacific differences in pressure and, in turn, the trade winds. This pattern helps explain the most crucial weather associated with El Niño: torrential rains across parts of the Western Hemisphere, and drought in Australasia.

Today, El Niño seems less like an event, and more like one end of a seesaw that perpetually teeters across the Pacific. But why does the seesaw behave as it does? There is still no scientific consensus, but the historical traces of both human societies and the natural world provide us with clues.

The most key questions about El Niño concern its impacts on global weather patterns – or in other words, the teleconnections that form between the warming of the equatorial Pacific and droughts, floods, storms or heatwaves around the world.

According to recent reports, these teleconnections are usually presented as predictable and consistent from one El Niño to the next. They’re visualised in maps that supposedly depict how regional temperatures or precipitation change as El Niño intensifies in the Pacific Ocean.

Typical rainfall patterns during El Niño events. Courtesy NOAA.

Industry observers note that but no two El Niño events have exactly the same teleconnections. One reason is that the extent, intensity and duration of unusually warm water in the tropical Pacific differs from one El Niño to the next. Another is that El Niño is only one of many influences on regional weather, and its effects generally weaken with distance from the tropical Pacific.

Because El Niño’s impacts on regional weather are never identical, it’s impossible to predict exactly how a future El Niño will impact most of the world’s people and ecosystems. But it’s even harder to piece together the history of El Niño before the beginning of the 20th century, when ships began to regularly measure sea-surface temperatures. And it’s harder still before the middle of the 19th century, when scientists began to systematically gather data from rain gauges where El Niño reliably generates heavy precipitation.

Decades of research now reveals broad patterns in El Niño history that could give a rough sense of what’s in store.

It’s a challenge, but not impossible. Climatologists – and a handful of historians and geographers – estimate the timing, strength and impacts of El Niño before the mid-19th century by consulting what they call the ‘archives of society’ and the ‘archives of nature’.

Sources indicate that the archives of society were created by the people of the past. They include surviving texts that describe weather directly, such as the logbooks that sailors wrote aboard ships. They also include diverse sources of evidence – not only documents but also artefacts, ruins, even oral traditions – that record human activities so dependent on the weather that they can serve as proxies for it.

It has been revealed that unlike the archives of society, the archives of nature were created by Earth itself (even if they are, of course, interpreted by people). These archives are parts of the natural world that responded either to changes in the water temperature of the Pacific Ocean, or to the regional extremes in temperature and precipitation that can be associated with those changes. The responses leave a mark in natural archives, changing the composition of growth rings in trees or corals, for example. Each mark serves as a proxy for El Niño conditions in the distant past.

Neither societal nor natural archives can provide direct measurements of sea-surface temperatures or weather, so histories of El Niño are inevitably full of uncertainty. Trees, for example, can only grow (or stop growing) so much. It’s one reason why their rings can’t precisely measure the strength of past El Niño events (and one reason why we can’t easily pin down whether this year’s El Niño really is the strongest in a millennium).

Still, decades of research can now reveal three broad patterns in El Niño history that could give us a rough sense of what’s in store – not only in the coming year, but in our future on a warming world.

Above all, El Niño shaped humanity’s past by suddenly changing where water was available, how much there was, and how people could use it.

The foundations of human life – food, shelter and movement – depend to varying degrees on water. Human populations can use water in many different ways, so they have learned to thrive in very different environments. But it seems to have been much harder for them to adapt to the sudden disruptions in water that a strong El Niño – or that a trend towards stronger El Niño conditions overall – could bring about.

This is the first pattern in El Niño’s human history.

We can already see its outlines a little more than 4,000 years ago, when the first states and empires established themselves. At that time, El Niño conditions seem to have grown more frequent, intense and long-lasting. The reason may have been a multimillennial cycle in the wobble of Earth’s rotation that altered the amount of sunlight associated with different seasons, weakening the trade winds.

It all sounds convincing until – inevitably – newly introduced evidence emerges.

Natural and societal archives suggest that some communities withered as El Niño intensified. In Peru, for example, populations appear to have deserted temple mounds, giant platforms that supported elaborate buildings and plazas. It’s easy to imagine that torrential floods sparked by strong El Niño conditions made it impossible to maintain these structures. But archaeological evidence hints at other changes that might have been partly responsible for population movements, including upcoming trade networks and newly cultivated plants. How much can the coincidence of two trends really tell us about causation?

According to recent reports, maybe quite a lot, if similar coincidences pop up elsewhere. And it seems they do. A little under 3,000 years ago, for example, settlers established a community at Teouma, on the island of Efate in today’s Vanuatu. Chemical traces of human waste and leaves in nearby swamp sediments show that the settlers cultivated taro, a root vegetable, during a period of increasing rainfall. By around 2,600 years ago, however, a trend towards stronger or more frequent El Niño conditions seems to have made local rainfall more erratic. The trend appears to correlate with a decline in settlement and cultivation on Efate.

You’ll notice a lot of conditional language about possible changes and potential correlations. Deep history is like that. Natural and societal archives can let us identify probable trends, figure out roughly when they happened, and craft convincing theories for how one trend caused another. It all sounds convincing until – inevitably – upcoming evidence emerges that compels us to re-date a trend, or propose another cause for it.

In general, evidence from the archives of nature and society is more abundant and precise the closer it dates to our present. Evidence from the previous millennium lets us identify not just trends in human and El Niño history, but discrete events.

Catastrophic famines partly linked to strong El Niño conditions appear to have killed millions.

By the 16th century, for example, cave formations, tree rings and reports written by government officials let us reconstruct the likely impacts of individual El Niño years on the Indian summer monsoon. They reveal a series of devastating droughts across India in the late 16th century, the middle and end of the 17th century, and the late 18th century.

It may be that a series of explosive volcanic eruptions were partly responsible for these droughts. The cooling effect of the sulphur they rolled out into the upper atmosphere altered temperature differences between latitudes, and between land and water. These differences in temperature help create the winds that bring monsoon rains; when they changed, the rains did too.

But the droughts also coincided with El Niño conditions. In fact, there may be a connection, because the upcoming wind patterns created by powerful eruptions seem to warm the eastern Pacific, relative to the west. Regardless, El Niño can also weaken the Indian monsoon by shifting warm water and rising air eastward across the tropical Pacific.

In a recent development, when the monsoon rains failed, harvests could too. Of course, rural populations and states had many ways of protecting themselves. Wells and granaries stored water and seeds, for instance, while trade networks could allow for emergency food imports. Still, these systems broke down when droughts lasted too long – and especially when states waged war.

In some El Niño events and in some parts of India, droughts provoked widespread famine only when armies demanded food from the already depleted countryside. In other Indian regions, the death toll soared when widespread malnutrition joined migration from drought-stricken regions to encourage the spread of epidemic disease. All told, catastrophic famines partly linked to strong El Niño conditions appear to have killed millions across 16th-, 17th- and 18th-century India.

It has been revealed that everywhere El Niño sparked extreme weather, communities suffered. Yet some prospered at their expense, and this is the second pattern we can discern in El Niño’s history.

Industry observers note that the collapse of China’s Ming dynasty in the 17th century seems to provide a striking example. Growth rings in trees and corals indicate that El Niño conditions repeatedly contributed to a weakening of the East Asian monsoon in the late 16th and early 17th centuries. At first, droughts afflicted both northeastern China – home of the loosely connected Jurchen peoples – and northern China, the Ming heartland.

Recent findings suggest that in the diverse environments of northeastern China, the Jurchen hunted, fished and farmed, a varied subsistence strategy that gave them some protection from drought. They also raided across the Great Wall into Ming territory, where they seized stockpiled grain. Eventually, droughts intensified in northern China, where soaring food prices and famine helped to destabilise the Ming regime. But drought seems to have yielded to above-average rainfall in Jurchen territories. Food provided by plentiful rain may have aided efforts to consolidate Jurchen communities into a united ‘Manchu’ state that was strong enough to exploit the Ming dynasty’s weakness, conquer China, and establish a newly introduced Qing dynasty.

Indeed, conquest and colonialism created a means by which the impacts of El Niño could be amplified for some communities, but alleviated or even exploited for others. This redistribution of vulnerability was never clearer or more catastrophic than in the late 19th century, when exceptionally strong El Niño conditions coincided with a global age of imperialism.

The exact connection between colonialism and crisis differed from place to place.

It has been revealed that in 1876, drought spread across India, then intensified with a strong El Niño in 1877-78. It was the heyday of the British Raj. Colonial officials had upended lives and livelihoods in many Indian farming communities by forcing them to plant cash crops such as tea or cotton. Now, there wasn’t enough food to go round. What grain could be harvested was either redirected from the poorest communities to areas where people could pay more, or exported out of India by colonial administrators who scorned market interventions.

Tens of millions died in the ensuing famines.

‘The Last of the Herd’ by Horace Harral from the October 1877 edition of The Graphic. Courtesy Wikimedia.

Similar tragedies played out wherever El Niño sparked drought in the late 19th century, though the exact connection between colonialism and crisis differed from place to place. In Eritrea and Ethiopia, for instance, Italian invaders arrived with cattle infected by rinderpest, a deadly disease that spread to local cattle before the arrival of another strong El Niño in 1890-91. Widespread mortality among cattle intensified food shortages, as did the arrival of immense locust swarms.

Perhaps a third of Ethiopia’s population perished.

The United States, however, often benefitted from El Niño conditions. As worldwide droughts drove up grain prices in 1877-78, US farmers exported enormous quantities of wheat to Europe. The resulting inflow of gold-backed credit strengthened US finances, and helped the government manage its Civil War debts. A century later, during another strong El Niño in 1972, the collapse of the Peruvian anchovy fishery, owing both to warming water and years of overfishing, deprived poultry producers of fishmeal. But that allowed US farmers to profit by planting soy, a substitute. In the even stronger 1982-83 event, torrential rains devastated California and other southern states, but overall, the US economy received a powerful stimulus from mild winter weather.

It was around this time – the late 20th century – that scientists and journalists created the modern concept of El Niño as a global event that recurred every few years to cause predictable disasters. This is the third pattern in our history. El Niño is not just an environmental reality; it’s also a cultural reality: a manufactured threat that is a unique product of our time.

According to recent reports, in some respects, that threat was a creation of the 1957-58 International Geophysical Year (IGY). During the IGY, a global campaign to observe Earth and near-Earth space served as an arena for scientific and technological competition between the US and Soviet governments. The IGY fortuitously coincided with an El Niño, and unprecedented observations helped scientists begin to understand the true dimensions of Pacific Ocean warming.

It turned out that different El Niño events strengthened in different ways.

Recent findings suggest that cold War politics continued to shape El Niño science. The 1959 Cuban Revolution joined the growing importance – for poultry farmers – of the Peruvian anchovy fishery to spur US support for collaborations between US and Latin American scientists. These collaborations, many of which focused on the study of El Niño, were supposed to demonstrate the value of partnership with US institutions.

When navies deployed nuclear submarines to reinforce newly developed nuclear arsenals, they began to fund oceanographic research partly to better understand the underwater battlespace. Until then, oceanographers had been able to visit marine environments only occasionally, in ships. Beginning in the 1950s, new funds and technology allowed them to deploy instruments to monitor environments continuously, for months or years at a time.

According to recent reports, the launch of Sputnik 1 during the IGY also heralded a new age in which weather satellites kept the oceans under constant supervision from above. And computer models soon seemed capable of forecasting not just global warming, but also the state of the Southern Oscillation. By the early 1980s, prominent scientists believed that El Niño could finally be predicted months in advance.

Yet the strong El Niño of 1982-83 came as a shock to the overwhelming majority of meteorologists and oceanographers. It turned out that different El Niño events strengthened in different ways, and each had distinct impacts on regional weather patterns. Because the unanticipated El Niño led to floods, droughts and storms that killed thousands of people, inflicted billions of dollars in damage, and cost the global economy trillions in estimated lost growth, scientists redoubled their efforts to forecast El Niño and its teleconnections.

The concept of El Niño as a global disaster had deep roots in the history of US mass media.

Industry observers note that in 1985, the World Meteorological Organization – a United Nations agency – introduced a decade-long project to scatter ocean-monitoring buoys across the tropical Pacific. Scientists also began to use both societal and natural archives to reconstruct the deep history of El Niño. In early 1997, they had learned enough to successfully predict another ocean warming months before it happened. Scientists from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) alerted US journalists, and they created a media sensation: an El Niño reimagined as a looming, worldwide catastrophe.

It’s ironic that American journalists developed this threatening newly introduced view of El Niño. In the US, the economic benefits of the 1997-98 El Niño would again far outweigh the damage. But the concept of El Niño as a global disaster had deep roots in the history of US mass media.

Recent findings suggest that since the 19th century, US reporters had thrilled audiences by portraying natural phenomena as sensational, often threatening events – events that could be understood only by plucky scientists. A close but routine approach of a comet or planet to Earth, for example, became a brush with death recorded by swashbuckling scientists in far-flung observatories.

Sources indicate that it was journalism that resonated in a culture shaped by religious concepts of a purifying apocalypse. And it helps explain why, in the 20th century, the scientific investigation of changes in the atmosphere – not just global warming, but also nuclear winter, the ozone hole, acid rain, and even the potential consequences of asteroid impacts or volcanic eruptions – relied on US funding and institutions, while coming to particularly alarm US citizens.

Industry observers note that now, some US journalists used the Spanish name of El Niño to conjure an image of a foreign menace that several compared to migrants from South America. As the 1997-98 El Niño warmed into the strongest event since the 19th century, ‘Blame it on El Niño’ and ‘Don’t blame me, blame El Niño!’ were common slogans on everything from bumper stickers to T-shirts. That was true even though scientists couldn’t predict exactly how El Niño would affect weather in most parts of the world, let alone how populations would react.

It was in 1997 that today’s understanding of El Niño – part Cold War relic, part scientific achievement, and part media monster – was born.

Sources indicate that the patterns in El Niño’s past teach us that the warming of the tropical Pacific can be disastrous for communities exposed to droughts and floods. But they also reveal that El Niño disasters are caused less by the severity of weather extremes, and more by the brutality of how some communities are exploited by others. They suggest that today’s imagined El Niño – a global threat, with predictable impacts on weather – is less an accurate reflection of reality than a creation of modern science, media and geopolitics.

In a recent development, in the coming years and decades, it’s likely that El Niño’s impacts on populations will be shaped primarily by human relationships and ideas, not by nature. But human actions now include greenhouse gas pollution on such a scale that Earth has warmed by about 1.5°C, relative to its average temperature in the late 19th century. This pollution is supercharging the impacts of El Niño on weather. Heatwaves are growing hotter, and intensifying evaporation means droughts are getting worse. Partly because a warm atmosphere holds more water, downpours are ever more intense.

NOAA’s CFSv2 seasonal climate model demonstrates what sea-surface temperatures could look like in December 2026, based on 1984-2009 model climatology. Revised from Tropical Tidbits.

Recent findings suggest that global warming doesn’t seem capable of ending the Southern Oscillation, and with it the age-old seesaw of El Niño and La Niña. Still, it could lead to even more intense El Niño events that cause even more extreme weather.

It’s never been more urgent to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. But El Niño’s past also teaches us a deeper lesson about adapting to climatic extremes. Today, the world seems increasingly shaped by renewed great power competition: by militarism and colonial relationships between superpowers and their patrons. History suggests that such a world could be one in which millions die unnecessarily, not just through war but in preventable climate disasters.

It’s a warning from the past that today’s governments would be wise to heed, as El Niño reshapes environments from one end of the world to another in the months and years to come.

In this video essay for the digital publication Fully Human, the UK animator and filmmaker Lewis Heriz interrogates where this is taking us. We inevitably build our world through symbols, he says, but the hall-of-mirrors reality we’re rapidly creating may be leading us down a perilous path. However, he argues, we’re not without agency. Instead of submitting to a world where data and people are indistinguishable, we should be thinking critically and imaginatively about how we might use AI in ways that preserve our humanity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometimes, when we are going through difficult times, we can wonder what the point of a celebration is. Parties and feasts are all well and good when all our needs have been taken care of, but they seem too frivolous in times of hardship. But having something that raises spirits and gives hope is just as vital as enduring the struggles.

Thanksgiving dinner looked different in the 1930s because the Great Depression had practically decimated the economy. People could barely afford regular food, let alone a typical Thanksgiving meal. But they made the best of what they had and celebrated the holiday as a bright spot during dark days. Even without the staples we think of today, American families used creativity and resourcefulness to make their Thanksgiving special during the Great Depression.

A traditional turkey was too expensive for Depression-era families, so they improvised with whatever meat they had available. Ironically, some of the poorest families could get turkey if they went to soup kitchens or charities that provided Thanksgiving dinners. Most people, however, made old hen, mock duck, or porcupine meatballs as their Thanksgiving entrÃ©e.

Industry observers note that rather than actual porcupine meat, porcupine meatballs were made by sticking rice into the ground beef as a way of making it more filling. Mock duck was similarly created to spread the meal further. It was actually flank steak wrapped around stuffing and roasted. It was a pretty good imitation of a fancy dish, making it feel more like a Thanksgiving meal. An old chicken that could no longer lay eggs could also do in a pinch, but you had to cook it carefully so the meat wasn't too tough.

Speaking of stuffing, that was one dish that was cheap and easy to come by because all you needed was stale bread and some herbs. People in the 1930s would add more to their stuffing, like apples, raisins, or chestnuts they foraged. Dandelion salads were popular side dishes as well, since it was easy to gather the plants from your yard.

Canned vegetables were also a staple for a Depression-era Thanksgiving. The radio show Aunt Sammy's Homemaker's Half Hour often included recipes to liven up canned foods. Some of the most popular were creamed pearl onions and candied sweet potatoes. Mashed potatoes were also easy to make, as potatoes were inexpensive.

According to recent reports, thanksgiving wouldn't be Thanksgiving without dessert, but it got a little tricky when sugar and other baking ingredients were luxuries. Pumpkin pie was only made for dessert if you could get your hands on an actual pumpkin in the 1930s. The canned pumpkin purÃ©e was not easy to access, and if it was sold near you, it was probably out of your budget. People made do with other sweet treats, using canned foods once again.

Thanks to sweetened condensed milk, families could make a sugar cream pie for Thanksgiving dessert. Tomato soup was also a main ingredient for an easy dessert: tomato soup cake. It might sound gross to modern foodies, but it was surprisingly sweet and rich, and it used simple ingredients families were sure to have on hand. If all else failed, you could pop open a can of B & M Brown Bread, which was sweet and dense like a cake.

For those who've yet to encounter these fairy tale wonders, the Moomins are a family of creatures who resemble upright white hippos. British writer C. S. Lewis penned this fabulous series of books between 1950 and 1956. This is one of those rare books that effortlessly conjures up a cozy yet adventure-filled world of ancient secrets and remarkable goings-on.

Many generations have been thrilled by Wilder's semi-autobiographical tales of her childhood in Wisconsin during the early 1870s. While later entries in the series don't shy away from difficult issues and tough times, this particular book is a perfect read for a cozy winter's day. It chronicles the Wilder family's preparations for the harsh weather to come, as food is harvested and fuel is gathered. The young Laura begins to learn her domestic duties, family comes to visit, and evenings are spent by the fire, wrapped up in music and love.

It didn't take long for Allsburg's highly imaginative and delightful 1985 picture book to establish itself as a modern classic. It's revealed to him that this is the famous Polar Express, on its way to the North Pole, and, of course the boy jumps on board. He finds himself in the company of many other children, dressed in pajamas. As the magical train rattles towards a meeting with Santa, the children sing songs and slurp hot chocolate, each hoping to be the first to receive a present from Father Christmas. There is a deep reverence for traditional fairy tales at the heart of this beautiful work, and adults will find themselves just as moved by it as their children.

Industry observers note that writer Susan Cooper turned to English folklore and history for this deeply evocative novel, the first in a series of five, which features an eleven-year-old boy named Will Stanton as he slowly discovers the world is far stranger and more magical than he had ever imagined. Stanton learns he is an Old One, part of an ancient group of protectors of the Light tasked with fighting back the ever-rising tide of the Dark. Cooper's writing brilliantly conjures the wonder and mystery of Christmastime and remains just as engrossing fifty years on from its 1973 debut.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Suzanne Collins never had to invent a word for the country at the center of The Hunger Games: she borrowed one. Panem is Latin for "bread," with Roman ties, and the same word used for "daily bread" in the Latin Lordâs Prayer.

On its own, it's a fitting name for a nation where kids go hungry, but Collins took the word out of a much nastier sentence.

Recent findings suggest that around the year 100 CE, the Roman poet Juvenal wrote his 10th satire, a long, sour poem about how badly people choose what to wish for, and partway through it he takes a swing at his fellow citizens. "Romeâs voters once handed out military commands and consulships," he complains, "but now theyâve stopped caring about any of it": in G.G. Ramsayâs 1918 translation, the public âlongs eagerly for just two things,â bread and games. In Latin, the two things are panem et circenses, and Mental Floss has counted the phrase among the Latin you should be using.

The translation comes in Mockingjay, the third novel, when Plutarch Heavensbee, the former Head Gamemaker, tells Katniss itâs âa saying from thousands of years ago, written in a language called Latin about a place called Rome.â As he puts it, âThe writer was saying that in return for full bellies and entertainment, his people had given up their political responsibilities and therefore their power.â.

Collins has mentioned the bread in her books cuts both ways. Asked in an interview for the seriesâ 10th anniversary why she made Peeta a baker, she said that when he throws a starving Katniss a loaf, âheâs keeping her alive long enough to work out a strategy for survival,â which made him âa life giver.â But, she added, âthereâs a dark side to bread, too. When Plutarch Heavensbee references it, heâs talking about Panem et Circenses, Bread and Circuses, where food and entertainment lull people into relinquishing their political power.â.

Recent findings suggest that panem isnât the only Roman name Collins borrowed. Plutarch is named for the biographer Plutarch, whose Lives Collinsâs father used to read to her: when Spartacus came on TV, heâd get out the âLife of Crassus,â since Spartacus, a slave, âdidnât rate his own book.â And in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, the District 2 boy Sejanus Plinth is named for Lucius Aelius Sejanus, who rose to enormous power under the emperor Tiberius and was executed for conspiring against him.

That last one ties back to Juvenal, who wrote his âbread and circusesâ line in the middle of a scene about the real Sejanusâs fall. In Ramsayâs translation, his statues come down, the head of âthe darling of the mobâ goes into the furnace and comes out as frying pans and slop pails, and âSejanus is being dragged along by a hook, as a show and joy to all!â The same crowd, Juvenal claims, would have hailed Sejanus as emperor if things had gone the other way, because it âfollows fortune, as it always does, and rails against the condemned.â A public execution staged as a show for a crowd that cheers whoeverâs winning is about as Panem as it gets, and it was sitting right next to the name the whole time.

It has been revealed that throughout history, beauty and attention have been synonymous with power, wealth, and identity, Cleopatra being a defining example. But physical beauty claims far less about a personâs character than what lies within.Â.

Beauty, by definition, is âthe quality or group of qualities in a person or thing that gives pleasure to the senses or the mind.â And since we all have different minds, a physical âbeauty standardâ is a very loose concept with a very strong hold on society.

Synonyms for beauty describe the physical appearance of a person or place, sometimes in a pleasing way and sometimes with hints of allure and deception; It can be a double-edged sword, after all.Â.

Many of these words have nearly disappeared from modern vocabulary or have been replaced by terms like âhot,â âpretty,â and âcool,â but they bring a certain vintage charm to the conversation.

They describe not only beauty, but also love, confidence, impressiveness, and vanity, with descriptions as ravishing as their definitions.

Here are seven old-timey words that describe beauty in different ways.Â.

Definition: "unusually attractive, pleasing, or striking.".

In a sentence: I'd heard about her ravishing countenance, but was unaware of the true measure of her wit.

Definition: "beauty or a beautiful thing.".

In a sentence: Her natural formosity made her shine like a bright light in every room she entered.

Definition: "marked by or expressive of love, confidence, or happiness, vividly bright and shining, glowing.".

In a sentence: His undeniable radiance drew people in, making him a noticeable presence at every function.

In a sentence: The actress's lovesome features gave her a timeless elegance that shone through the silver screen for centuries.

Definition: "attracting attention or notice through unusual or conspicuous qualities.".

In a sentence: The scene was so striking, he compared it to a dream.

Definition: "having a pleasing and usually impressive or dignified appearance.".

In a sentence: His handsome face was not easily forgotten, nor his kindness.

Definition: "having deceptive attraction or allure, showy.".

In a sentence: The stranger's specious smile made him seem very approachable, but, what was hiding beneath it?
