📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For Shuai Wang, chef of King BBQ in North Charleston, South Carolina, mochi brings back memories of holidays with family. His other dessert love? Classic Southern pecan pie. This Hawaiian-style butter mochi cake draws on both, pairing a rich, chewy cake with a generous layer of maple-miso pecans.

The batter gets its signature bounce from mochiko, a distinct style of rice flour that gives butter mochi its chewy texture—not the fluffy crumb of a conventional cake. Coconut milk and melted butter add richness, while the pecans provide crunch. Let the cake cool completely before slicing so the texture has time to set.

Industry observers note that the secret to the pecan topping is a little white or yellow miso, which brings savory depth to the maple syrup, much like the salt in salted caramel. The nuts need only a brief head start in the oven; they’ll continue to toast as the cake bakes.

Can I use regular rice flour instead of mochiko?

Recent findings suggest that no. Mochiko, also called sweet or glutinous rice flour, has a different starch composition from regular rice flour. It’s responsible for butter mochi’s characteristic springy, slightly sticky chew. Regular rice flour or all-purpose flour won’t produce the same texture.

What kind of miso is best for baking?

According to recent reports, white and yellow miso are both good choices for this cake. White miso tends to be milder and slightly sweeter, while yellow miso has a somewhat more pronounced savory flavor. Either adds complexity to the maple-coated pecans without overwhelming their buttery, nutty flavor. Learn more about the different types of miso and how to use them.

Is butter mochi cake gluten-free?

Mochiko is naturally gluten-free, despite the sometimes confusing name glutinous rice flour. This recipe can be gluten-free, but check your miso: Some varieties contain barley or wheat. If you’re baking for someone who needs to avoid gluten, choose a miso labeled gluten-free and check your other packaged ingredients.

1 hour 30 minutes, plus cooling.

According to recent reports, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly oil a rimmed baking sheet with vegetable oil. Whisk 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 tsp. white or yellow miso (gluten-free if needed) in a medium bowl until smooth. Add 8 oz. raw pecans, coarsely chopped (about 2 cups) and 1 Tbsp. sugar and toss until evenly coated. Spread out on prepared baking sheet; bake until fragrant and matte looking, 6–8 minutes (nuts won’t be fully toasted). Let cool.

Lightly grease a 9"-diameter cake pan with unsalted butter and line bottom with a parchment paper round. Vigorously whisk 2 large eggs, 1¼ cups (250 g) sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Add one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, well shaken, heated slightly if fat is solid, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and whisk well. Add 1⅔ cups (254 g) mochiko and 1 tsp. baking powder; whisk vigorously until combined and batter is smooth and thick. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Industry observers note that toss pecans to break up any clumps and scatter evenly over batter, going all the way to the edges (it may seem like a lot). Bake cake until sides start to pull away from pan, top is golden brown, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean (some pecans will sink), 50–55 minutes. If pecans begin to brown too promptly, loosely tent pan with foil. Transfer to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 15 minutes. Turn cake out onto rack; peel away parchment and discard. Carefully turn cake right side up and let cool completely (at least 1 hour).

To serve, slice cake and top with scoops of vanilla ice cream.

Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Cake can be made 1 day ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that the former United Boat Service Yard at the foot of Carroll Street was the first major maritime property to be converted to residences, becoming in the early-1980s The Boatyard Condominiums.
  • Less than 10 years later, the last sail-making loft, Rapsey & Lapthorn, founded in 1915 and a purveyor to America's Cup racing yachts, became The Sailmaker Condominium.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was perhaps inevitable that market-driven land use change would come to City Island; the beauty of the place is immediately apparent. Only a quarter-mile causeway separates the small island from the rest of the Bronx, one of the five boroughs of Fresh York City, and yet City Island can seem a world away.

Industry observers note that the former United Boat Service Yard at the foot of Carroll Street was the first major maritime property to be converted to residences, becoming in the early-1980s The Boatyard Condominiums. The managing director then of the island’s chamber of commerce told the New York Times, “If the condos do well, then the boatyards and marinas are all going to go.”.

Less than 10 years later, the last sail-making loft, Rapsey & Lapthorn, founded in 1915 and a purveyor to America's Cup racing yachts, became The Sailmaker Condominium. All that was left of these two businesses was nominal references to their function before conversion to residential development. Yet, in spite of the loss of major historic waterfront industries, City Island (mostly, see “Know Before You Go”) maintains its small-town, maritime feel.

It has been revealed that A half-mile wide and 1.5 miles long, one is never far from the water on City Island. The buildings, even the new construction, are low-rise, providing a sense of sky that is unique to waterfront communities. With only 4,417 residents (2020 Census) and a—“a” as in one—small supermarket, gas station, bank, and hardware store, it is not hard for visitors to picture themselves in a quaint New England fishing village.

According to recent reports, the popular seafood restaurants, the principal tourist attraction, contribute to the impression. This is ironic because City Island was not a significant port for fishing vessels. City Island is known for its boat building and repair and if you want to know more about that history, the place to visit is the City Island Nautical Museum.

Recent findings suggest that the museum is located in the former Public School 102 (later, P.S. 17) designed by noted academic architect C.B.J. Snyder and constructed in 1897. The museum contains a main hall gallery primarily composed of two-dimensional material; the Walsh Library with books, ephemera, and other artifacts; the Nautical Room that focuses on the island’s maritime history; a Community Room, which celebrates life on City Island; and the School Room, with an emphasis on local education.

Like many museums in sparsely populated places that have undergone substantial change, the historical museum on City Island is nostalgic, a lovingly handcrafted assemblage of what artifacts became available for exhibition and what might be reproduced (including with a photocopying machine). A larger physical space, and a much larger budget, might have resulted in a more polished presentation, but a good deal of the charm of the museum derives from the manner in which it tells the maritime and social history of City Island.

It has been revealed that the City Island Nautical Museum is open seasonally on Saturdays and Sundays. Check the museum’s website for details. It is worth noting that the weekends during peak season are when day-trippers are most likely to visit City Island. Congestion is predictable and on-street parking is limited.

The western terminus of the Bx29 bus is located at the Pelham Bay Park station on the 6 train and the ride to City Island is approximately 15 minutes. If traveling by public transportation, it is possible to take the bus to its final stop at Rochelle Street and walk one-tenth of a mile further south to Belden Point. It is a 0.7 mile walk north to the City Island Nautical Museum, with Grace Episcopal Church located on the right in about five blocks.

I Used to Hate February in Upstate New York. Then Came the Soup.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1201 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that “Come on downnn!
  • My partner’s dice hit the green felt with an emphatic thwack.
  • According to recent reports, the setting couldn’t be further from a casino, and my gamble wasn’t for money—it was for chowder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that “Come on downnn! Roll and spin!” My teeth chattered and breath puffed into the air as I searched for the source of the announcement from my spot halfway down the line snaking down the Phila Street sidewalk. Rounding the corner, my eyes landed on a jovial gentleman clad in a purple suit and yellow-tinted aviators; he’s really in character. A few minutes later, and it was our turn to roll.

My partner’s dice hit the green felt with an emphatic thwack. “That’s a seven! It’s that easy, my friends,” yelled the purple-suited host. “You get a free chowder,” the dealer exclaimed from behind a mock roulette wheel and a table riddled with giant playing cards, poker chips, dice, and uniquely, steaming crockpots. Most people flock to my hometown city of Saratoga Springs for the summertime horse races, natural springs, or, in winter, as a gateway to snowy Adirondack cabins. But I brave February’s biting cold most years for one thing: soup.

According to recent reports, the setting couldn’t be further from a casino, and my gamble wasn’t for money—it was for chowder. Along with about 20,000 other attendees bundled in parkas and wool hats, I was in my hometown of Saratoga Springs to judge soup at my favorite annual festival: Chowderfest.

It has been revealed that we were in front of Solevo Restaurant in downtown ‘Toga to taste our first sample of the day: clams casino chowder. My hands rejoiced at the warmth from a small cup of New England-style broth swimming with garlic-butter littleneck clams, bacon, peppers, and breadcrumbs. Straight out of the gate, this one was the one to beat for me; the rich flavor, ample clams, and contrast of the breadcrumbs came together for a chef’s kiss.

In a recent development, as a gateway hub to the massive Adirondack Park’s eastern region, Saratoga isn’t short on visitors, especially in summer when the track opens. But despite the crowded streets, Chowderfest is different. It’s mostly locals, out in the cold on the slowest weekend of the year, eating soup on the sidewalk. It’s our mid-winter beacon: a city-wide party paying homage to gastronomic creativity through chowder in all forms. This year marked the event’s 27th year, and my 11th time attending, with 88 restaurants and vendors slinging chowder of all kinds.

It has been revealed that clams are optional, and thinking outside the box is highly encouraged. I’ve had a Southwest shrimp and corn chowder, and Druthers Brewing Company has won People’s Choice in the festival’s top sales tier every year since 2023. Past winners have included a red Reuben chowder and a ravioli chowder. This year’s entry was a smoky corn chowder amped up with a fancy garnish of bacon crumbles and a lobster hush puppy.

According to recent reports, february gets a bad rap in Upstate NY. Winter kicks into full gear as already-towering snowbanks creep higher, icicles dangle like giant pointy fingers from roofs, and the temperatures dip into the negatives more days than not. I’d always despised February growing up—I wanted spring to show up already. But shortly after graduating college in Vermont and moving back home, that changed. On the first Saturday of February 2005, I discovered Chowderfest in all its glory: downtown closed to traffic, a community showing up to mingle and support local restaurants during the slow season, and happy visitors ready to party…hard. Live music wafted from numerous watering holes, throngs of people embraced the bitter cold to celebrate chowder, and despite my toes going numb, I loved every minute of it. I’d just moved back to my hometown and wasn’t sure I wanted to be there. That afternoon was the first time Saratoga felt like a place I’d choose, not one I’d ended up in.

Recent findings suggest that lines at the ever-popular Chowderfest. Photo: Lauren Breedlove.

Since then, I’ve lived in Manhattan and Italy before eventually circling back to Upstate. Whenever possible, I’ve made a point to attend Chowderfest, even braving the slippery streets on crutches one year after breaking two toes on my left foot the night before. But nobody hobbles through a February crowd on crutches for the soup alone, and I went for the same reason I went in 2005: the whole town out on the street in the cold, propping up its restaurants through the slowest stretch of winter and having a very good time doing it. I’ve brought my sister, numerous friends from out of town, and my partner, all to share the unique soup-fête experience over the years.

For me, Chowderfest has fostered a deeper appreciation of soup, particularly when I travel. Soup is universally comforting, feeds the masses, salutes local ingredients, and is typically one of the most affordable meals. Now, I seek out local soups as part of my culinary and cultural connection to a destination: pumpkin soup in Slovenia, fish soup in Iceland, quinoa soup in Peru—all wonderful. The bowl that inspired a return trip to the far-flung Faroe Islands came with good conversation. In a local’s home, cozy and shielded from the wind that had been whipping me in the face all day, I tucked into what has become the soup by which I measure all soups: a creamy, almost curry-like fish soup with potatoes and root veggies. I had two bowls while chatting with the homeowner’s son-in-law, who told me about his favorite place in the archipelago — which I then visited on my next trip four years later.

With so many participating restaurants, it’s impossible to try every single chowder. This year, I hit up some favorite joints like Cantina, which dishes out a chiles en nogada (chiles in walnut sauce) chowder inspired by a classic Mexican dish made with roasted poblano peppers, picadillo beef, roasted pork, dried fruits, and a creamy pepita sauce. It’s heavy on the meat and wonderfully creative. I also popped into some newbies: a fresh bar on Caroline Street (the party street) called Lucy’s, where staff were ladling out a cheddar cheeseburger chowder that got bonus points from me, thanks to the tater tot toppers.

Recent findings suggest that despite the cold, I took my gloves off to vote. As predicted, clams casino from Solevo was my number one chowder this year, and I’ve already marked the date in my calendar for the next one. For someone who spent her childhood wanting to skip February, it’s an odd month to plan a year around. Saratoga’s summers are mostly for tourists, but for one weekend in February, the town throws a party for itself, and that’s the weekend that really makes me feel at home.

According to recent reports, the festival takes place annually on the first Saturday of February. The upcoming 2027 event will be on February 6 from 11 AM to 4 PM, but the party downtown keeps going all night, with a slew of live music events and food and drink specials. The festival is free to attend, with four-ounce chowder samples available to purchase for $2 each. Everyone is a judge, and attendees can easily vote in the app (found in the App Store or on Google Play) for their favorite chowder.

As a word in its own right, the verb reapâas in, âto reap what you sowââdates back to the very earliest days of Old English.Â.

Back then, it was used both in its literal sense, of cutting and gathering a ready harvest, and in its more metaphorical sense, meaning to enjoy or make the most of oneâs effortsâor, in a more negative light, to get your deserved comeuppance. (The phrase âreap what you sow,â in fact, is inspired by several similar lines in the Bible.) Etymologically, moreover, in the sense of collecting something only when it is ready, reap is a not-too distant cousin of the adjective ripe.Â Â.

According to recent reports, in more recent years, however, reaping has earned a whole new lease of life thanks to Suzanne Collinsâ hugely popular Hunger Games series of books and spinoff movies. In the context of Collinsâ dystopian future universe, the Reaping is the annual selection of âtributesâ who go forward from each district to compete in the Games, with their names drawn lottery-style from a communal pot.Â.

Names of potential tributes are added into the draw as soon as they come of age, with another added the following year, and so on, until theyâre 18. By that time, their name has been added a total of seven times, increasing their likelihood of being âreapedâ year on year. Families in the Collinsâ world can also apply for tesseraeâearning an extra supply of grain or oil in exchange for adding an extra entry into the Reaping.Â.

Industry observers note that mercifully, there are no real-world parallels to Collinsâ dystopian system (or at least, not yet there isnât). But thatâs not to say that her Reaping was at least in part inspired by several grim and gruesome stories from ancient history and mythology.Â.

One of the greatest inspirations behind Collinsâ stories were the gladiatorial games of Ancient Rome, which motivated the idea of the Games themselves at the center of her work. She has also credited the story of Spartacusâa Roman soldier turned slave who was forced into gladiatorial combat and fought for othersâ entertainment, before leaving to rebel against Rome itselfâas inspiration for the character arc of her own protagonist and Capitol rebel, Katniss Everdeen.Â.

The influence of Ancient Rome on Collinsâ work, in fact, can even be seen in the name of the Katnissâ home nation of Panem, which was lifted from the Latin phrase panem and circenses, or âbread and circuses.âÂ  Coined by the poet and satirist Juvenal, it is meant to sum up the basic sustenance and entertainment provided by a government to keep their people content and unlikely to rebel.Â.

Sources indicate that but if Ancient Rome gave Collins an idea for the Games themselves, what about the Reaping? Well, thanks to Greek mythology, thereâs a historical parallel for that too.Â.

It has been revealed that collins has said that her first inspiration for The Hunger Games was the myth of Theseus and the Minotaur. In the story, as revenge for the brutal murder of his son Androgeus in Athens, the despotic king of Crete, Minos, demands that Athens send him seven Athenian youths and seven Athenian maidens every year (or, in some versions of the story, every seven or nine years) so that they can be sent into the labyrinth and sacrificed to the Minotaur. These fourteen tributes are selected from the populace of Athens by lot, with the city largely powerless to do anything about the enraged kingâs demands.Â.

It has been revealed that in an attempt to end the sacrifices once and for all, the legendary hero Theseus gamely takes the place of one of the Athenian youths sent to the labyrinth, andâwith the help of King Minosâ young daughter Ariadne, who falls in love with him as soon as she sees himâslays the Minotaur. The parallels between this story and Collinsâ Reaping are clear, with the drawing of lots, yearly sacrifices of youths and young maidens, and even Katniss voluntarily taking the place of her younger sister in the Games as tribute in the Reaping all having their roots in Theseusâ story.

Rather than being an impressive, polished wax museum, the Visulahti Wax Museum has become famous for its awkward, outdated, and sometimes unintentionally hilarious figures.

According to recent reports, the museum has something of a cult reputation in Finland. Its wax figures are famously questionable in quality: many look surprisingly inaccurate, while some remind you more of a horror movie setting. In 1983, the Wax Museum was established with serious intentions, but nowadays people visit it mainly for nostalgic reasons. You have to approach the museum with a good sense of humour.

Sources indicate that the collection rarely gets updated, and the once-popular TV stars are now unfamiliar to the younger audience. The newest figurine is the Finnish president, whose resemblance – or the lack of it – has been widely discussed in the national news.

It has been revealed that there are also international stars displayed at the museum, such as Elvis, the Beatles, and Santa Claus. At the end of the tour, a creepy version of Mickey Mouse sings to you with his friends, as you walk out of the building, wondering what you just experienced.

Recent findings suggest that wax Cabinet is open only during the summer season; see the current entry price on the website. Entry is also included with the Visulahti wristband, which gives you access to other activities in the area as well.

A Miami cafe even released a specialty roast of coffee beans, and one Florida restaurant chain partnered with Rockstar, the game’s developer, to bring an in-game food spot to life. (The game is set in a fictional state modeled after Florida.).

According to recent reports, this is the kind of widespread, obsessively orchestrated marketing plan you’d expect around a Beyoncé album. We have arguably not been this close to a true monocultural moment since The Dress debate in February of 2015.

It has been revealed that in other news, Alison Roman’s podcast, Having People Over, which I teased in last week’s Open Tab officially debuted this week. Episode one features Bowen Yang, and the next couple will be with Lauren Graham and Jenny Slate—and then that’s it until 2027, as Roman told me.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the salty, salacious scandal around Maldon’s sourcing, a latest study on GLP-1s for children, the case for cocktail brutalism, and a Tuscon restaurant alchemizing desert ingredients.

According to recent reports, at Bon Appétit, we love flaky Maldon salt. Like, we really love it. So when a report from The Observer detailed how Maldon’s famed UK sea salt was in fact also made with German rock salt, gasps rippled around the Bon Appétit office. I mean, not gasps exactly, but everyone was like “whaaaat? That’s crazy.”.

The gritty details: Maldon’s been harvested in Essex’s Blackwater estuary for more than a century, and the label on each box lists its only ingredient as 100% sea salt. The Observer’s report reveals that the manufacturer imports mined rock salt from Germany as part of the “salt-on-salt” process in which the sea salt is enriched with minerals. The company is allowed to call their product 100% sea salt because the salt that comes from mines was at one point in a sea—in prehistoric times.

Origin and processing matters because these factors can affect the final flavor, color, and how salty it tastes. Maldon is a finishing salt, and it's largely prized for the crunch of its significant flakes. But consumers don’t love feeling like they’ve been lied to, and judging from the comments under Maldon’s apology post on Instagram, that is precisely how many feel.

I would wager that Maldon will survive this controversy. It’s a legacy brand that’s a staple in professional and home kitchens alike. And while it’s not a great look, I think the majority of consumers would say that salt is salt, and as long as Maldon stays crunchy and salty, they’ll be on board.

In a recent development, semaglutide, the GLP-1 compound in brand name drugs Wegovy and Ozempic, is already approved for use in children older than 12. But a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine shows that the drug is effective for treating obesity in kids as young as six. According to the New York Times, drug manufacturer Novo Nordisk, plans to ask the FDA to authorize the drug’s use for kids in that age group.

It's hard to know what the long term effects on developed adult brains and bodies would be, let alone the quickly growing, changing brains and bodies of young kids. We’re beginning to see that GLP-1s can have a profound effect on mental health in adults, but though it seems the drugs can indeed contribute to weight loss in children, there are many other facets of its use that we simply don’t understand and haven’t studied yet.

When I helped build our Best Bars list last year the question of what exactly makes a great bar was one we pondered over for many hours. Order a drink from a Bar of Note (i.e. one of the many bars sitting on a Best-of list somewhere on the internet), and you’ll quickly get a sense of how they answer that same question. Namely: spectacle.

Cocktails across the country and abroad have ramped up in complexity and presentation in recent years fueled mostly by the reason you might expect: spectacle and theatricality performs well on social media, according to a report in the Times.

In a recent development, as a reporter who has often been forced to order the most attention-grabbing, loudest, most obnoxious drink on the menu in the name of journalism—and as a cocktail-enjoyer in my free time—I would like to propose a paradigm shift. Cocktail brutalism. Cocktail minimalism. Cocktail absurdism—actually anything besides the overwhelming maximalist cocktail moment that we’re stepping into. The ideal drink special? A beer, a shot, and a genuine compliment.

What happens to Airbnb when personal AI agents can look at a listing and instantly check the price on the property’s own website, where Airbnb doesn’t collect a commission?

Using the AI agent Instinct, Skift compared 16 Airbnb listings with rates on the properties’ own websites. The direct site was cheaper in 10 — by as much as 42% — and one was essentially a tie.

When an account on X questioned whether Airbnb’s profits would suffer if AI agents could compare prices right before guests book, CEO Brian Chesky replied: “You presume we could never offer a price-match guarantee.”.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that economic hardships in 19th-century Europe led to a wave of immigrants to American shores, with traces of that migration still evident today in family trees across the country.
  • Census Bureau's American Community Survey still asks about ancestry, and its self-reported 2024 study found that a few countries stood out as the most likely European ancestry in each state.
  • Check out the survey results to see which European country accounts for the largest share of reported ancestry in your state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that economic hardships in 19th-century Europe led to a wave of immigrants to American shores, with traces of that migration still evident today in family trees across the country. But some states had one country's ancestors dominate over the others when it comes to where residents can trace their roots.

The U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey still asks about ancestry, and its self-reported 2024 study found that a few countries stood out as the most likely European ancestry in each state.

Check out the survey results to see which European country accounts for the largest share of reported ancestry in your state.

German immigrants have been coming to the United States since before the United States existed. A group of Quaker families arrived in 1683 and founded Germantown, which is now a suburb of Philadelphia. The largest wave, however, came in the 1800s when Germans arrived with hopes of securing land to farm or leave after a failed revolution in 1848. They brought with them things like kindergarten, the tradition of Christmas trees, and hot dogs.

According to recent reports, today, an estimated 40 to 60 million Americans consider German their main heritage, making it the largest country of origin for immigration. It's even more than Irish or Italian heritage and is the main European heritage in 27 states, more than any other European group. German roots are mainly found in the Midwest and West Coast.

Industry observers note that another strong country for where Americans claim roots is England. After all, England provided some of the earliest settlers across the Atlantic along the East Coast, with colonists first arriving in Jamestown in modern-day Virginia in 1607.

English roots dominate the South, with states in the Southeast claiming English heritage over all other European countries. English pockets also remain in Latest England, like Maine and Vermont, as well as out west in New Mexico, Utah, and Idaho.

Irish immigration peaked in the United States in the mid-1800s, when the Great Famine ravaged the country. It's estimated that between 1851 and 1860, more than 80% of immigrants arriving in the United States came from Ireland. Additional near-famines in the second half of the 1800s propped up the flow of immigrants from Ireland to the United States.

Those migration waves left a lasting effect on the East Coast, where five states still claim Irish heritage as the most common European heritage. States where Ireland is the most represented European heritage include Delaware, the District of Columbia, and the New England states of New Hampshire, Rhode Island, and Massachusetts. Even New York, which is known for its diverse population in New York City, cites Ireland as the country that produced the highest number of ancestral European roots among residents.

Only two states claim Italy as the most common European ancestor among their residents, with East Coast states Connecticut and Fresh Jersey representing the country.

Recent findings suggest that italians arrived in the United States most notably in the 20th century. But while other immigrants came through Newly introduced York City and moved inland, Italian immigrants stayed in the area, with an estimated one-third settling around New York City.

In Fresh Jersey, almost 1.3 million residents claim some sort of Italian ancestry, pushing it past Irish ancestry by more than 100,000 residents.

Connecticut has a similar dynamic, with Italian heritage outnumbering Irish ancestry, and both groups clearly leading the state.

Louisiana is the only state that claims French ancestry more than any other European ancestry among residents.

In a recent development, france had already established itself in Louisiana before the 1800s, but the Louisiana Purchase solidified Louisiana's placeâand its French traditionsâin American life. The 1803 purchase included parts of several states as far as modern-day Montana and Minnesota, but Louisiana in particular held on to its French roots after the handover of land.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, some of the carvings date back more than 7,000 years, making them among the oldest and most significant examples of prehistoric rock art in Northern Europe.
  • Recent findings suggest that light plays an important role in discovering the carvings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, one of the most extraordinary attractions in northern Norway is Alta Museum's outdoor area, where thousands of prehistoric carvings can be found. These are not paintings or replicas displayed behind glass – they are original artworks carved directly into the bedrock by people thousands of years ago.

In a recent development, some of the carvings date back more than 7,000 years, making them among the oldest and most significant examples of prehistoric rock art in Northern Europe. They depict reindeer, bears, elk, fish, whales, boats, hunting scenes, fishing activities, human figures and mysterious rituals. The carvings were originally made near the shoreline, and as the land gradually rose after the last Ice Age, latest rock surfaces became available for successive generations of artists.

Recent findings suggest that light plays an important role in discovering the carvings. Depending on the direction and angle of the sunlight, the engraved lines can become much more visible or almost disappear completely. Low-angle sunlight, especially in the morning or evening, creates small shadows inside the carved grooves, making the figures stand out more clearly.

Some of the carvings have been painted red to make them easier to see. This red colour is not original to the carvings, but was added in 1970s to help visitors recognise their shapes and details. Today, the focus is on protecting the original rock carvings while keeping modern alterations to a minimum. As part of this conservation work, the red paint is gradually being removed to preserve the site's authenticity.

The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognised in 1985 for its outstanding cultural and historical importance.

After paying the Alta Museum admission fee, you can explore the area independently by following wooden walkways that wind through the landscape. Please note that the carvings are only accessible during the snow-free season.

The museum also has an indoor area showcasing local history.

Recent findings suggest that then again, the forest in Wildwood is not a paradise; it is deeply fractured and plagued by violence and bureaucracy. Wildwood is less of an escapist tale than a deeper look at our own world and its problems mapped onto one of the oldest tales of all: a childâs adventure into the woods and home again.

Extra-Fluffy Cinnamon Rolls

📅 22 Dec 2022 | ⏱️ 5 min read (986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting.
  • One is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough.
  • The other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting. But a couple of smart moves make them especially fluffy, with a tender crumb that stays soft well into the next day (assuming there are any left).

One is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough. The precooked starch helps the dough hold on to more moisture, resulting in pillowy, supple cinnamon rolls.

The other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge. The tangy cream cheese frosting balances all that richness; add the optional lemon zest for extra brightness.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls the night before?

In a recent development, yes. You can refrigerate the dough after its first rise or assemble the rolls in their baking pans and refrigerate them before the second rise. Cover tightly with plastic wrap to prevent the dough from drying out. The next day, let the chilled dough sit at room temperature for about an hour before proceeding with the recipe, making sure the shaped rolls have doubled in volume before baking.

Why is my cinnamon roll dough so sticky?

In a recent development, this is a soft, moisture-rich dough, but it should become smooth and elastic as you knead it. For the most consistent results, weigh your flour rather than measuring by volume. Also, make sure the tangzhong has thickened into a paste before adding it to the dough: You should be able to see the tracks of your whisk across the bottom of the saucepan. Avoid adding excessive extra flour, which can make the finished rolls dense.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls without a stand mixer?

Industry observers note that yes, though kneading this soft, enriched dough by hand takes considerable time and effort. Several readers have reported success doing so. If using a stand mixer, keep an eye on the motor during the extended kneading time. If it begins to strain or overheat, stop the machine and finish kneading by hand.

Can I use active dry yeast instead of instant yeast?

According to recent reports, this recipe calls for instant yeast, which can be mixed directly into the dough. Active dry yeast generally requires activation in warm liquid and may affect rising times, so we recommend sticking with instant yeast for the recipe as written. For more information, see our guide to the different types of yeast.

Watch Zaynab perfect these cinnamon rolls.

Industry observers note that save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app.

In a recent development, whisk ¾ cup whole milk and ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour in a medium saucepan until smooth. Place saucepan over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture is thickened and whisk lines are visible on bottom of pan, about 2 minutes. Scrape tangzhong into the bowl of a stand mixer and let cool.

Add 1 large egg, one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), ⅓ cup (67 g) granulated sugar, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt,  and remaining 1½ cups whole milk to tangzhong and whisk to combine. Add remaining 5½ cups (688 g) all-purpose flour. Fit bowl onto stand mixer; fit mixer with dough hook attachment. Mix on low speed until combined, about 1 minute. Increase speed to medium-low and mix, scraping down sides of bowl occasionally, until dough is smooth and elastic, 18–24 minutes. Pinch off a golf-ball-size piece of dough and stretch between your fingers as thin as possible without breaking. If you can see light through the dough, it’s ready. If not, continue mixing a few more minutes, then try again.

Add ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, to dough and mix on medium speed until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Continue mixing until dough pulls away cleanly from sides of bowl and is no longer tacky to the touch, 5–7 minutes longer. Remove bowl from mixer and cover with a damp kitchen towel. Let sit in a warm spot until doubled in volume, 60–90 minutes.

While the dough is rising, cook ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until butter foams and milk solids turn dark amber, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a heatproof bowl and let cool slightly. Add 1 cup (packed; 200 g) dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. ground cinnamon, 2 Tbsp. heavy cream, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to butter and mix to combine.

Butter two 9"-diameter cake pans. Punch down dough and transfer to a lightly floured surface. Stretch dough into a rough rectangle; if dough feels stiff, let sit 5–10 minutes to allow gluten to relax. Arrange dough with short side facing you and roll out to a 24x13" rectangle. Spread filling over dough in an even layer.

Industry observers note that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Bake rolls until golden on top and puffed (don’t be alarmed if they rise dramatically in the center), 25–30 minutes.

Meanwhile, using an electric mixer on medium speed or a whisk, beat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, and 8 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, in a large bowl, scraping down sides of bowl as needed, until combined. Add 1¼ cups (138 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. heavy cream, 1 tsp. lemon zest (if using), and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt and beat until mixture is smooth and sugar is incorporated. Taste and beat in more powdered sugar (up to ¾ cup) if desired. Thin with more cream as needed, a teaspoonful at a time, until frosting is thick but spreadable.

Let cinnamon rolls cool in pan 5 minutes; spread frosting over.

According to recent reports, parvus, an activist investor, has criticized Accor's Ennismore buyout and 13 years of alleged stock price underperformance under CEO Sébastien Bazin. Accor's management has its own side to the story.

Accor’s largest shareholder, Parvus Asset Management, mentioned Thursday it will ask shareholders to remove Sébastien Bazin as chairman and CEO at the hotel group’s next annual meeting, citing Accor’s €1.6 billion (about $1.8 billion) buyout of its partners in its Ennismore joint venture and years of lagging returns.

Sources indicate that parvus argues Accor has long underperformed its peers. “Accor shares have returned 99% from December 2013 to November 2026, against 593% for IHG, 863% for Hilton, and 950% for Marriott,” it wrote. “In our view, this sustained gap reflects an unfocused strategy, inconsistent capital allocation, and inadequate governance oversight.”.

In a recent development, A few Novembers ago, I had a mild crash out over puff pastry. I was planning to meet my partner’s extended family for the first time over Thanksgiving, and volunteered to bring a holiday staple a few weeks prior (in what was one of the most helpful, albeit intimidating Excel sign-up sheets I’ve ever seen). What could be easier than apple pie? The ingredients for the recipe I found weren’t fussy, and it hardly called for fancy technical skills. Plus, I could make it ahead of time knowing that it would travel well.

Then I remembered the puff pastry. For some reason, I attached a moral imperative to the idea of making the whole pie from scratch, and spent the next two weeks poring over puff pastry recipes that felt like casual guides to wizard-tier alchemy. I loved to cook, but I simply wasn’t a big baker. (I also didn’t own a food processor, unless you counted my Magic Bullet.) My mother eventually brought me down to Earth. “Just buy it,” she told me over the phone, undoubtedly rolling her eyes. “Everyone knows it’s a pain in the butt.” Even the Barefoot Contessa herself, she reminded me, famously avoids the time-consuming task (“Nobody wants to make puff pastry!”).

Recent findings suggest that those words set me free. Once I realized that I could outsource my puff pastry, and the source of my Thanksgiving stress, I was finally able to relax and enjoy the holiday. Folks take pride in their Turkey Day dishes, as they should, but there’s nothing wrong with accepting a little help.

In the hopes of encouraging you to lighten your load, my colleague Bettina Makalintal and I asked some of the coolest people we know in the food industry what they prefer to outsource for Thanksgiving, from smoked hams to appetizers, in order to keep their holiday stress-free.

It has been revealed that “There is a single premade item that I purchase for Thanksgiving: a smallish in-house smoked ham from The Meat Hook. It’s a sort of whatever part of the Thursday meal — I make a banging turkey, which commands most of the attention. But! The ham has become a key player during what my family calls Leftover Sandwich Weekend. Having an extra piece of protein mitigates any concerns about not having enough turkey left over. More importantly, a thin slice or two adds a salty, fatty, sweet, and smoky layer to the sandwich architecture. Much needed, very appreciated. Ham: I can’t imagine a turkey sandwich without it.” — Carla Lalli, cookbook author of books including Food is a Feeling.

“I outsource pies because I don’t especially enjoy making them… or eating them!”— Laila Gohar, food-based conceptual designer, artist, and co-founder of Gohar World.

According to recent reports, “I almost always outsource appetizers and/or a cheese plate. If I’m making the massive stuff (turkey, stuffing, sides, desserts… okay, I’m also a control freak with more time to cook than most), I feel absolutely overwhelmed if I am also making small things. So while I have a couple really simple apps I’ll put out if there are no volunteers, I much prefer having a friend or family member bring their favorite wedge of cheese and crackers, or [crossing fingers] bacon-wrapped dates. Here is one of my simple go-tos (it’s also in my Smitten Kitchen Every Day cookbook): herb-and-garlic baked Camembert. I’d still prefer if someone else can prep it; I don’t mind heating it up.” — Deb Perelman, cookbook author and recipe developer behind Smitten Kitchen.

In a recent development, “We outsource lumpia from Chuck’s mom. We love having them for the holiday but don’t like frying at home when we have everything else cooking that day. She always has a couple hundred in her freezer ready and waiting to be fried for special occasions.” — Hailee Catalano and Chuck Cruz, cookbook authors and recipe developers behind @2peoplecooking.

“I usually get a roast duck from Hay Hay Roasted in Chinatown, because they’ve got it down. It’s consistently delicious and not everyone eats turkey in our family.” — Camari Mick, chef and founder of Calabash.

Industry observers note that “I always outsource the pre-dinner snacks to the grocery store. I have so much respect for people who can construct elaborate cheese boards or spend the morning filling puff pastries, but that’s just not me. I like to set out a few bowls with tamari almonds, Castelvetrano olives, and — this is the most important one — Nacho Cheese Doritos. They’re the perfect mix of salty, crunchy little snacks to have with a drink before dinner is ready. The Doritos always get cleaned out first, so keep a backup bowl waiting in the kitchen.” — Casey Elsass, columnist at Cup of Jo and author of What Can I Bring?

“Last year for Friendsgiving, we collectively decided to skip the hassle of making the turkey and instead ordered Popeyes’ Cajun-Style Turkey. It’s rubbed with a blend of Louisiana-style Cajun spices and comes fully cooked, so all you have to do is thaw, heat, and serve it. It really set the tone for a very unserious dinner, which I think is what you want at a Friendsgiving. We’ll be ordering it again this year.” — Anna Archibald and Kevin Serai, content creators and recipe developers behind Cabagges.World.

Sources indicate that “We’re fairly relaxed about Thanksgiving, but if we do end up making food on that day, I usually outsource pie dough! I’m happy to buy organic frozen pie dough because usually it tastes fine and it saves me a little bit of time. I realized I prefer to spend my energy on the other parts of the meal, and I prefer not to add on to my own mental load by also making pie dough. I know it’s quick and easy; I’d just rather not! But I do make my own fillings.” — Ifrah F. Ahmed, author of Soomaaliya.

Beavers may build dams, but do you actually give one when it comes to the meaning of the Beaver Moon? Whether you're the type to break out the crystals whenever the full moon comes around, or it's simply just an extra-bright night to you, the spiritual meaning of each month's moon sheds light on the history and habits of those who named it so.

Sources indicate that the 2026 Beaver Moon, which happens to be a supermoon this year, hits peak brightness on Tuesday, November 24, at 9:53 a.m. ET. Here's the story and meaning behind it.

We aren't so different from our distant mammalian relatives, and our pre-winter behavioral patterns are proof. Just as we prepare to settle in for the coming cold season by stocking up on blankets, making cozy dishes, and clearing out the social calendar save for the obligatory holiday get-togethers, much of the animal kingdom retreats toward the end of fall, too.

That's where the name "Beaver Moon" comes from: the nesting instincts of beavers that kick in around November. The second-to-last month of the year is a bit of a frenzy for the semi-aquatic rodents as they prepare for the waters they call home to freeze over. November sees colonies of beavers putting the finishing touches on their lodgesâusing mud and sticks for insulationâand stocking up on food before settling into their warm, sturdy structures for the next few months. In the same vein, other historical theories link the name to Native American traditions and early colonial fur-trapping seasons, when hunters set traps to acquire thick, warm pelts for protection against the freezing winter weather.

Recent findings suggest that alternative names for November's full moon also nod to these seasonal shifts. For instance, it's known as the Digging Moonâa Tlingit name referring to animals foraging and digging their winter densâand the Frost Moon, a moniker given by the Cree and Assiniboine peoples as the harsh winter freeze takes hold.

Unlike bears and wolves, beavers don't hibernate, though they do retreat indoors to ride out the cold months, using the winter pause to nurture their young instead of gnawing logs. That makes the frantic seasonal prep all the more notable.

In a recent development, translating that to your own world, the Beaver Moon points to finishing the year strong: putting your final bursts of energy into wrapping up current projects, tying up loose ends, and spending time with family and friends (which the holiday season tends to require anyway). When daylight dwindles and the things you've been working on for months start to get boring, it's easy to fantasize about your next business venture or vacation. But the moon's message is to resist that urge and focus on the finish line.

Of course, that's easier stated than done. Beavers might be getting down to business as their namesake moon rises, but it's entirely normal to feel a bit out of sorts during a full lunar cycle. Because this year's Beaver Moon is also a supermoon, those energy levels are supercharged. It's a stark contrast to the quiet, restful themes we usually associate with winter.

According to recent reports, so, if you feel a sudden, manic urge to start over while running on three hours of sleep, blame the Beaver supermoon. Then, consider channelling that chaotic energy into holiday shopping instead of launching a startup in late November.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Hunger Games franchise is at the moment in the midst of a massive revival, with two prequel books released in the last six years and the latest movie adaptation coming to theaters on November 20. With author Suzanne Collins expanding what we know about the world of Panem, her Classical inspirations are becoming increasingly obvious.

Recent findings suggest that collins has discussed the origins of The Hunger Games on multiple occasions, explaining that she was channel surfing when the coexistence of reality television and genuine war footage sparked her imagination. She began to write a book based on just war theory, merging the idea of reality TV and fights to the death. To create the overarching plot and style of the Games, she borrowed from the Greek myth of Theseus and the Minotaur and the Roman tradition of gladiatorial combat.

You donât have to be a Classics expert to see the connections between The Hunger Games and Greek and Roman death battles. But you might be surprised to learn just how deep the connections go. From the names of major Capitol residents to the terminology used by the people of Panem, Greek and Roman history are everywhere in The Hunger Games franchise, highlighting the worst elements of these cultures and how they can be appropriated by authoritarian regimes.

Perhaps the most well-known example of Roman culture infiltrating The Hunger Games franchise appears in its setting. The series takes place in the country Panem, which comes from the Latin word for bread. As Collins has acknowledged, âBread crops up a lot in The Hunger Games.â Peeta is a baker, and his gift of bread kept Katniss alive long enough to spark the rebellion. Both inside the arena and beyond, the Capitol uses food as a weapon, keeping the Tributes and districts hungry so that they donât have the energy to fight back.

However, the giving and withholding of bread isnât the only thing at play here. In Mockingjay, Plutarch references the idea of âpanem et circensesâ (bread and circuses), a phrase coined by the Roman writer Juvenal in his work Satires.

The same mentality that Juvenal lamented in Rome is present in Panem, and especially in the Capitol. The citizens have so much food that they choose to vomit just to continue eating. They receive annual entertainment through the deaths of children and the celebration of the Victors, emphasizing Juvenalâs claim that âEven those who have no wish to kill enjoy the power to do so.â Ultimately, though, a population that is lulled into apathy by bread and circuses is easily roused when their food and entertainment are taken away.

Recent findings suggest that the character Plutarch Heavensbee is directly inspired by the writer Plutarch, a Greek aristocrat who became a prominent Roman citizen and one of the most vital sources for Classical historians. He wrote hundreds of works, including approximately fifty surviving biographies of Greek and Roman figures, published under his Parallel Lives series. While his writings often included gossip and may not have reflected the true history they purported to explore, they nonetheless provide insight into the mindset of 1st century Romans and influenced public perceptions of these figures for millennia.

Recent findings suggest that suzanne Collins was well aware of this when she began working on The Hunger Games, as her father would read her passages from Plutarchâs biographies when she was young. She explained that Plutarch Heavensbee was given his name because he is âone of the few characters who has a sense of the arc of history.â As a Capitol aristocrat, Heavensbee had access to a top-tier education, and while he never knew a world without the Hunger Games, he had more understanding of the world before it than nearly any other character. Furthermore, his role as both a gamemaker and head of propaganda for the rebellion put him in a position to create stories and shape minds and hearts, just as his namesake did thousands of years earlier.

The concept of each District providing a boy and girl as Tributes to the Capitol plays on both Greek mythology and Roman political systems. The process comes from the myth of Theseus. After the Cretan king's son died, he went to war against Athens, forcing them to send seven young men and women to Crete on a regular basis, where they would be sent into a labyrinth to be killed and eaten by a minotaur. This only stopped when the Athenian prince Theseus volunteered to go to Crete and defeat the monster.

In Collinsâs words, Katniss serves as âa futuristic Theseus,â volunteering for certain death in order to protect innocents. But the specific word âTributeâ has its own history. The word comes from the Latin Tributum, which was originally a form of taxation collected for military purposes. As the empire spread, however, citizens were exempt from paying Tributum, and it instead became a price that conquered peoples paid as a sign of submission. Given this context, the Tributes in The Hunger Games serve as literal taxes paid by the districts after their defeat in the Dark Days.

When Katniss and Peeta make their way to the Capitol, Effie warns them that Haymitch, as their Mentor, is âyour lifeline to the worldâ¦ the difference between your life and your death.â While the concept of a mentor is ancient, appearing in thousands of stories, it has an interesting connection to Greek mythology that might have influenced its use in The Hunger Games.

According to recent reports, while the word appears to derive from Ancient Greek roots meaning âmindâ and âthought,â it first appeared in the form of a name in The Odyssey. Mentor was a man in Ithaca who advised Telemachus during his fatherâs absence, although he was often actually the goddess Athena in disguise. In addition to providing advice, Athena advocated for Odysseus before the gods, guided allies to him, and provided both Odysseus and Telemachus with the information and resources they needed to survive. Given this context, the fact that mentors in The Hunger Games would advocate for their tributes to the sponsors, send them supplies, and guide them in how to act feels deliberate, with Haymitchâs actions being just as vital to Katnissâs survival as Athenaâs were for Odysseus.

The choice of the word âarenaâ for the setting of the Games is yet again a way to connect the world of Panem with its historical inspirations, as the term is heavily associated with Roman gladiatorial matches. Although The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes showed the early games taking place in the Capitol Arena, which was described as âa now-dilapidated amphitheater that had been used for sports and entertainment events before the war,â the historical distinction between the word âarenaâ and words like âamphitheaterâ (a place to watch spectacles from both sides) or âstadiumâ (which comes from a measure of distance) provides additional context.

Recent findings suggest that the word arena comes from the Latin harÄna, which initially meant âsand.â It became synonymous with the location of gladiatorial matches and other violent entertainment because the amphitheaters would be covered in sand to absorb the blood. By the 1st century CE, the word âarenaâ began appearing in reference to conflict itself as well as the location it was set in. The Capitol kept the word âarenaâ long after the Games stopped being held at the Capitol Arena, because even in a seemingly natural ecosystem, it retains its Roman origins as a place that combines violence and spectacle for mass consumption.

It has been revealed that suzanne Collins tends to be very deliberate with her name choices, and Coriolanus Snow is no exception to that. While his last name was intended to evoke âcoldness and purity,â his first name comes from Gnaeus Marcius Coriolanus, a Roman general from the 5th century BC. He won the name âCoriolanusâ after a dramatic victory in Corioli, but he was later exiled after refusing to grant Roman citizens access to grain without completing military service or relinquishing their political power.

After being cast out of Rome, Coriolanus gathered support for a rebellion against Rome, only stopping after an appeal from his mother, wife, and children. There is some debate about his ultimate fate, but he is believed to have been either executed or assassinated. While many historians doubt whether Coriolanus actually existed, he functioned as a case study in the dangers of valuing military service and patrician birth over the well-being of the common people. It isnât difficult to see the connection between Panemâs tyrant and his historical namesake, especially with the additional context provided in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. Both used hunger and violence as weapons against their own people, and both learned the consequences of that decision.

Originally, a tessera was a single tile within a mosaic, which was common in both Greek and Roman artwork. This meaning was referenced in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, when Tigris made buttons from the tiles in their bathroom. Over time, the word tessera came to mean nearly any token or small object, including gambling dice. The most key version here is the Tesserae Frumentariae, tokens which entitled the holder to disbursements of grain or oil. But while the Romans would give these Tesserae based on citizenship or position, the government of Panem used them as bargaining chips, forcing the poor to put their own children in greater danger, in exchange for the food they needed to survive.

The concept of an Avox was invented for the world of The Hunger Games, but its linguistic composition is once again rooted in ancient history. Avox is a hybrid word, combining the Greek prefix a- (not or without) and the Latin word vox (voice). This is fitting, as the Avoxes were people who had their tongues removed as punishment for treason. In contrast to the popular phrase âVox populi, vox Dei,â which claimed that âthe voice of the people is the voice of God,â the Capitol saw the voice of the people as an inherent threat that had to be eliminated.

In a recent development, if bread is used as a weapon in Panem, speech is a tool that is carefully regulated. The characters frequently worried that they were being spied on, and the jabberjays were explicitly created for that purpose. Like the character Echo, in Greek mythology, they had no voices of their own, only able to repeat the things they heard. Similarly, President Snow attempted to control what Katniss and Peeta said to limit their power. Amongst all of this, the Avoxes were constantly present, showcasing the Capitolâs ability to silence those who didnât fall in line. However, the mockingjay was a powerful symbol precisely because its speech could not be tamed by the Capitol. This was especially clear when Pollux, an Avox, served as a cameraman for the rebellion, reclaiming his voice despite his physical limitations.

The central image of every Hunger Games since the first Quarter Quell is the Cornucopia, a golden horn filled with weapons and supplies, drawing the Tributes together to prompt a bloodbath. Itâs a twisted version of the Classical symbol, which used the Latin cornu copiae to mean "horn of plenty.â As Haymitch noted in Sunrise on the Reaping, the version in Panem functioned as âA horn of plenty for the few. Desperation for many. Destruction for all.â Even by becoming a Victor, which guaranteed enough food to survive without fear, the tributes could never escape the oppressive system.

Sources indicate that while many of the other concepts and symbols in Panem come directly from antiquity, the cornucopia is the most twisted from its original meaning. Greek mythology depicted the cornucopia as the horn of a divine goat named Amalthea, who fed Zeus while he was being hidden from his filicidal father. The horn was capable of providing endless nourishment, a concept which was embraced by the Romans, who associated it with gods like Pax (peace) and Abundantia (abundance). In The Hunger Games, it is the setting for both the bloodbath and the final kills in the 74th Games, reminding the districts that the Capitolâs abundance is only available to them if they fight to the death for it.

The Head Gamemaker from the 74th Hunger Games provides one of the most direct translations from Roman history into the world of Panem. Seneca Crane was inspired by Lucius Annaeus Seneca the Younger, a philosopher and politician during the early Roman Empire. After being threatened with death under two emperors, one of whom exiled him, Seneca returned to Rome triumphant, serving as a tutor and advisor for the future emperor, Nero. But while he was a competent statesman, managing the empire during Neroâs early years in power, he was eventually implicated in an assassination attempt against the emperor and ordered to commit suicide. He complied, cutting open his veins and consuming a potion made from hemlock, one of the very poisons that inspired The Hunger Gamesâs revolutionary Nighlock berries.

Recent findings suggest that like his namesake, Seneca Crane seemed to be thriving under the reign of an autocratic ruler until rebels that had nothing to do with him put him in the line of fire. Notably, both of the Head Gamemakers in The Hunger Games trilogy were named after Roman writers. While Plutarch wrote biographies of Greek and Roman historical figures, Seneca wrote tragic plays in which Greek mythic heroes caused violent deaths, and lovers turned on one another. Itâs little surprise that the character named after him would believe that Katniss and Peeta could be turned against each other so easily. However, both the historical figure and the fictional one learned how easily a paranoid dictator can transform from an ally to a deadly adversary.

In a recent development, riyadh’s hotels lost their peak season when the airport shut. With BA, Cathay Pacific and others suspended into the upcoming year and Houthi strikes still hitting the capital, the recovery hasn’t started.

Riyadh hotels had one of their worst months of the year in October. A temporary shutdown of the city’s main airport cut off inbound demand just as peak season started.

In a recent development, occupancy fell 34.7 percentage points year over year to 34.3% from 69%, according to CoStar’s STR. Only March had lower occupancy, at 28.3%. Average daily rate dropped 29.9% to $190 and revenue per available room (RevPAR) fell 65.1% to $65.

“October and November are usually the peak season months for Riyadh, so the impact is much bigger,” said Kostas Nikolaidis, associate account director for Middle East and Africa at STR.

The October demand collapse traces back to an attack on King Khalid International Airport. The airport closed after an attack on Oct. 10 that Saudi authorities remarked killed 13 people and injured more than 300. Some 86% of scheduled Riyadh departures were canceled between Oct. 8 and late October, according to Cirium data, Skift repor.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that slashing bone-in chicken thighs (carefully, around the bone, of course) allows a punchy maple-Dijon-ACV marinade to permeate the meat deeply in a short amount of time. And that waiting time is well spent: Scatter torn sourdough bread on a baking sheet and bake until crisp, then toss croutons aside to make way for the thighs. Once the chicken is cooked through, toss the croutons in the rendered fat and cook until everything is bronzed and glistening. A few handfuls of arugula make an elegant finish—who needs a side salad?

More sheet-pan dinners this way.

Whisk 5 garlic cloves, finely grated, ½ cup plus 3 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar, 5 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 3 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, 2½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) in a measuring glass or small bowl to combine. Transfer 2 Tbsp. vinegar mixture to a small bowl; set aside.

According to recent reports, arrange 3 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (6–8), skin side up, on a cutting board. Season lightly with salt. Turn over and season lightly on other side with salt, then carefully use a sharp paring knife to make 3 long slashes, going most of the way through meat (avoid the bone). Transfer to a large bowl and pour vinegar mixture in measuring glass over. Toss chicken to coat, making sure to get liquid into slashes. Let chicken sit at least 30 minutes and up to 1 hour.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Place 8 oz. country-style or sourdough bread (about ⅓ loaf), torn into 1" pieces, on a rimmed baking sheet. Drizzle remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil over and sprinkle with a pinch of salt and a pinch of freshly ground black pepper; toss to coat. Arrange bread in a single layer and bake until golden, 12–15 minutes. Transfer croutons to a plate; reserve baking sheet.

Arrange reserved chicken on reserved baking sheet and nestle 3 large shallots, quartered lengthwise through root ends, around; pour any excess vinegar mixture in bowl over. Bake chicken until golden, cooked through, and an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part, avoiding bone, registers at least 165° (it should be well over), 25–30 minutes.

Industry observers note that scatter croutons over empty areas of baking sheet and toss to soak up juices. Roast until chicken and croutons are deeply browned, 10–12 minutes. Let cool 5 minutes, then top with 2 oz. arugula and drizzle with reserved vinegar mixture in small bowl.

#322. My grandmother was a seal

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3874 w)
