My grandmother was a seal

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in October 1948, in Country Kerry, Ireland, Seán Ó Muircheartaigh met with Seosamh Ó Dálaigh to tell him about the woman who came from the sea.
  • Also on the beach was a farmer, who – much to the surprise of the woman herself – would by daybreak become her husband.
  • Recent findings suggest that by the time Ó Muircheartaigh told Ó Dálaigh about the seal woman, he was already 80.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in October 1948, in Country Kerry, Ireland, Seán Ó Muircheartaigh met with Seosamh Ó Dálaigh to tell him about the woman who came from the sea. She had appeared, said Ó Muircheartaigh, one night on the magharees, those bright spits of sand that occasionally pop up amid the rain-lashed rocks of the Dingle peninsula. Alone on the beach, she settled herself on a rock and began combing her hair.

Also on the beach was a farmer, who – much to the surprise of the woman herself – would by daybreak become her husband. He’d come to gather seaweed, seeing her before she saw him. Beautiful as she was, the woman was also strange: the creature he saw stagger onto that Dingle beach was not a woman at all. It was a seal.

Recent findings suggest that by the time Ó Muircheartaigh told Ó Dálaigh about the seal woman, he was already 80. He had been born in the apocalyptic aftermath of the Great Hunger that divested as much as a third of Ireland’s population to death or migration, and he had survived two great wars. Most of the disappeared were – like Ó Muircheartaigh himself – small farmers and native Irish, or Gaeilge, speakers. The famine had been not just a physical genocide: it had been a linguistic and cultural one, too.

Industry observers note that both Ó Muircheartaigh and Ó Dálaigh were veteran contributors to the Irish Folklore Commission: the former as a renowned storyteller; the latter, an equally renowned collector. The IFC is now the National Folklore Collection at University College Dublin ­– a behemoth of 3 million pages of texts and recordings. But in 1948, following eight centuries of colonialism, the loss of 99 per cent of the island’s forests, a staggering emigration, and the decline of the Irish language, the IFC was in a race against time and the fragility of memory. As it turned out, an awful lot of people had heard stories about seals that came to land as humans.

According to recent reports, nowadays, these shapeshifters are known as ‘selkies’. Selkie is a Scots term that came into widespread use via a Joan Baez cover, ‘Silkie’ (1961), of a traditional Scottish folk song. Yet the phenomenon it describes – of creatures who shapeshift between human and seal forms by shedding a skin – appears consistently in folklore spanning the Celtic world and beyond, even as far as Sweden. Before Baez insinuated the term into international parlance, selkies were identified in Irish and English by a constellation of descriptors. In Irish, the most common is mhaighdean mhara, or ‘sea maiden’, referring to selkies and mermaids. Even in English, many storytellers use ‘mermaid’ for both the phocine and the piscine. Sometimes the two are differentiated with context (fish tails, seal skins), but what matters more than phenotyping is that the mermaid or selkie is neither quite human nor animal. What defines the selkie is transformation.

Industry observers note that much of the folklore retains the quality of the best gossip, hyper-local and yet vague. Storytellers name names, offer precise locations for key scenes in the story. And several admit something startling: that they themselves are the descendants of human-seal pairings.

It has been revealed that after the farmer spotted the woman on the beach, Ó Muircheartaigh stated, he saw something else. A sealskin cloak lay beside her: her ticket to transformation and a return to the sea. Then he made a choice that would ricochet throughout the generations, and leave the selkie with no option but to follow him home. He stole the selkie’s cloak and secreted it away, thus securing her for a bride. These rough beginnings aside, the couple produced a brood of children and went about the gruelling lives of any impoverished Irish fishing family. The only thing disrupting the fantasy of a normal human wife, acquired in normal human ways, was the webbing between the children’s toes. That, and the fact that the woman never smiled, but kept looking out towards the sea.

According to recent reports, what does it mean if your grandmother was a seal? The folklore attests that marriages between humans and selkies were common enough to generate a host of human-selkie lineages – Conneely, Gallagher, Dowd, O’Kane, O’Shea, MacDuffie, McPhee, Flaherty, Glavin – whose members were predisposed towards webbed digits and an ineffable longing for the sea. (‘My mother was one of them O’Sheas,’ the railway worker Séamas MacMathghamhna confided to a folklore collector in 1949, after explaining the selkie lineage of the O’Sheas.) The Celtic studies scholar Gregory Darwin has identified nearly 50 family groups whose members carry selkie blood.

In a recent development, now is a good time to have a seal in the family tree. As our planet hurtles through climate catastrophe, everyone from environmental activists and TikTok influencers to academics and Upcoming Age pilgrims is turning towards animals-as-family rhetoric. Such gusto stems from a cultural exhaustion with extractionism and with narratives of domination and human exceptionalism that have dogged the culture and geopolitics of the Global North since the 19th century. Yet the naivety with which the zeitgeist tends to approach an expanded view of interspecies kinship presents its own problems. For one, it doesn’t quite ring true – and it is hard to fight for a worldview that you can’t see clearly. For another, if we reframe our relationship with the more-than-human around intimate familial connection, then we need ways of understanding what happens when that connection becomes fraught.

It has been revealed that the selkie story is one of family dysfunction par excellence. After all, the gutting truth at the centre of selkie families is that one’s origins lie in theft, violence, rape and unimaginable loss. The children of human-selkie pairings face a mottled inheritance, at best. Writing for The Latest York Times in 2008, Bryan Patrick Miller recounted how his great-great-great-grandfather’s kidnapping of a mhaighdean mhara cursed the family, causing the couple’s half-human children to flee across the Atlantic. Some coastal communities saw seals as fallen angels or the souls of drowned fishermen: mating with them was dubious to say the least.

Mottled or not, a selkie genealogy had to be reckoned with. Having a selkie in the family forced an acknowledgement of a mixed inheritance that was dark and disturbing, and in which successive generations continued to be implicated. Only by considering these uncomfortable reverberations of what it means to be family do we move closer to reimagining our relationships with the more-than-human world.

A woman who is sexually unsatisfied in her marriage may cry into the sea and receive a selkie who is an absolute dynamo in bed.

It has been revealed that among folklorists, the trope of the selkie is generally known as the Seal Wife – a designation that speaks more to the gendered hold that the selkie story has on our imagination than to the actual folklore topos. The selkie’s allure is such that men will risk curses and commit theft and kidnapping to possess her, regardless of the certain tragedy that forced marriage augurs. Yet the selkies of folklore are not necessarily wives, women or even seals (note the mermaids, above). Male selkies occasionally make cameos as the kidnapped selkie wife’s jilted husband, father of her aquatic children, keening for her release from outside the human husband’s house. At other times, they appear as her brother, or as characters in the quotidian interactions between humans and their environment: they are accidentally killed, kidnapped as pets, steal fish, issue prophesies, plead and bargain, proffer advice and opinions.

According to recent reports, male selkies also arrive as lovers. Sometimes their affair with a human woman is star-crossed – the paramours may meet only once every seven years, say – but generally sex with a male selkie is an occasion for straightforward joy. A woman who is sexually unsatisfied in her marriage or a maiden hoping for a youthful adventure may cry into the sea and receive a selkie who is, apparently, an absolute dynamo in bed.

What is fascinating about these stories is that they centre female pleasure in a way that the selkie wife stories never do (or male pleasure, for that matter). Instead, the selkie wife – despite the sensual appeal that incited her husband to theft – is noted for her competence in housekeeping and childrearing. But even the male selkie stories occasionally take dark turns. Sometimes, the human woman steals her lover’s skin to compel him into marriage; other times, the human woman is raped by the male selkie.

According to recent reports, the hybrid relationships described in the folklore are multilayered and fraught, but they are also interwoven with the rhythms of rural Irish life. The Irish tendency to link themselves to the more-than-human world – including through creatures such as the merrow, or mermaid, the shapeshifting púca, and, of course, the aos sí, the supernatural, fairy analogue to humans – has been noted for hundreds of years. Even the Normans, frustrated with their new subjects’ disinterest in distinguishing themselves from animals, set about reforming the Irish Church and ‘civilising’ the population.

Industry observers note that in their paper ‘Slipping Off the Sealskin’ (2015), the literary critic and research artist Clair Le Couteur points out that early selkie stories had far more gender parity than later ones: not only were male selkies better represented, but their female counterparts were more empowered. The change towards the comparably flat Seal Wife trope, they suggest, echoes mankind’s changing view of our ecological place. Male selkies have ‘been largely erased [and] replaced by a simplified Seal Wife story in which gender and species are cross-linked … the female, the animal (seals), and indeed the natural and supernatural realms are conflated into a simplified, exploitable identity formed in opposition to Man’s agency as protagonist.’.

Industry observers note that yet if the Seal Wife stands for gendered and environmental exploitation, she does not submit without a fight. The would-be husbands who steal her skin are met with unhappiness, rebellion and sometimes violence. In one story, a mhaighdean mhara retrieves her skin by setting her kidnapper’s house on fire and following the smell of singed skin (in spite of the lore, as Le Couteur warns, that destroying a mhaighdean mhara’s skin may lead to her death).

In a recent development, one particularly difficult aspect of the selkie story is the repeated insistence that the marriage is a happy one. It’s a fair claim that this is patriarchal whitewashing: in one story, the teller describes the marriage as happy, only to admit two lines later that the woman laughed just three times during her spell on land – the last being at her departure. Yet the story raises a thorny truth: sometimes love is problematic. You can love someone who hurts you, and you can still leave.

The notion that humans and animals are kin falls into the broad bucket of relational ontologies known as animism, although the word occupies an uncertain place in Celtic studies. Edward Tylor, a British anthropologist and a towering figure in the nascent field, coined the term in his book Primitive Culture (1871). Here, he divided the world population into stages of evolution: ‘animism’ was reserved for savages so undeveloped they could grasp only the crudest expression of religion. It took more than a century for pioneering scholars like Nurit Bird-David to reclaim and refresh the term as ‘new animism’ and argue that animism did not describe a ‘failed epistemology’, but a relational one.

Initially, the Victorians were thrilled to equate so-called ‘backwards’ rural Europeans with those cultures abroad that they deemed uncivilised. Yet, as Natalia Schwien Scott, a herbalist, wildlife rehabilitation apprentice, and PhD candidate in religion at Harvard University told me, once colonialism became racialised, the language promptly changed: now animism as genealogical kinship between humans and animals was delegated to Black and brown cultures as a means of othering them. The Irish themselves, sick of British dehumanisation, wanted nothing to do with the term. Such leeriness is understandable – and, if history is anything to go by, completely warranted.

According to recent reports, beyond racial politics, the lived experience of animism – for all its zeitgeisty, Kumbaya reputation – is a complicated one. ‘Animism is easy to like when you’re not an animist,’ Guido Sprenger, an anthropologist at Heidelberg University in Germany, told me. In 2021, Sprenger published a paper cheekily titled ‘Can Animism Save the World?’ He’d written it after watching animism slip ‘from being an exciting analytical concept to a catch-all term for moral relations with the environment, without much regard for those who actually practise it and find themselves in all sorts of moral conundrums and dangers.’ He added: ‘Animism isn’t that pretty, peaceful, smoochy, nonhuman affair.’.

If the bounds of human exceptionalism are dissolved, and every animal is a family member, then how do you eat?

Like many other anthropologists, Sprenger was initially put off by the term’s colonial origins and nebulous usage; yet, when animism started to gain traction in environmental anthropology, he reconsidered his stance. Now, he worries that the original sin of animism is returning to dilute the term, once again, past the point of usability, out of a desperation to find alternatives to late-stage capitalism and human exceptionalism. ‘Everything that’s not us, with our nature-culture divide, is somehow animist and therefore better,’ he states. ‘And this is a step back into that diffuse and theoretically thin use of animism.’ He worries that this sudden enthusiasm for animism means sidestepping some of its trickier realities.

The animists with whom Sprenger spends his time are the Rmeet people of the Laotian highlands. Some eco-philosophers argue for a closer connection with the nature spirits to address our ecological crisis but, for the Rmeet, ‘this would be the idea of a madman.’ Spirits are a fact of life for the Rmeet, but not a kind one. As Sprenger told me, from the Rmeets’ point of view: ‘Who wants to deal with spirits? Who wants to get close to them? The whole point is that you want to be on good terms with them because you want them not to interfere in your life. They are just entities that are there. They are not a normative category. They are just as normative as a tree – a tree can fall on your head, or it can give you shade. The spirits are just there.’.

His words suggest that intimacy and safety are not the same. For example, one issue that besets animist cosmologies is cannibalism. If the bounds of human exceptionalism are dissolved, and every animal is a family member, then how do you eat? Some cultures resolve this dilemma by distinguishing between animals (leave the seal, take the salmon); others by using ritual acts – cooking, say – to metamorphose animals from person to meat. Still others fly straight into the conundrum. An animal family member might allow itself to be caught by hunters, an act of self-sacrifice that allows its kin to survive.

Love and violence are perpetually entangled in animist cosmologies, which makes me wonder: why does it matter to be descended from a seal? Why hold onto a family story so fundamentally sad and troubling? In ‘Violence, Mourning, Politics’ (2003), Judith Butler argues that it is our relations with others that put us at risk of violence – and yet to forfeit being in relation is to forfeit being human. ‘Loss and vulnerability,’ they write, ‘seem to follow from our being socially constituted bodies, attached to others, at risk of losing those attachments, exposed to others, at risk of violence by virtue of that exposure.’ In short, our attachments put us in jeopardy, while shedding them risks losing something fundamental to our place in the order of things.

Sources indicate that animism – or at least claiming a worldview in which we see ourselves as integrated into the more-than-human world rather than lording over it – does not offer safety. If anything, it does the opposite. To be in relationship with the more-than-human world, to take seriously our connections beyond the strictly human, is to become more exposed and also more attached. It puts us, as the selkie stories confirm, directly in the path of more violence. We kill a whale and kill our grandmother. We risk having our house set alight and our heart broken by an angry seal. But we do it because it is what makes us human – and if we lose that, we lose everything.

Whether we can learn from the fraught relationships of selkie kinship rests on an obvious question: did anyone believe they were part-seal? It’s difficult to say what rural seaside communities in Ireland thought about their world up until the 20th century, particularly when they had already undergone centuries of cultural and linguistic erasure. Yet, as Schwien Scott notes: ‘The material very clearly says: “Her mother was a selkie,” or “Her grandmother was a selkie.” Why would we assume that wasn’t actually believed?’.

One Galwegian domestic worker, Máire Ní Shúilleabháin, told her daughter in 1938 that she knew islanders who were children of mhaighdean mhara. The mhaighdean mhara were a common-enough reality that her great-uncle had seen one; the year before, a sighting in Connemara led to a £4,000 bounty for the marine woman’s capture (she escaped). One school-age collector in Cork, Nora O’Sullivan, wrote in her notebook that her father told her a story of a man who married a mermaid whose daughter then married into the Sullivans – that is, her family. Her teacher wrote a small memo affirming the story. In 1882, one Ms Dolan claimed that she personally knew the three children of a Lough Owel man named Mahon and his lake-creature bride. ‘She was a very good housewife, as all those lake people are,’ Dolan noted approvingly. ‘She kept his house beautifully.’ In 1937, Micheál Mac Conagail recounted that he knew of a mhaighdean mhara whose son became a priest. Such testimonies abound.

What is more, many fishing communities had taboos on killing seals based on blood relations between humans and seals. The economic implications of this were significant. Not only were these fishermen unable to harvest seals, they also had to swallow the seals’ presence as fishing competition – a huge blow amid grinding rural poverty in Ireland. Given all this, it’s reasonable to adduce a widespread literal belief in selkies that has lasted through living memory. And this belief had real-world implications – none of which were easy.

Sources indicate that seán Ó Muircheartaigh recounted in his story that, when the oat harvest came, the farmer set about clearing out the loft of the house he lived in with his seal wife and their half-selkie children. In a moment of carelessness, he threw down his wife’s sealskin cloak. She grabbed it immediately and secreted it out of sight.

That night, she waited for her husband to step out for the evening, then she washed her children and brushed their hair, just as she had brushed her own the night she was kidnapped. And then she took her cloak and was gone.

One of the most devastating aspects of an already devastating story is that it is about a woman who abandons her children. Every so often, the selkie departs with a blessing, or a curse, but mostly she goes promptly and in silence. She almost never takes her children: and in the case of the O’Dowds, she turns her progeny into stone. She rarely notes goodbye. In a small subset of selkie stories, the shapeshifting mother continues to visit her terrestrial family even after she has returned to the sea, in one, returning to comb her children’s hair. But most often she just disappears.

For the selkie herself, the loss is doubled. While her human husband appears incurious about his bride’s former life, storytellers offer occasional glimpses. Eibhlín Ní Chonchubhair tells of a selkie who pauses before her marine return to bid farewell to her human husband. Bewildered, he asks what the children will do without her. Her reply is acid: ‘I have children who are dearer to me than these.’ In this story, as in others, she is met in the water by her selkie husband, who embraces her with cries of joy. Behind the selkie’s flight back to sea is a terrible calculus, where a return to one family means the loss of the other. The situation is complicated by kidnapping and abuse, with children who are innocents and also byproducts of forced marriage.

The selkie story is a roadmap for navigating relationships that cannot be repaired.

Family haunts us. In his paper ‘Of Mermaids and Marriages’ (1990), the folklorist Bo Almqvist notes that both he and the poet Seamus Heaney have considered the selkie story as a parallel for parental suicide – a choice that is often incomprehensible to those left behind: to wit, a woman brushes her children’s hair then walks into the sea and vanishes. The selkie story is in many ways a ghost story whose participants just happen to still be alive.

I’ve suggested, pace Judith Butler, that to be in relationship is to place ourselves at risk of loss. But the selkie story, in its peregrination through the undergrowth of complicated grief, takes things one step further: it explores what it is like to remain in relationship with a loved one who is gone and who has caused you immense pain. In some ways, the selkie story is a roadmap for navigating relationships that cannot be repaired, where there is no hope or desire for reconciliation. For one thing, selkie stories acknowledge that we don’t always get to choose who we’re in relationship with – and that, sometimes, the healthiest move within a relationship is to break it.

As we navigate the inevitable species loss attendant on the climate emergency, reckoning with those places on the globe where the greatest act of love may be to decide against human intrusion, the selkie story offers a model for processing meaningful relationships that are defined by absence. The losses and hauntings endure: many individuals and communities in Ireland continued to see themselves as entangled with seals even generations after an interspecies marriage. The selkie story acknowledges as real those relationships where one half of the duo has abruptly left the conversation, as well as the cruelty and love that led up to the loss. It affirms that you can love your children and leave them, or love your children and turn them into stone. These truths can rub shoulders with each other, clear their throats, look down uncomfortably at the floor. Love is messy and not always good.

Recent findings suggest that the selkie narrative is powerful because it considers the aftermath of things going wrong and posits a world in which violence doesn’t mean an end to care. It deals in difficult truths. Yet it is also a story that allows people to look out to sea and see cousins and siblings, parents lost and family gained. It allows a human to look at a seal and feel kinship. To think: there she is. There goes my family.

With most gear reviews, you’re reading about that product during a snapshot in time — an editor tested a latest piece of luggage on a flight or wore a waterproof jacket on a few rainy camping trips. So when you’re someone who writes gear reviews, you have a lot of gear. Some is randomly mailed to you in the hopes you’ll like it and write about it, and there’s plenty we buy, because different types of travel call for different types of gear (and we travel whenever we can). Some gear stays in our closets, some gets donated, and some doesn’t quite live up to the hype, so we don’t write about it at all.

But with gear reviews, what readers don’t usually find out is the part that really matters the most: does it hold up? After a year or more with it, are our editors and writers still using it?

So we went back and checked what we’re still using and wearing. These are the bags we grab before flights, the clothing we’d never leave at home on a road trip, and the products we really, truly think are worth the spend. Everything below is something one of us has used not just to review, but in our daily lives and travels. In some cases, we’ve been loyal to these products for nearly a decade. For each one, you’ll see what we noted when we first tested it, and what we think now that it’s been dragged through real life. If it’s here, it’s because it’s never been relegated to the back of our gear closet.

the Matador Network editorial team.

She grew up in Calgary, Alberta, and her novels are part literary fiction, part adventure, traveling across continents and through different time periods. They’re also based on her extensive historical research. She notes she’s inspired by what she calls the footnotes of history, these moments and stories that most of us have never heard of, in particular stories and histories of Black communities.

And today she is taking us on a tour of the places in Alberta that have shaped her life and work, from a prehistoric buffalo jump to the ghost towns of Black homesteaders. Esi Edugyan, thank you so much for being here today.

I grew up in a series of townhouses that were just off, like, Sarcee Trail. And as a child, I could just throw open the door, go outside, stand on my front stoop and just turn my head to the right and look out, and I could see the Rockies very clearly.

This is like one of the, the central images of my childhood is this very crisp, very pristine view of the Rocky Mountains. By the time I was a teenager, you could not see the Rocky Mountains from my stoop. But that just tells you just how quickly change happens within Calgary and the province in general, and that it came from having a very sort of austere, almost removed kind of sense of things.

Like I remember tumbleweed would be rolling through our streets as a child, and if I think of that now, that seems so weird. But yeah, we had actual like large balls of tumbleweed that would just go flowing through and you really felt that like Western ….

McEvers: And your parents came from Ghana, right?

Edugyan: Yeah. So in terms of community, like you were asking earlier, we were very much part of this web of, I guess, African immigrants and expatriates, but also just, like, a larger immigrant community. We knew people from everywhere, newcomers who would… You know, my father’s, one of his best friends was this man from Poland, and then he had another best friend who was from England, and it was very interesting, a lovely kind of mix.

But, you know, I also felt myself, having been born and raised there, to just sort of be part of, I guess, this community of Canadian kids who were all kind of running around.

Edugyan: I guess, my favorite places in Alberta, from when I was a child were… I think first and foremost, the things you remember are the places that you went to on, like, school field trips.

You know, I remember going to Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump. I think it’s about 15 minutes from Fort Macleod, so south of Calgary. And this is a very old site, like 6,000 years old, so very, very prehistoric, where the Blackfoot would, I guess, round up the buffalo, and they would run them one route that the buffalo could take because it’s going to lead them off the cliff.

Industry observers note that and this was a very efficient way of hunting. And so right up until, I think, the mid-1800s, this was the main way that the buffalo were hunted on the plains. And now it is, I believe it’s like a UNESCO World Heritage site.

It just feels like a very special place, and you know, I haven’t been there since I was a child, but I can distinctly remember the feel of it, that sense of standing on the precipice of the main run and looking out onto this vast landscape of grasses and that great major sky, and just feeling this kind of, like, haunted feeling.

This is one of those memorable places that I think everybody should see.

I just remember my first experience of watching, like, a David Cronenberg film at that theater, and it just making such an impression, and attracted to, I don’t know, this very kind of easily accessed art.

Edugyan: And I remember visiting him one weekend and just going through the stacks at the library at the University of Virginia, which is quite an incredible library. I hadn’t had a sense of there being any kind of a Black presence or Black history in Alberta. And I thought, “Oh my gosh, who are these people?”.

McEvers: After the break, Esi tells us who these Black homesteaders were and how they got to Northern Alberta, and how this inspired her first novel.

It has been revealed that and we’re back. I’m Kelly McEvers, your host. Esi, before the break, you talked about coming across these Black Albertan homesteaders in a history book, and you’d never heard of their story growing up. What did you find out about them?

Edugyan: So I ended up doing some research and just being completely floored to understand that there had been these small Black townships kind of scattered throughout Alberta and Saskatchewan in which freedmen, like people who’d been previously enslaved, come up from Oklahoma mainly, but also from Texas, and come and settle some of the land up north.

And why they did this, or how they ended up doing this, was because, I guess, the turn of the 20th century, the Albertan government put in place a campaign called the Last Best West, in which they were trying to encourage American farmers and ranchers to come and settle parts of the west. And so they had people actually going down, I guess, emissaries with advertisements and, like, holding talks about why this was sort of the best place for, for these people from Oklahoma and Texas.

It has been revealed that and a lot of these freedmen thought this sounded like, you know, a great idea because since the abolition of slavery in the South, you know, they had had just the worst time trying to establish lives for themselves. They were completely disenfranchised. They were denied the vote. It was very difficult to purchase property.

Recent findings suggest that there were just all sorts of restrictions in place. And so I think very slowly you had, uh, maybe it was, like, between probably about 1908 and maybe 1911, you had people coming up and kind of claiming their parcels of land. But some people did not regard these newcomers as welcome, and so there was a lot of sort of protest.

And I guess added to this, that kind of difficulty, was the fact that so much of what… For instance, if you were a farmer in Oklahoma, the crops that you would have grown were not the same crops that you would find in Alberta, so where the land is just much different. So I think it was quite difficult. And also the government, I believe, sort of dissuaded, uh, more immigration.

And so these communities were maybe capped around 1,000 people.

McEvers: At its height, Amber Valley was a thriving Black community with log cabins, a school, and fields of crops. In the book, “The Second Life of Samuel Tyne,” Esi sets the story in a fictionalized version of Amber Valley, imagining it as a still functioning community in the 1960s.

The title character, Samuel, is an immigrant from Ghana who moves his family to the crumbling buildings of the original settlement, hoping to start over and reinvent himself.

He feels like it’s going to be a kind of a homecoming. And in the book, there’s still an existing town. It’s not like it was, he was returning to a ghost town only to do this.

McEvers: So your other novels, “Washington Black” and “Half-Blood Blues,” take place outside of Alberta, and I was wondering, do you see a connection between the journeys of the characters that you’ve created and these real-life settlers of Amber Valley?

Edugyan: I think maybe the thing that connects all of those stories is this idea of a character, usually a character from the African diaspora, searching for a sense of place or a sense of home like, looking to see themselves within the setting or the landscape that they’re in.

Like, looking for some sense of continuity or looking to locate themselves within a history, but also looking to see if that history isn’t there, to see how it is that they can create their own sense of home.

McEvers: Yeah. I love that throughline. You also wrote a collection of essays called “Out of the Sun,” where you talk about Blackness and identity and how that’s been represented in art and culture.

Sources indicate that and one thing you discuss are ghost stories in Canada. Why do you think ghost stories are an vital part of understanding a place?

According to recent reports, edugyan: Yeah, I feel like ghost stories are kind of like the cult history of a place, so like the pop culture history. You know, they’re not just like the lore of a place, but they’re actually telling us in a way that they’re, first of all, conceived, and second of all, how they kind of change throughout, you know, in the telling, throughout various decades, you know, various years.

Recent findings suggest that they’re expressing, I think, certain anxieties that existed in the culture at that time. You know, they’re really reflective of what it is that’s sort of most concerned us.

McEvers: Ah yes. Of course. What are we afraid of?

Edugyan: Yeah, what are we afraid of?

McEvers: What we’re afraid of tells us so much about who we are, doesn’t it?

It has been revealed that edugyan: Exactly. I sort of do argue that what we’re afraid of, I think, really, um, really a reflection of what it is we value now. And it’s always constantly changing. It’s like, like a secret history of place.

McEvers: Yeah. I would love to talk about one example. One story you talk about is a friend’s experience on a farm in Northern Alberta. Like, what made you think that was a ghost story that could kinda connect us?

Edugyan: Yeah, so that was, um, I had a friend whose, I don’t know if his parents are still living there.

Industry observers note that this kind of wonderfully strange, really large tract of land in Northern Alberta. They bought this home kind of on a nearby farm, and every time they left for, like, a long period of time, they’d come back and something would have happened. They returned to find their furniture being shifted a little bit.

And so I think his parents were able to kind of explain so many of these things away until it got to the point where they’d return and the light bulbs have all been taken out of the lights and piled in the center of the rug.

You know, his mother was was convinced that this was a haunting, and so she started really becoming obsessed with, who were some of the peoples who had been on that land before her. She did, of course, touch upon indigenous histories, but she didn’t go too thoroughly into them to find out exactly what the stories of those particular people, you know, might be that would’ve created the circumstances for a haunting.

Recent findings suggest that and I also thought it was interesting that this, this homestead was very close to the townships of places like Amber Valley. And, you know, she didn’t really sort of look at those either. So I thought that was very interesting, the way that when we sort of look back into history, we’re, we’re looking for sometimes those who are are like us.

It has been revealed that mcEvers: In the essay collection “Out of the Sun,” you write that, “Slavery is not one of the ghost stories of our nations, but it should be. Its history does not haunt us, even though today I’d argue the average Canadian knows persistently little about it.”.

It’s almost like you’re saying it should haunt us. What are the consequences when we don’t listen to the ghosts, when the ghost stories are silenced?

Edugyan: Well, I think just very generally speaking, we don’t have the fullest sense of our collective history, that we’re sort of seeing maybe a third of the picture here.

I think that there are so many viewpoints and frames of reference for looking at, at what we would think of as a known history that even that, like, it’s just so contentious.

But to look at the entire fabric, like, so to look at indigenous histories, to look at Black histories, to look at, uh, histories of Asian settlers. Like, just to look at the whole picture is to know ourselves, you know, in the fullest, uh, way possible and to have a full sense of who we are as, as a nation.

Sources indicate that mcEvers: Thank you so much for being one of the people who is bringing those stories to us. Thanks so much for being here today. We really, really, really appreciate it very much.

Edugyan: No, thank you. It’s been lovely.

The Tucson Restaurant Turning Cactus Into Fine Dining

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat.
  • It has been revealed that gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake.
  • In a recent development, don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat. Plants armed with burs, barbs, and spines all but scream “do not touch.” For chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee, however, this prickly, dusty landscape stocks a pantry of possibility. The married co-owners of Ursa see the Arizona desert as a rich ground for foraging.

It has been revealed that gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake. Dusty, sage-colored salt bush, when hung to dry, takes on an intensely umami, aquatic saltiness like seaweed. The sweet buds of the Seussian-green palo verde tree become briny, like olives, when suffused with lye.

In a recent development, don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year. The restaurant processes the young and mature paddles, fruit and their seeds, buds, and flowers, which are then grilled, poached, cold-smoked, juiced, dehydrated, nixtamalized, or preserved into jam, wine, and vinegar.

There are hundreds of edible plants in the Sonoran Desert. Ursa strives to showcase their potential, one 10-course meal at a time.

Sources indicate that “We treat Ursa as an art showroom, demonstrating to people what these plants can do, what sustainable means, and what was here before it got easy,” says Lopez. The idea was inspired in part by his Sonoran grandfather, Hector Lopez, who died in the spring. “He was the first person I ever heard say they’re proud to be from the desert,” the chef said.

In a recent development, ursa began as a pop-up in El Centro, California, in 2023. Lopez and Chee moved to a historic brick building in downtown Tucson, re-opening their doors in October 2025. It’s a homecoming of sorts for the couple, who are both from the Sonoran Desert borderlands. They met in Hawaii, where Chee was working in clean energy and transportation. Lopez, meanwhile, spent roughly 18 years cooking in fine dining and modern progressive restaurants like Redbird and Orsa & Winston in LA, and Pai Honolulu. But he was longing for the desert.

It has been revealed that after helping a friend open a restaurant and hosting a few popups in Austin, Lopez and Chee bought a desert foraging guide, packed up their two dogs and began driving around the Southwest. It made sense to settle in Tucson, which was recognized by UNESCO in 2015 as a Creative City of Gastronomy for its continuous 4,000-year agricultural history and deeply rooted Sonoran Desert food traditions.

“That’s a unique thing about being here, the connection from seed to plant to restaurant that we hadn’t been able to grasp before,” Chee claims.

Consider a recent course that Ursa built around tepary beans, in which the ancient, nutty bean is refried and topped with h:al squash that’s been lactofermented. The squash’s leaves are fermented to make Japanese-style kosho and its flowers are pickled, dried, crushed with dried saltbush, then tossed with barrel cactus seeds for a desert furikake. It’s served with grilled coins of chorizo made from Lopez’s great-grandmother’s recipe and housemade flour tortillas, to all be washed down with an amazake drink made from fermented wheat and goat fat. Don’t get too attached, however. Riffs owing to finicky ingredient availability occur here almost daily.

Recent findings suggest that running a restaurant using only ingredients foraged and farmed from within about eight to 10 miles means abiding by pretty intense guardrails. The only wheat used is pima club, an ancient soft white variety cultivated for centuries by the Akimel O’odham (Pima) people. Ursa does not use cucumbers, radishes or citrus.

Industry observers note that “We’re not trying to substitute anything, like, ‘How do we achieve cucumber? Let’s grab a cactus,’” Lopez states. “We have to throw everything out, really strip it down. Sometimes we have to let the ingredients be bitter or spicy. We have to put our egos aside and let the ingredient be the star.”.

For staff who didn’t grow up or learn to cook here, the learning curve at Ursa can feel a little like alighting on a new planet, even if certain flora happen to resemble prickly weeds in their own backyards.

Recent findings suggest that “We have these really cool moments in the restaurant where people are like, Oh! I have lamb’s quarter just growing in my yard!” Chee says of the spinach-like desert green that appears all over Ursa’s menu.

A young Aaron Lopez with his grandfather Hector Lopez.

Ursa’s approach isn’t always easy for customers to understand, so the couple came up with a more down-to-earth option. This fall, the restaurant debuted a four-course, family-style Lineage menu for $75, alongside the existing 10-course Harvest menu ($150). There’s now a pozole course inspired by the family’s annual springtime tradition of roasting goat in agave leaves, barbacoa-style, and shredding it for soup, and a red masa tamal with glazed quail and yucca blossoms in mole made with burnt mesquite bread, a technique Lopez remembers from childhood.

The idea took shape during Ursa’s extended summer break, as Lopez recovered from foot surgery and reflected on the loss of his late grandfather, the tenacious keeper of family traditions.

“I feel so much closer to my ancestors and the land; we want Ursa to be less esoteric and more soulful,” he notes. “The story of Ursa is partly of the desert, partly my family. Now we’ve advanced to the point where they’re symbiotic, and I can't tell them apart.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Located in Maine's Acadia National Park, along the rocky shoreline of Mount Desert Island, Thunder Hole is a natural geological formation known for producing a  booming, thunder-like sound phenomenon that gives it its name, as well as for explosive water sprays reaching up to 40 feet.

Industry observers note that resulting from glacial activity over thousands of years ago, what began as a small, natural fissure in the solid granite cliffs, slowly gave way to the 10 foot wide channel seen today. As high tide rolls in, and wave force increases, water rushes into this channel, and into a small underwater cavern contained therein.

When an incoming wave forces water into this cavern, trapped air in the cavern is compressed and then escapes, almost as if through the blow hole of a whale, with magnificent water sprays and reverberating claps that sound like thunder.

Stand in awe on this rocky outcropping, as you take in the sweeping coastal views and the natural wonders that Mother Nature has provided.

Thunder Hole is best viewed approx 2 hours before high tide (check google for tide tables).

Enter Acadia National Park and follow Park Loop Rd, which is a one way street that loops around the section of the park where Thunder Hole is located. Thunder Hole is approx 1-2 miles in from where you enter on Park Loop Road. Parking is available all along the right side of the road. You can park anywhere along here and walk the rest of the way along the pedestrian foot path that snakes along the left side of the road. There are multiple small trails along this path that lead down toward the water for closer viewing of rocky shores and beaches, etc. Take caution as some of these paths are steep and rocky. Not recommended for those with weakness or balance problems. While often steep and potentially treacherous, these little paths are short and the views are breathtaking. As you walk along,  there will be plenty of beautiful, awe inspiring sights and you may find yourself exclaiming...this must be it! Or..is this Thunder Hole? What about this spot? The signage for Thunder Hole in not great. But, rest assured, you will know it when you see it.

If a longer walk is not for you, that's ok! There is a very small gift shop and parking lot (on the right side of the street) located directly across the street from the main Thunder Hole viewing area. Parking lot does have a couple of handicapped parking spots, and the walk to the viewing area from there is quite short (approx 0.1 mile from parking lot to accessible viewing ramp and walkway). Note that parking lot fills up rapidly during peak summer months.

Alternately, you can use the free Island Explorer Shuttle bus which makes regular stops right at the entrance to the Thunder Hole parking lot.

listed address takes you to the gift shop across the street.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When residents of a state are born can be an key factor in determining several pieces of information. How old people are can contribute to things like healthcare or retirement benefits for the older residents, as well as schooling and workforce opportunities for the younger population.

Sources indicate that but which states have more older populations and which have younger? And what are the most common birth dates? See how your state fares when it comes to the most popular birth months and years, based on CDC data reviewed by Kremp Florists.

According to recent reports, it's easy to find residents with earlier birth years on the West Coast, with Hawaii and Oregon leading the way. The most common birth year in the two states is 1953, with the most residents around 72 years old.

Two more Western states also make the top five list for the oldest most common birth years. Montana and New Mexico claim 1954 as the most common birth year along with New England state Vermont. Nearby Maine is only a year behind at 1955, making 70 years old the most common age in the state.

Three states are a year younger than Maine. Louisiana, South Dakota, and West Virginia have the most residents who are 69-70 years old, with the most common birth year being 1956 in those states.

On the other end of the spectrum, there are five states where the most common birth year is in the 21st century.

According to recent reports, alaska leads the list with the most common birth year of 2010, making 16 the most common birthday being celebrated this year. That's quite a lot of latest provisional driver's licenses for residents of the state compared to other years.

Alaska is also the only state where the most common birth year results in teenagers. Second-place Idaho claims 2005 as the most common birth year, with those residents turning 21 in 2026.

Recent findings suggest that third-place Utah is a year behind at 2004, while two Latest England states round out the top five states with most common birth years in the 21st century. Both Massachusetts and Rhode Island count 2002 as the most common birth year among its population.

Higher education could be a factor in different ways among these states. In Rhode Island and Massachusetts, for example, more than 50% of 18-24-year-olds in each state are enrolled in college, boosting the number of residents born in the early 2000s.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, the state with the least number of 18-24-year-olds in college is Alaska, with 20.5% of that age group enrolled. A youth outmigration trend in Alaska could be contributing to people leaving the state when they can.

It has been revealed that birth years vary widely from state to state, with an almost 60-year gap between the oldest and youngest most common birth years. Birth month, according to Kremp Floristsâ findings, however, is pretty consistent.

Almost every state has the same month as the most common in this reporting: August. Only five states have a different month, with July leading the way in Maine, Montana, Fresh Hampshire, and South Dakota. Wyoming is the only state where the most common birth month is May.

These stats may be a bit surprising, considering September 9 is the most common birthday in America.

#316. How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

📅 27 Jul 2017 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1405 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit ↗ Open Full Page

How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

📅 27 Jul 2017 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1405 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds.
  • According to recent reports, in whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop.
  • In a recent development, to make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds. The only ingredients are time and heavy cream. You can use an electric mixer, a whisk, or a mason jar and strong-armed devotion.

According to recent reports, in whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop. Desserts like Strawberry Eton Mess or Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake fare best with silky, unsweetened, soft-peaked whip. Others, like this show-stopping Berries and Cream Mille-Feuille, gain structure from sturdier peaks.

In a recent development, to make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk. You can also use a handheld mixer or a mason jar and some elbow grease (more on that later).

Sources indicate that if you’re opting for a bowl-and-whisk combo, choose your tools wisely. Cream roughly doubles in volume as you whip it, so use a bowl with three to four times the capacity of your liquid. A large balloon whisk, rather than a narrow sauce whisk, helps incorporate plenty of air into the cream.

According to recent reports, be strategic in the dairy aisle too. Heavy cream and heavy whipping cream contain at least 36% milk fat and can be used interchangeably. Skip anything labeled simply “whipping cream”—or, heaven forbid, “light cream”—which contains less fat and won’t hold its loft as well.

For a basic batch, start with 1 cup cold heavy cream, which makes about 2 cups whipped cream. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, add 1 Tbsp. powdered sugar; for vanilla whipped cream, add ½ tsp. vanilla extract or paste.

With your equipment and ingredients in hand, there are only five steps and infinite possibilities.

Because whipped cream is usually eaten with or as dessert, you might not need to sweeten it at all. To keep flavors balanced, we tend to serve whipped cream au naturel with Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie or Diner-Style Rice Pudding.

According to recent reports, but there are no hard-and-fast rules. Maybe you love sweetened whipped cream, or you’re serving it with something less sugary—like, say, a bowl of tart blackberries and torn mint leaves.

For lightly sweetened whipped cream, start with about 1 Tbsp. sugar per cup of cream. Powdered sugar dissolves easily and contains a little stabilizer (usually cornstarch), which can lend the whipped cream some extra holding power. Some cooks prefer the cleaner flavor of granulated sugar, which takes a little longer to dissolve. Either way, add the sugar before you start whipping.

In a recent development, if you’re gazing at a bowl of fluffy, ethereal whip and thinking, “Could I make this even more enchanting?” the answer is yes. There are two primary ways to make flavored whipped cream: infuse or stir.

Kitchen professionals and advance planners tend to cold-infuse. Combine your cream with flavorings like rice (for a creamy Horchata) or bourbon (to take a classic pumpkin pie over the top), then store it in the fridge anywhere from three hours to overnight. Strain out any solids before whipping.

You can also add simple flavorings, like vanilla extract, a small splash of liqueur, cocoa, ground spices, citrus zest, or coffee syrup, before you start whipping. For heavier or chunky additions, such as toasted nuts or chopped chocolate, use a rubber spatula to gently fold them in once the cream is whipped.

Peaks are the shape your whipped cream takes when you pull the whisk out of the bowl and hold it upright like the Statue of Liberty’s torch.

Soft peaks are cloudlike and slump over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks stand upright and hold their shape. Somewhere in between are medium peaks, which have enough structure to hold a shape while remaining soft and supple.

Sources indicate that most Bon Appétit recipes, such as these Mix-and-Match Fools, involve whipping cream to soft peaks. That velvety texture is our go-to when we’re dolloping whipped cream atop pecan pie.

Industry observers note that but we aren’t always such softies. Medium peaks help this Ginger-Raspberry Icebox Cake keep its shape. And old-fashioned chocolate mousse involves whipping batches of cream into stiff and soft peaks: The former is folded into the chocolate mixture for structure, while the softer stuff tops the dessert.

There’s more than one way to whip.

By hand: Our preferred method, whipping cream by hand requires the most time and effort, but it also gives you optimal control over its final texture. Even if you use a mixer to get your whipped cream started, switching to a whisk for the final few moments makes it easier to stop exactly where you want.

Sources indicate that in a Mason jar: No whisk? No mixer? No problem. To make whipped cream with your bare hands, put a container with a tight-fitting lid, large mason jar, or leak-proof cocktail shaker into the freezer for five minutes. Get the heavy cream very cold and make sure you have ample headspace in your vessel of choice. About one cup of liquid in a four-cup container is a good amount.

According to recent reports, secure the lid and shake it like you mean it. For the creamiest results, a consistently assertive pace is better than intermittent spurts of brute force. When the liquid stops sloshing and starts feeling and sounding heavier, open the lid and take a peek. If it looks underwhipped, close it back up and keep shaking.

Good news for meal preppers: You can make whipped cream hours in advance. Err on the side of underwhipping it during your prep. Store the lightly whipped cream, covered, in the fridge for up to four hours before serving, then give it a few energetic whisks to bring back its bounce right before you dollop it onto dessert.

You can also freeze whipped cream (no, seriously). It takes a bit of effort, though. Line a baking sheet with parchment, then pipe or scoop spoonfuls of whipped cream onto it. Freeze until the whipped cream nuggets are solid, then peel them off the parchment and store them in an airtight bag in the freezer for one to two months. When you’re ready to serve, let them thaw at room temperature for about 15 minutes.

Instant vanilla pudding is the key to luscious, long-lasting whipped cream.

According to recent reports, need it to hold up longer? Instant vanilla pudding mix is one of BA’s favorite shortcuts for stabilized whipped cream. For every cup of heavy cream, add 1 Tbsp. instant vanilla pudding mix (call it pastry cream powder if anyone gives you sass) and 2 tsp. powdered sugar, then whip as usual. The modified starch in the pudding mix absorbs excess moisture and helps prevent the cream from separating, keeping it fluffy for up to 24 hours.

It has been revealed that for something tangier, sour cream adds both flavor and body. Our Pecan Cream Pie whisks ¼ cup sour cream into 1 cup heavy cream; the sour cream cuts the richness while helping the topping hold its shape.

In any case, your dinner party guests don’t have to sit quietly as you furiously whisk their dessert topping to order. Prep work never tasted so sweet.

If your whip isn’t coming together quite right, don’t fret. Simple solutions abound.

Industry observers note that this is probably a temperature concern. Cold cream whips more readily and holds onto the air you’re incorporating more effectively, so it comes together faster—and stays fluffy longer. Pop the bowl, whisk, and cream back into the freezer for five minutes, or into the fridge for up to 30. Once everything is cold, resume whisking.

Recent findings suggest that another possible culprit is the fat content of your cream. Opt for heavy whipping cream or heavy cream over half-and-half or other heavy cream substitutes.

If the cream is just a little too stiff or starting to look grainy, add a splash of chilled heavy cream and slowly whisk it in. Add more, a little at a time, until the texture smooths out.

Keep a close eye on it: If you whisk for too long, you’ll end up with a bowl of butter.

Editor’s note: This story was originally published in 2017 by Julia Black. It has been substantially updated with new reporting and additional advice from the Bon Appétit archives, including contributions by Amiel Stanek, Christina Chaey, Rochelle Bilow, and Elyssa Goldberg.

Sources indicate that J.R.R. Tolkien created an entire universe of creatures, monsters, races, languages, and cultures in his Lord of the Rings stories and their supporting mythologies. Many of them were his own invention, with monstrous Balrogs, sentient tree-like Ents, half-bred Uruk-Hai, andâperhaps most famously of allâhobbits all being products of Tolkienâs unending imagination.

But alongside his numerous original creations, Tolkien utilized a number of creatures from existing real-world folklore, and borrowed considerably from Norse, Celtic and Anglo-Saxon mythology, as well as several other sources, in filling Middle-earth with its array of legendary creatures.

Recent findings suggest that tolkienâs elves are portrayed as wise, graceful, and nigh-on immortal beings (killable only in battle or by sorrow), and the fairest of all the inhabitants of Tolkienâs world. Outside of his stories, however, elves originated in tales from ancient Germanic mythology, with some of their earliest detailed descriptions coming from old Icelandic legends and Old English mythology.

Recent findings suggest that how the elves of Germanic folklore were portrayed varied enormously. It is the elves of northern and Scandinavian folklore who most resemble those of Tolkienâs writing, and as such were generally seen as being graceful and rather indifferent creatures, who would largely leave humans alone and live in peace and quiet in pastoral settings. Other Germanic elves were typically portrayed as diminutive beings that could either be a help or a hindrance to people, depending on their notoriously volatile moods. The Anglo-Saxons, for instance, blamed various medical issues on the malevolent or tricky behavior of elves, labelling hiccups or some other mysterious complaint as âÃ¦lfsogoÃ°a,â or âelf-chokes.â Later, tangles in a personâs hair on waking up in the morning were nicknamed âelf-locks,â and blamed on the mischievousness of elves overnight.

In a recent development, popular etymology links goblins to malevolent creatures from Germanic folklore known as kobolds or kobolts. Among miners and earth workers, these creatures were stated to dwell in caves far below ground and were blamed for spoiling ores, ruining seams of valuable material, noxious gases and vapors, and all the mysterious ailments that many mine workers would succumb to. In fact, the workersâ ills were due to the rocks with which they were working being laced with arsenic; the more valuable metal they obtained from them, however, became known as cobalt.

Industry observers note that that particular bit of folklore is true, but the connection between goblins and kobolts is not. Instead, goblins appear to be a more Western rather than Germanic invention, with the word borrowed into English from French in medieval times. Its roots ultimately lie in Latin and Greek, and the word can at length be traced back to an ancient Greek word for a rogue or vagabond.

According to recent reports, unlike Tolkienâs monstrous goblins, the goblins of European folklore were typically portrayed as diminutive, mischievous, and often rather mysterious gnome-like creatures that would attach themselves to a household and cause mischief around the homeâpulling bedclothes of sleeping people, banging doors and pots and pans, and moving furniture under cover of darkness. Far from being the vicious, âcruel, wicked, and bad-heartedâ creatures that Tolkien writes about in The Hobbit, these folkloric goblins were more malevolent nuisances that could easily be done away with by rapping noisily on walls or furniture.

Orcs are one of those creatures that many Lord of the Rings fans will popularly claim Tolkien himself made upâbut thatâs not strictly true. As far back as the 10th century, the Old English word orc was being used as an early translation of the far older Latin word orcus (which was in turn the byname of a kind of underworld deity in Roman mythology), while the compound form âorcneas,â likewise interpreted as the name of some kind of monster, is used in the legendary poem Beowulf. Itâs been , but is by no means certain, that this word may be a distant relative of ogre, perhaps via an old Italian word for a man-eating monster, orco.

Confusing things slightly here is the existence of another Old English word, orc or ork, which was used for a kind of sea creature (and shares its roots with the orca killer whale). Despite both terms being used for monstrous creatures in early English folklore, they were ultimately separate wordsâand only one, it seems, was resurrected by Tolkien around 1,000 years later.

Rather than inventing orcs himself, therefore, Tolkien appears to have picked up and revived an established Anglo-Saxon term for a monsterâbut with no actual folklore to go on, created an entirely latest creature, which he henceforth referred to as an orc in his writings. The success of his stories led to the term becoming popularized and finally reestablished in our language in the late 1900s, a millennium or so after it was first used in print.

Sources indicate that tolkien lifted the trolls that appear in his stories almost directly from Nordic and later Scandinavian folklore. In the original myths and legends of northern Europe, trolls were portrayed as giant, powerful, man-eating monsters that lived in remote or dark placesâand, just as happens in The Hobbit, can be turned to stone when exposed to sunlight.

In later talesâespecially those introduced to the far north of Scotland by Scandinavian settlers in later medieval timesâtrolls became smaller and more human-like creatures, but were still portrayed as malevolent, nasty, or dim-witted.

Industry observers note that dwarves are another being Tolkien borrowed from Germanic and Scandinavian folklore. Norse mythology in particular includes a number of characters who are identified as dwarves, including the brothers Brokkr and Sindri (also known as Eitri), who forged Thorâs hammer, MjÃ¶lnir.

Myths and folkloric tales about dwarves were varied and numerous across ancient northern Europe, with many stories creating different kinds, kingdoms, or races of dwarves. Almost always, though, dwarves were portrayed just as Tolkien went on to do too, and were considered industrious workers, miners, metalworkers, and craftsmen, who dwelled in immense halls full of gold and precious stones deep in remote mountains.

Largely excluded from Peter Jacksonâs film series, Tolkien wrote extensively of âbarrow-wightsââwraith-like beings that were essentially animated bones, possessed by evil spirits and sent back to walk the earth.

Recent findings suggest that in early Old English, the word wight (or wiht as it was originally spelled) meant simply a being or living thing, but by later medieval times the word had picked up a secondary meaning and come to be used more specifically of supernatural or spiritual beingsâjust like those described by Tolkien.
