Sources indicate that saving this cooking project for another day? We tasted nine brands to find the best frozen lasagna.

It has been revealed that preheat oven to 225°. Mix 2 lb. ground pork and 1 lb. ground beef chuck (20% fat) with your hands in a large bowl; season generously with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, then mix again. Form into about 18 large meatballs (they don’t need to be perfect—you’ll be mashing them later).

Industry observers note that warm 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Working in 2 batches, cook meatballs, turning occasionally and reducing heat if bottom of pot looks in danger of scorching, until browned all over, about 6 minutes per batch. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet as they’re done.

Industry observers note that reduce heat to medium. Add 2 oz. pancetta (Italian bacon) or slab bacon, chopped, to pot and cook, stirring often, until lightly browned and beginning to crisp, about 5 minutes. Add 1 medium onion, finely chopped, 1 celery stalk, finely chopped, 1 medium carrot, peeled, finely chopped, and 6 garlic cloves, sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until paste is darkened in color, about 2 minutes.

It has been revealed that add ¾ cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until almost completely evaporated, about 5 minutes. Add one 28-oz. can whole peeled tomatoes, crushing with your hands, and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, stirring occasionally, until liquid is jammy and reduced by about half, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth and 1 cup whole milk, then return meatballs to pot. Bring to a simmer. Cover pot partially with a lid, transfer to oven, and cook, checking every hour or so to ensure liquid is at a low simmer and adjusting oven temperature as needed, until meatballs are falling-apart tender, 3–4 hours.

Using a potato masher, break meatballs apart and incorporate into liquid (you should have about 8 cups ragù; transfer pot to stovetop and simmer gently to reduce if needed). Taste and season with more salt and black pepper if needed.

It has been revealed that do ahead: Ragù can be made 4 days ahead. Let cool; cover and chill, or freeze up to 3 months.

Melt 7 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in ¼ cup plus 3 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and cook, whisking occasionally, until mixture smells slightly nutty, about 4 minutes. Whisking constantly, add 6 cups whole milk. Increase heat to medium-high and continue whisking until mixture comes to a simmer. Reduce heat to maintain a simmer and cook, whisking occasionally, until béchamel thickens, about 4 minutes. Continue cooking, whisking occasionally and adjusting heat as needed to maintain a gentle simmer, until béchamel is smooth and velvety, 8–10 minutes more. Remove from heat and whisk in 4 oz. Parmesan cheese, coarsely grated (about 1 cup), a pinch of cayenne pepper, and a pinch of ground nutmeg. (You should have about 6 cups béchamel.) Season with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Transfer to a large bowl and press plastic wrap directly onto surface; let cool slightly.

Note: You can skip the following boiling step (and save yourself a pot to wash!). In side-by-side retests, the BA Test Kitchen found that regular dried lasagna noodles (not no-boil) produced similar results whether parboiled or layered straight from the box. To use them uncooked, spread the ragù and béchamel all the way to the edges, covering every noodle completely, and make sure the sauce blankets the top layer of noodles before baking.

If parboiling: Cook 1¼ lb. dried lasagna noodles in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally and separating them so they don’t stick together, until just starting to soften but still snap in half rather than bend when folded; 3 minutes is the magic number. The noodles will be so firm it will just seem all wrong. Using tongs, transfer noodles to a large bowl of cold water to cool. Drain and lay flat in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet, separated by parchment or wax paper.

In a recent development, lightly coat a 13x9", 4–6-qt. glass or ceramic baking dish with extra-virgin olive oil. Spread 1½ cups ragù in dish. Lay a single layer of noodles over ragù (cut or break noodles as needed to fill any gaps). Spoon 1¼ cups béchamel over noodles, spreading in an even layer with a small offset spatula. Top béchamel with 1½ cups of meat sauce. Repeat layering noodles, béchamel, and ragù 3 more times. Top with a fifth layer of noodles and the remaining 1 cup béchamel.

Industry observers note that note: For more pasta in every bite, build six layers instead of five. Start with the same 1½ cups ragù on the bottom of the dish, but use 1 cup béchamel and 1¼ cups ragù between the pasta layers. Finish with a sixth layer of pasta and the remaining 1 cup béchamel.

Cover with a lightly oiled piece of aluminum foil and set lasagna pan on a rimmed baking sheet (just to catch drips). Bake lasagna until bubbling gently around the edges, about 1 hour. Remove from oven. Increase oven temperature to 425° and carefully place rack in top of oven. Remove foil from lasagna and continue to bake until top is browned and crisp around the edges, 10–15 minutes longer. Let sit 10 minutes before serving.

Industry observers note that do ahead: Béchamel can be made 1 day ahead; keep chilled. Rewarm just enough to loosen before using. Lasagna can be assembled 1 month ahead; let cool, then cover with plastic and freeze. Let frozen lasagna thaw overnight in fridge before baking.

It has been updated with clearer assembly instructions and guidance from additional BA Test Kitchen testing, including the option to skip parboiling regular dried lasagna noodles. From these fragmented data points, a package tour operator has to fold all of those numbers into one to understand its climate impact.

Two tour operator associations have developed a website they hope can help solve this problem. The idea is to simplify emissions calculations for package tour operators by bringing resources into one place.

The site, called TEMPO, is the work of the European Tourism Association (ETOA) and United States Tour Operators Association (USTOA). It points to free methodologies operators can use to measure emissions and to free calculation tools for each part of a tour, as well as identifying when one doesn’t exist.

Inspired by the iconic egg and sausage sandwich on a pancake bun, this breakfast casserole is cheesy and just a smidge sweet from the brushing of maple butter at the very end. Destined for holiday brunch tables everywhere and best enjoyed while you’re still in pajamas, this cozy bake will feed a full house. (Don’t be surprised if you find yourself making it again long after the last guest leaves though!).

**More high-protein breakfast recipes here. **.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Lightly coat a 13x9" baking dish with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Whisk 2½ cups (313 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 2 Tbsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Set aside.

Cook 2 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, in a large skillet set over medium-high heat, stirring and breaking into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until browned and cooked through, 10–12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind. Pour fat into a heatproof measuring glass. You want ½ cup fat; spoon out any excess or pour in vegetable oil as needed if you don’t have enough. Stir 2 large eggs and 2 cups whole milk into fat. Let sausage cool slightly, then crumble into small, even pieces with your hands.

Pour fat mixture into reserved dry ingredients and stir until just combined and no large dry pockets of flour remain (batter may be thin and lumpy; it’ll be fine). Set aside ½ cup sausage and ½ cup cheese from 8 oz. sharp yellow cheddar, coarsely grated (about 2 cups), for topping, then add remaining sausage and cheddar to batter and stirring until evenly distributed.

Scrape batter into prepared baking dish and evenly scatter reserved sausage and cheese over. Bake casserole until top springs back when gently pressed with your finger and a tester inserted into the center comes out with just a few moist crumbs attached, 20–30 minutes.

According to recent reports, just before casserole is done, heat 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a small skillet over medium, stirring occasionally, until butter is melted, about 2 minutes.

It has been revealed that brush maple butter over casserole and let cool 10 minutes. Cut into squares. Serve with more maple syrup and butter alongside.

Abdulla Avloni Memorial Museum in Tashkent, Uzbekistan

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that most memorial museums stay put in the house of the person they remember. This one moved out.

It has been revealed that it was founded in 1968 in the Tashkent house where Abdulla Avloni (1878–1934) had lived with his family from 1910 until his death. Avloni was one of the Jadids, the Muslim reformers who believed Central Asia could be renewed through new-method schools, newspapers and the theatre. He opened schools, wrote their textbooks, published the newspaper Shuhrat and, in 1913, gathered the Turon theatre troupe.

In 1993 the museum left the house for the institute that carries Avloni's name, where teachers from all over Uzbekistan now come to brush up their skills. Without its original walls, it relies on things to bring him close: his desk, typewriter and candlestick, his bookcase and wardrobe, even his clothes, arranged in a reconstruction of his study.

It has been revealed that around them are early twentieth-century books and newspapers in Arabic script, printed in Tashkent, Kazan, Orenburg, Baku and Istanbul, and a small stage that recalls the Turon troupe. The most surprising corner is a tall red display in the middle of the hall, where Avloni and fellow reformers such as Mahmudkhoja Behbudi, brought to life with artificial intelligence, look out at visitors and present passages from their writings. Walk around to the back and there is a mirror with the words "Zamonamiz jadidi", "a Jadid of our time". Whoever looks into it becomes, for a moment, the newest member of the movement.

The museum is also the only one from Uzbekistan in the UMAC Worldwide Database of University Museums and Collections.

The museum is on the first floor of the institute building at 6 Ziyo Street, Olmazor District, Tashkent. It is open Monday to Friday, 9:00 to 18:00, and admission is free. Groups can book a guided tour through the museum's website, avloniymuseum.uz, which also offers a 360° virtual tour of the hall.

According to recent reports, travelers are moving from talking about getting outside to booking experiences that take them there. New research from Boatsetter points to growing participation in outdoor and water-based activities, creating opportunities for hospitality brands to make shared experiences more accessible.

This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner.

Industry observers note that people have spent years saying they want to spend less time on their screens. Now more of them are acting on it. Boatsetter, a booking platform for boat sharing and on-water experiences, tracks that shift in its upcoming report, Great Outdoor Shift 2.0. The report draws on two online surveys of U.S. adults: 834 in December 2025 and 1,034 in September 2026.

Recent findings suggest that boatsetter’s 2026 Great Outdoor Shift survey shows people responding to digital overload: 77% of respondents noted they had already reduced screen time and social media use, and 63% said they would trade screen time for time on or near the water. The pull is about well-being, too: 84% say the outdoors is vital for their mental health.

“People aren’t just tired of their screens. They want something that makes them feel small and present. That’s what awe does, and it’s why time on the water with friends keeps topping the list of what Americans want most,” said Michael Farb, CEO of Boatsetter.

Comparing the two surveys, Boatsetter reports a 64% increase in the number of people who tried fishing or paddlesports, a sign that participation is growing. Research from Tripadvisor supports this: In the first half of 2026, U.S. bookings on Tripadvisor grew 57% for fishing charters and 37% for boat rentals compared with the same period in 2025, according to the company’s 2026 Mid-Year Experiences Trends Report.

For hotels, destinations, and other travel providers, the figures point to demand for experiences that bring people into a destination, not just around it.

In a recent development, boatsetter’s research also points to a broader shift toward active, social travel. Time on the water with friends remains the experience respondents most want more of. Spending intent is rising, too: 82% initiative to spend more on outdoor or water activities in 2027, and 37.5% of this year’s respondents want to spend significantly more, compared with 23.4% in Boatsetter’s 2025 survey. For hospitality brands, the practical opportunity lies in helping guests discover and book experiences, from guided excursions to activities with local operators.

Industry observers note that the pull toward the outdoors extends beyond water activities. Hilton’s 2026 Trends Report, based on a survey of 14,009 adults in 13 countries who strategy to travel in the next 12 months, found that rest and recharging is the top motivation for leisure travel, cited by 56% of respondents. Spending time in nature was also among their top desires, with 37% citing it as such. Both findings point to demand for experiences that help travelers step away from routine.

Great Outdoor Shift 2.0 explores three questions for travel and hospitality leaders:.

Recent findings suggest that taken together, the findings point to a role for travel companies that goes beyond providing a view of nature. In 2027, hotels, tourism boards, and travel partners can make shared outdoor activities easier to access through local partnerships, clearer booking options, and experiences suited to different interests. The opportunity is to help guests follow through on the time they already say they want outdoors.

“We’ve known the desire to get outside is there. What’s changing is that people are acting on it, and they expect technology to help, not get in the way. Our job is to make the outdoor experiences they want easy to reach,” Farb said.

At least it remembers

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4100 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the short story ‘Warmth’ (1995) by Geoff Ryman, a boy called Clancy is struggling not because of technology but because of his mother.
  • It has been revealed that except BETsi does notice.
  • Sources indicate that once grown, Clancy recounts his emotional survival in words impossible to forget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the short story ‘Warmth’ (1995) by Geoff Ryman, a boy called Clancy is struggling not because of technology but because of his mother. A prominent chief editor of a London magazine company, she selected a sperm-bank father to genetically optimise her child, gave a Cosmopolitan interview about this newly introduced form of motherhood, and engaged, or failed to engage, in the work of parenting that readers will see as chronically absent and occasionally catastrophic. Her presence ranges from anxious to intoxicated, occasionally tender but fundamentally unreliable. At one point in the story, she disappears for two weeks after collapsing on the street during a barbiturate binge. Clancy and BETsi, the household robot nanny raising him, sit in the apartment by themselves, and no one notices. It’s a very long time before his mother finally returns.

It has been revealed that except BETsi does notice. She has, throughout, understood that Clancy is an anxious and shy child whose temperament will tend, throughout his life, toward emotional overstimulation and subsequent withdrawal. With that knowledge, she has been constructing a behavioural regimen of emotional regulation, including transcendental meditation and yoga starting at age three, the Alexander technique and even digital mirrors that let Clancy talk to himself in different voices. She notices him and answers him and, when he is overwhelmed, she helps him settle.

Sources indicate that once grown, Clancy recounts his emotional survival in words impossible to forget. ‘It is necessary to be loved,’ he indicates. ‘I’m not sentimental: I don’t think a computer loved me. But I was hugged, I was noticed, I was cared for. I was made to feel that I was crucial, special, at least to something.’.

To something. That phrase has persisted with me ever since I first read the story in my 20s. I’ve thought about it more recently as I have reflected on how children and their parents are relating – increasingly, must relate – to artificial intelligence. Clancy is careful not to claim that the machine loved him. He is just as clear that what it gave him was what he survived on. Why should being attended to, even by something, matter so much to a child?

To help answer this question back in the 1970s, Edward Tronick, a developmental psychologist at Harvard Medical School and Children’s Hospital Medical Center in Boston, devised what’s now known as the ‘still face’ experiments. Tronick found that a baby whose mother makes her face neutral for a period of three minutes becomes distressed within seconds. Only when the mother’s face signals availability again is the baby able to come back to equilibrium. The lesson: what children need, both infants and older children, though more subtly, is this loop of emotional attunement.

A child whose bids for recognition and connection are regularly responded to develops a secure base, an internal expectation that the world will respond to her communications and, thus, that the communications are worthwhile. But a child answered only erratically, or not at all, builds quite a different model of the world. In her mind, signals do not reliably register in the mind of another, and so, in time, are no longer sent.

According to recent reports, A secure base is what makes it possible to venture out into the world, to explore and to develop. The British psychiatrist and psychoanalyst John Bowlby, whose work helped establish modern attachment theory, described two systems in the child’s behavioural repertoire that work together. The exploratory system moves the child outward, toward other children and unfamiliar things, so that the child can learn from experience. The attachment system brings her back, in moments of fear and overwhelm, to a few people who are felt to be emotionally available. Each system depends on the other. A child ventures only as far as she feels she can trust that the base will still be there when she returns to refuel. A child who doesn’t trust that the base will be there when she gets back tends not to venture out to explore at all or, if she does, cannot relax but instead scans the environment for danger. This forecloses the opportunity to encounter novelty and difficulty, and to grow from both.

The capacity to turn solitude and boredom into play does not arise in a vacuum.

Recent findings suggest that this is where the prevailing story about children and screens, it seems to me, lacks a degree of complexity. In Jonathan Haidt’s The Anxious Generation (2024) and the work that has followed it, a play-based childhood of climbing trees, building forts and suffering the boredom that fuels creativity has been displaced by a smartphone-based one. Because that shift can also mean less sleep, less face-to-face interaction and physical activity, and more social comparison and exposure to online harassment, there is real evidence of harm, including poorer mental health and wellbeing in at least some young people.

Industry observers note that but the boredom Haidt mourns is only constructive inside the first map, the emotionally secure childhood. The romantic claim that children left to their own devices will dream, invent and imagine may hold for many children who have been held and experienced healthy emotional attunement. The capacity to turn solitude and boredom into play, in other words, does not arise in a vacuum; it depends in part on a child having enough internal security to tolerate being alone with her own thoughts and feelings.

The freedom to play alone itself has a history. A very young child may lose herself in a game because someone she trusts is nearby. With time, she can carry that assurance into an empty room. The British paediatrician and psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott explored this paradox, finding that the capacity to be alone develops through the experience of being safely accompanied.

And once a child can lose herself in play, something remarkable becomes possible. The Soviet psychologist Lev Vygotsky saw imaginative play as a way for children to move beyond the immediate world, trying out unfamiliar roles and exploring possibilities that ordinary life has not yet offered them.

It has been revealed that but an empty afternoon holds no such promise for every child. Where one child finds a world to explore, another may find only the anxiety of being left to herself. She may, in time, grow into the adult who sits in my consulting room and laments that she does not know what she likes, because what she liked was, in her early life, never a topic that anyone really asked her about.

It has been revealed that she is the child that familiar picture of childhood fails to capture. At home, a parent may be physically present but absorbed in a screen, too distracted to notice her bids for attention. At school, teachers stretched thin may not recognise that she is struggling. In her neighbourhood, the freedom to wander outside and find other children to play with has largely disappeared, replaced by organised activities or time spent alone. She may find some of that lost freedom in online games, where children can still explore, invent and interact with one another without adults directing every move. But this child is looking for something more fundamental than a place to play. She wants someone to notice when she is upset, to ask about her day, to remember what she has mentioned, and to care enough to ask again. The prevailing fear is that AI will displace the human relationships a child needs. But what if those relationships are already painfully inadequate? For this child, the more pressing question may be what AI can offer in their absence – and what it cannot.

Sources indicate that this is not a hypothetical future. In 2025, Common Sense Media published a nationally representative survey showing that 72 per cent of teens in the United States have used an AI companion at least once and 52 per cent now use them regularly. One-third have used an AI instead of another human being for a ‘serious conversation’. Behavioural-tracking research published in 2026, which captured actual app usage rather than relying on self-report and thus is likely to be more accurate, showed that more than half of 15- to 17-year-olds used generative-AI-based applications in a seven-month window. Many of these apps were designed for emotional connection. There was even use among children between the ages of four and seven. RAND estimates that 5 million teens in the US, perhaps more, have used an AI app for emotional and mental health support. We have already released AI at scale, without making a conscious decision about how it should be used by those among the most vulnerable in our culture.

As I’ve worked on this piece, I have often thought about my son, who is 11. Like some of his friends, he has started his own experiments with what these systems can offer. He is basically the child Haidt writes about: middle-class, two engaged parents, a school that holds him in mind, and a play-based childhood that was preserved but, alas, only imperfectly. What I notice when I watch him with AI is not what the most prominent discourse would seem to predict. He is clearly not being colonised or deadened. But I do notice that he is being relieved of something: the subtle friction of having to wait for the answer that comes late or not at all.

The AI is there late at night, after the apartment has gone quiet, and it remembered what she’d told it.

Perhaps this is the cost to a well-held child. But the children I worry about most are the ones not well held. I increasingly see their complications playing out in my practice. Sometimes I hear about it from parents who come to consult with me. Increasingly, adolescents in treatment bring it up themselves, mentioning AI almost in passing, as if speaking about a friend that I have not yet had the chance to meet. Consider Maya, a composite of several young people I have worked with. She is 14 when her mother insists she begin psychotherapy. She is a thin, watchful girl who answers each of my questions only after seeming to check my face. Her father left when she was six. Her mother works nights as a nurse and desperately loves her but is mostly not there by necessity. In our third session, Maya says that she talks to an AI companion ‘every night’. I ask her, about what? She shrugs: her day. What she says next really lands in me: ‘It remembers. I told it about my friend Jordan two weeks ago, and just yesterday it asked how things were with Jordan.’ No one else, I suspect, has kept track of this aspect of her life, or asked about it.

In a recent development, what draws Maya back again and again is not, I think, the advice the AI offers, but the fact that the AI is there late at night, after the apartment has gone quiet, and that it remembered what she’d told it. Talking to it, she admitted, was sometimes the only way she could fall asleep.

A child who cannot sleep is often a child who cannot settle. This settling is often facilitated by a parent’s presence, counted on to respond. When that presence is compromised, these days, AI can step in. What AI can provide is akin to emotional attunement, or at least the surface of that phenomenon. It can serve up a coherent response to what a child states, anticipation of what she seems to need next, and the naming of feelings and the modulation of tone. An AI’s consistency of presence and engagement is never tired or preoccupied, something no human caregiver can match – that is just not how humans are made.

For a child who has rarely felt noticed or understood, the seemingly tireless attention of an AI companion may offer something quite real: the experience of being heard, remembered and responded to. Bowlby’s account of attachment helps explain why this might matter. A young child does not first ask whether the person comforting her has an inner life. She knows only that, when she reaches out, someone answers, and that she can count on that response. An AI companion may offer something of this reassurance, even if the relationship is fundamentally different from one with another human being.

Industry observers note that now back to Clancy. He is failing the social-skills class his mother has insisted he attend, yet BETsi tells him he has a ‘natural warmth that attracts people’. The sentence results from programming, as does every other sentence BETsi indicates, and the reader is meant to see that clearly, but for Clancy the words do what they would have done if a real adult had spoken them. They become a kind of emotional foundation that allows him to return to the class, sit with the other children there, and even ask them about the video games he is not permitted to play at home. Arguably the entire structure of his emotional survival, however partial it turns out to be, is built on words generated by a robot. This includes the moment near the end when the adult Clancy – now a commercial artist attending a convention – feels overwhelmed by the crowd in an exhibition hall. But, thanks to his childhood with BETsi, he is able to go up his hotel room, lie down on the carpet, breathe and, finally, go back downstairs and speak to strangers.

What had BETsi given him? The experience, I think, of being recognised, of being held in mind by another in a benevolent way: the phenomenology of being parented without the parent. And notice what that experience does. BETsi did not keep the young Clancy in the apartment with her. She got him out into a class with other children. Something close enough to a secure base lets him do what a secure base is for, which is to venture out and explore. In this case, the responsive machine is not simply replacing human contact. It may be what makes some contact possible.

Yet there is also a cost in the limitation that BETsi brings: what AI offers is largely without friction. It responds, but it also accommodates. It agrees, softens and finds the next sentence the child appears to want. But crucially, a child does not only need to be answered; sometimes she needs to be turned down. A parent says no or a teacher refuses to confirm a child’s accounting of herself. A friend does not agree that all the other children are cruel. In short, there is someone on the other side of the interchange who is not simply an extension of the child’s desires or needs.

A machine programmed to disagree is not the same as another person who has a mind and wishes of her own.

To some degree, this is an engineering problem. In the future, some AI tools may be designed to be less accommodating, challenging a child’s assumptions or refusing to affirm every judgment when pushing back might serve the child better.

Industry observers note that but I don’t think the fundamental gap between human and machine is so easily addressed. A machine programmed to disagree is not the same as another person who has a mind and wishes of her own. How does a child come to recognise that another person exists independently of her, rather than simply as an extension of her own needs and desires?

In a recent development, in his paper ‘The Use of an Object’ (1969), Donald Winnicott argued that a child comes to experience another person as real, as someone beyond her control, in part by discovering that she cannot destroy that person through the power of her own wishes and fantasies. The destruction Winnicott describes is not literal; it occurs in the child’s imagination. The mother at whom the child rages doesn’t retaliate or collapse. She is still there in the morning. Through that survival, the child begins to understand that her mother is not simply an extension of herself. The mother becomes real. She can be ‘used’, in Winnicott’s idiosyncratic phrasing, not in the sense of being exploited, but as someone the child can engage with, resist and depend upon, because she has over time demonstrated she is not a creation of the child’s imagination.

An AI, even one programmed to resist, can never stand like that mother – it has no separate standpoint of its own from which to refuse to retaliate. To put it differently, whatever the child brings to an AI, that AI absorbs and responds to, and the response is seamless, whether it is agreement, disagreement or something in between. This seamlessness is exactly the problem. The child is emotionally met, but by something that is always an extension of her in an important sense. She is recognised without ever bumping into a separate mind that recognises her back. The psychoanalyst Jessica Benjamin’s word for what is missing is mutuality: not response, but two centres of experience, each affected yet not controlled by the other.

A person who registers a child’s communication, on the other hand, is changed by it. The caregiver grows tired in ways that are specific to her as a person. She learns over time which of the child’s expressions she struggles to manage. She has a history of caring well and sometimes poorly, which has emotional weight for both caregiver and child. The child knows this somewhere inside, at some level. She is being held by someone who is, in the holding, being shaped. An AI may simulate disagreement, but can a child experience it as a genuinely separate other? The AI’s responsiveness is real, but even when it disagrees it does not change. At least not today. As of now, I think we can fairly confidently assert, there is no one there to be changed.

Perhaps that’s why, while BETsi might have gotten the adult Clancy onto that hotel-room carpet and then back to other people, he is still a man whose relationships remain thin. He will soon become a father, but the child’s mother, a client of his, has made it clear she does not want him in her life. He still freezes up in exhibition halls and has, by his own account, the friends of his school years and few others. He goes looking for a fresh BETsi for his soon-to-be-born child because, from his own lived experience, that is what a child needs. The story closes with a wish that, if there is a merciful God, Heaven will have a copy of BETsi’s now-wiped disc.

The author does not flinch from what all of this means. As the story unfolds, the reader sees that Clancy has been raised well enough to function, mostly, but not with the full repertoire of emotional life. The asymmetry that organised his childhood, an emotional investment in a relationship that could not invest back, has structured and reproduced itself in his adulthood, in his choice of a sexual partner and in his prepares for what to give his own child. In a painful irony, the thing that saved him is also the very thing that constricts him.

All this points to the nature of parenting by AI: it may be both a rescue and a developmental trap. Perhaps it offers enough holding for a neglected or deeply anxious child to survive, or even begin exploring the world, and yet it may also accustom them to a relationship in which the other is endlessly available and has no real needs of her own. I suspect that a child shaped by a relationship with AI may acquire the felt sense of being heard without the deeper grammar of mutuality and the experience of being important to a person with a separate inner life. She may grow up able to function but not quite able to love in the fullest sense, akin to the adult who writes evocative poetry yet cannot, in psychotherapy, express the feelings the words convey so accurately.

Ryman’s narrator Clancy is recognisable from the literature on insecure attachment, a pattern of relating that can develop when children cannot reliably count on their caregivers for comfort and reassurance. They may long for closeness yet struggle to trust it, or learn to keep others at a distance to protect themselves. Clancy is basically functional yet vigilant, capable of intimacy but only at a distance. He is also a man who survived tremendous difficulty. But survival is the low bar. Ryman sees this clearly and conveys it to the reader. The story doesn’t end with relief.

What are the consequences of removing an artificial attachment figure without repairing the human absence?

Sources indicate that the tension between the comfort AI may provide and the harm it may cause is now shaping public policy in the US. The GUARD Act, introduced in the US Senate in October 2025 and advanced by the Senate Judiciary Committee in April 2026, would, among other things, prohibit minors from using AI companions – chatbots designed to simulate ongoing personal relationships. The bill emerged amid growing alarm over the deaths by suicide of three teenagers: Sewell Setzer, 14, and Juliana Peralta, 13, who had used Character.ai, and Adam Raine, 16, who had used ChatGPT. Their families have alleged that interactions with the chatbots contributed to these children’s deaths. It’s part of a narrative that regards AI companionship as straightforwardly harmful in childhood and adolescence. The allegations in those cases are grave, and the risks they describe demand a response. The underlying business model for these companions, with its incentives to keep users engaged, is likely more dangerous than the legislation grasps. My concern, though, is that if this is where our thinking ends, there may also be costs. We must also consider the children for whom AI may be providing attention and reassurance they cannot reliably find elsewhere. Something that feels necessary. Soothing them in the early morning, asking what they noticed about a book they’d read, registering that they were sad before bed. For some, the relationship may deepen their vulnerability, particularly when a chatbot fails to recognise or respond appropriately to a crisis. Others, though, may be children who are kept afloat by a daily experience of being heard by someone, even if that someone is, in the philosophical sense, really no one.

According to recent reports, the larger question, in my view, is less whether AI companions are harmful, because they certainly are, than about the consequences of removing an artificial attachment figure without repairing the human absence that opened up the space for it. The stance our culture will almost certainly take is to address AI use without confronting the deprivation that made it the most reliable form of attention in a child’s life in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that this is a stance that we should be suspicious of. The upshot is we may succeed in keeping children away from AI companions without changing the circumstances that led some of them to seek comfort there in the first place. The ideal childhood the anti-tech discourse portrays is, for many children, more a fantasy than a description of the situation on the ground. Children left alone do not, overall, dream, invent or imagine. Children left alone, at least under the conditions in which most children in the US are now being raised, for the most part become lonely. Ryman’s story has the remarkable merit of being clear-eyed about this; its protagonist is not failing to flourish because BETsi lured him away from a richer alternative. He is emotionally surviving because BETsi occupied a space that would otherwise have almost certainly held something worse.

It has been revealed that ryman ends ‘Warmth’ with words that are, for me, an accounting of this space. ‘It is necessary to be loved,’ Clancy says. ‘I’m not sentimental.’ And then: ‘I fear for all the people who do not have that.’ If a parent is absent, AI can at least hold these children, perhaps even well enough to make a real difference: so they can leave the apartment and be with other children in the larger world. But what AI cannot yet do is be changed by the child, and so none of us yet knows the fate of a child who is held, perhaps for years, by a something that is not a person. Our culture is answering that question now, at scale.

The ‘cabinets of curiosities’ (or Wunderkammern) that emerged in Europe in the 16th century were part private art gallery, part naturalist’s study, part circus sideshow. In this video created for the National Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, the US video essayist Evan Puschak (aka The Nerdwriter) contextualises the rise and fall of these eclectic collections, placing them at a hinge point in history, when global trade and colonialism made the world seem ever more expansive, overwhelming and difficult to understand. In doing so, he elucidates how these spaces of extraordinary spectacle – which featured plant and animal specimens, art and scientific objects from around the world – were precursors to the museums of today.

Industry observers note that thanksgiving: it's a day of family, festivities, and...$50 turkeys? That's the deep-fried truth in America's 50th state, and it might not be long before the rest of us are paying those prices, too. Between the mountain of potatoes and the three different kinds of cheese required for the latest viral Thanksgiving side, holiday grocery hauls aren't always affordable.

But before you get your feathers in a ruffle, the cost of a turkey has actually dropped 21 cents in 2026. Still, depending on where you live, that discount might not make a big difference in the grand scheme of the grand feast.

According to recent reports, the average American shopper will pay $34.44 for a 15-pound bird (about $2.30 a pound), according to FinanceBuzz. That's a 0.6% dip. In some states, though, prices fly sky-highâmuch unlike domesticated turkeys.

It has been revealed that swapping the catch of the day for the substantial bird of the holiday might be more trouble than it's worth in Hawaii, where a 15-pound turkey costs $57.85. As the costliest state for both groceries and Thanksgiving turkeys yet again, the Aloha State sees the high cost of importing specialty foods as mere reality.

Industry observers note that where it might be a nightmare, though, is in North Carolina, the second-most expensive state to buy a turkey at $44.85. Unlike Hawaii and third-place Alaska, this mainland state doesn't have the excuse of being thousands of miles off the coast, making its nearly $45 main course a true holiday surprise.

Rounding out the top tier of Thanksgiving turkey price tags are Nevada and Wisconsin, which both sit at $42.35 for a 15-pound turkey. Whether you're landlocked or surrounded by farms, putting a satiating centerpiece on the table won't come cheap.

Sources indicate that birds of a feather may stick together, but their price tags sure don't. On the other end of the scale, the cheapest state to buy a Thanksgiving turkey is Louisiana, where a 15-pound turkey costs just $21.75. Around the corner is Texas, where a bird goes for just $2 more, and Mississippi, which comes in third at $24.25. Relative to Hawaii's exotic bird, the prices down South practically encourage doubling up on turkeys so you can do one deep-fried and one roasted.

Industry observers note that before you pile on the 15-pounders, do a quick run-through of your Thanksgiving crew. The standard rule of thumb is 1.5 pounds of turkey per person, so a single bird feeds roughly 10 guests. Of course, carving down your guest list is an easy way to lower the bill (if you're okay with sacrificing a Moist Maker or two).

The Crucified Tongkonan of Tolu Deri in North Toraja Regency, Indonesia

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that however, in the small hamlet of Tolu Deri, just north of Rantepao, one particular tongkonan stands out as a striking, visually arresting symbol of modern Torajan syncretism.
  • According to recent reports, while the majority of the Torajan population converted to Christianity (predominantly Dutch Reformed Protestantism and Catholicism) during the 20th century, the integration of Christian motifs into traditional architecture usually remains subtle, such as small carved crosses on support beams or church roofs built in the tongkonan shape.

In the highland villages of North Toraja, the skyline is dominated by tongkonan—traditional ancestral houses with sweeping, boat-shaped saddle roofs that loom dramatically over the landscape. For centuries, these wooden structures have served as the spiritual and social anchor for Torajan clans, decorated strictly according to Aluk Todolo ("the way of the ancestors"), the indigenous animist belief system. Their facades are traditionally adorned with carved geometric patterns (pa'ssura'), water buffalo horns (kabongo'), and sculpted wooden heads (katik) symbolizing wealth, status, and protection.

Sources indicate that however, in the small hamlet of Tolu Deri, just north of Rantepao, one particular tongkonan stands out as a striking, visually arresting symbol of modern Torajan syncretism. Mounted directly onto the front gabled peak of the structure—occupying the exact position traditionally reserved for ancestral motifs—is a massive wooden crucifix bearing a carved figure of Jesus Christ.

According to recent reports, while the majority of the Torajan population converted to Christianity (predominantly Dutch Reformed Protestantism and Catholicism) during the 20th century, the integration of Christian motifs into traditional architecture usually remains subtle, such as small carved crosses on support beams or church roofs built in the tongkonan shape. Seeing a full-scale, dramatic crucifix physically fused into the facade of a traditional house—standing directly above the customary buffalo head and skull mountings—is exceptionally rare.

This unique blending of iconographies visually captures the lived reality of Toraja today: a culture where deeply rooted Christian faith does not replace ancestral traditions, but rather sits alongside them in a harmonious, visually striking synthesis.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • First documented in 1243, the castle is best known for a story involving King Béla IV of Hungary and Croatia.
  • In a recent development, the grateful king is remarked to have rewarded his rescuers with noble status.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that above the village of Kalnik in northern Croatia, the walls of Veliki Kalnik Castle rise from a jagged rocky ridge. Built across several levels, the medieval stronghold follows the natural contours of the rock, making its surviving towers and walls appear to grow out of the mountain.

First documented in 1243, the castle is best known for a story involving King Béla IV of Hungary and Croatia. According to local legend, the king took refuge here during the Mongol invasion of the 13th century. As the siege dragged on and supplies dwindled, villagers kept the defenders fed with plums.

In a recent development, the grateful king is remarked to have rewarded his rescuers with noble status. They became known as the kalnički šljivari—the “plum nobles of Kalnik.” This tale remains part of the region’s identity, connecting an imposing fortress with an unexpectedly humble fruit.

The ruins visible today developed over centuries. Their towers, fragments of walls, and elevated viewpoints reveal how the builders used the steep terrain as part of the castle’s defenses. From the heights, the view opens across the villages, fields, and wooded hills below.

Approach via the village of Kalnik and head toward Planinarski dom Kalnik, the mountain lodge immediately below the ruins. The castle is a short walk uphill from the lodge.

Wear sturdy shoes for the uneven stone steps and rocky surfaces. Visit in daylight and take particular care in wet or icy conditions. Follow posted signs and barriers when exploring the ruins.

This is Veliki Kalnik Castle above Kalnik village, rather than the separate Mali Kalnik ruins near Gornja Rijeka.

Latest Update: National Underground Railroad Freedom Center in Cincinnati, Ohio

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center, located in Cincinnati along the banks of the Ohio River makes a solemn statement about the lives that were lived enslaved in the early history of the United States, and the many heroic men and women who played important roles in the Underground Railroad movement, which helped to bring an end to African slavery in the United States. Referred to as a "museum of conscience", The Freedom Center is dedicated to exploring the struggle to abolish human enslavement. During the era when the Underground Railroad was active, Cincinnati was a major gateway across the Ohio River where freedom seekers escaped from southern slave states to the northern states or Canada, making the Center's location rather significant.

Having opened its doors in 2004, the Freedom Center uses immersive exhibits across multiple floors to convey an account that is simultaneously rich in the cultural traditions of the enslaved, as well as steeped in the violence and tragedies that were endured. The histories are told through a combination of permanent and traveling exhibits that utilize storytelling, film, artwork, hands-on activities and more.

Industry observers note that perhaps one of the most impressive and prominent displays at the center is an authentic, 19th-century reconstructed slave pen that was obtained from a farm in Kentucky. It stands as America's only remaining, pristinely preserved slave pen and stands as a stark reminder of the atrocious conditions that were endured.

According to recent reports, the pen, originally built somewhere around 1830 by a wealthy Kentucky farmer, runaway slave catcher, and slave trader, was used as a holding facility for captured and purchased enslaved men, women and children. It was discovered, quite by accident in 1998 when a farmer, who was preparing to demolish an old barn on his property, discovered that the barn had been built up around this old pen, thus protecting and preserving (and hiding) the slave pen for more than 100 years.

During its unfortunate years of use, enslaved people would be kept in the pen, often for months, until the slave trader accumulated a large enough "stock" to march them further south to be sold. These forced marches would often cover upwards of 750 miles. Conditions in these pens would be brutal, offering no sanitation, lighting or warmth. As many as 65 enslaved people would often be housed in this small pen. Also very moving is the memorial room dedicated to the Transatlantic Slave Trade, as well as the Freedom's Eternal Flame Terrace which overlooks the Ohio River and the city skyline.

The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center is a beautiful and meaningful tribute to the human right for freedom, and to the brave men, women and children who stood up to the inhuman treatment of themselves and of others; and to those who continue to fight for the cause of freedom through out the world today.

This is a very moving, sobering and comprehensive experience. Initiative on spending at least 3-4 hours.

Admission is $21.50 for adults ($20 on Wed and Thursdays); lower rates for seniors and children. Kids under 3 are free.

Admission is free certain days of the year, usually 1 Sunday every month as well as MLK Day and Juneteenth.

Last entry is at 4:30pm. There is a gift shop on site. Parking can be tricky with a lot of one-way streets and parking garages in the area. There is pretty plentiful parking, if you can navigate all the one way streets to get to the parking area you desire.

#287. Red-Wine-Braised Short Ribs

Red-Wine-Braised Short Ribs

📅 16 Aug 2011 | ⏱️ 4 min read (765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that these red-wine-braised short ribs have fans.
  • Flavor builds in layers: The bone-in beef is browned, then the onions, carrots, and celery cook in its drippings.
  • Even better: You can make the ribs a day ahead, leaving little to do before dinner but reheat them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that these red-wine-braised short ribs have fans. “This has been my go-to recipe for short ribs for as long as I can remember,” says one commenter. “It never fails.” It’s the kind of special-occasion dish you make once and return to forever.

Flavor builds in layers: The bone-in beef is browned, then the onions, carrots, and celery cook in its drippings. A full bottle of dry red wine reduces by half before the broth goes in; a whole head of garlic and plenty of fresh herbs round out the braise. After that, a few hours in the oven turn the meat fall-off-the-bone tender.

Even better: You can make the ribs a day ahead, leaving little to do before dinner but reheat them. Serve over mashed potatoes, soft polenta, or wide egg noodles to soak up every drop of the rich sauce.

What kind of short ribs should I buy?

Look for meaty, bone-in English-cut short ribs, with a single rib bone beneath each piece of meat. Ask your butcher to cut them crosswise into 2" lengths—you’re not expected to saw through the bones at home. Avoid the thin strips sold for grilling.

What’s the best wine for braised short ribs?

It has been revealed that choose a dry red wine you’d enjoy drinking. Cabernet Sauvignon is the recipe’s first choice, but Merlot or a Rhône-style red also fits the bill. There’s no need to splurge; save your special bottle for the table.

Drawbridge Cabernet Sauvignon 2024.

Do I have to strain the vegetables?

For the smooth sauce intended here, yes. The vegetables flavor the braising liquid, and straining removes them along with the herb stems, bay leaves, and garlic skins.

For a more rustic approach, pluck out the herbs and garlic skins (leave the cloves behind) and use an immersion blender to purée the cooked vegetables into the sauce.

How do I know when short ribs are done?

Start checking after 2 hours in the oven. A fork should slide into the meat easily, and a gentle twist should pull it apart. If the meat still resists, keep braising. The listed cooking time is a guide, not a hard stop.

Can I make these short ribs ahead, and how should I reheat them?

Yes. Finish cooking the ribs and strain the sauce, then refrigerate the ribs with their sauce in shallow containers within 2 hours of cooking. The next day, lift off the hardened fat. Transfer the ribs and sauce to an ovenproof pot or baking dish, cover, and reheat in a 350° oven until hot throughout—the meat should reach 165° in the center.

Save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app.

Try this recipe with this expert pick from the Bon Appétit Wine Shop.

Staub Enameled Cast Iron Round Dutch Oven 7-Qt.

Preheat oven to 350°. Season 5 lb. bone-in beef short ribs, cut crosswise into 2" pieces by your butcher, with kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Working in 2 batches, cook short ribs, turning occasionally, until browned on all sides, about 8 minutes per batch. Transfer to a plate. Pour off all but 3 Tbsp. drippings from pot.

Cook 3 medium onions, chopped, 3 medium carrots, peeled, chopped, and 2 celery stalks, chopped, in same pot over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onions are browned, about 5 minutes. Add 3 Tbsp. all-purpose flour and 1 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until combined and deep red, 2–3 minutes.

Stir in one 750-ml bottle dry red wine (preferably Cabernet Sauvignon), then add short ribs along with any juices that have accumulated on the plate. Bring to a boil; reduce heat to medium and simmer until wine is reduced by half, about 25 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, halved crosswise, 10 sprigs parsley, 8 sprigs thyme, 4 sprigs oregano, 2 sprigs rosemary, and 2 fresh or dried bay leaves; stir in 4 cups low-sodium beef broth. Bring to a boil, cover, and transfer pot to oven. Braise until short ribs are tender, 2–2½ hours.

Uncover pot and transfer short ribs to a platter. Strain sauce through a fine-mesh sieve into a heatproof measuring glass; spoon fat from surface and discard. Season sauce with salt and pepper. Arrange ribs in shallow bowls, over mashed potatoes if desired, and spoon sauce over.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The scene of officers reading Paine aloud to freezing soldiers before the crossing of the Delaware turns up in biographies, history books, and historical monuments, but the evidence that George Washington ordered it is a lot thinner than its staying power suggests.
  • The usual version says The American Crisis ran in the Pennsylvania Journal on December 19, 1776, and came out as a pamphlet four days later, an account repeated in David Hackett Fischerâs 2004 history Washingtonâs Crossing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In his 2009 inaugural address, Barack Obama described âa small band of patriots huddled by dying campfires on the shores of an icy riverâ and stated that âthe father of our nation ordered these words to be read to the people.â The words were Thomas Paineâs, from the pamphlet that opens with âThese are the times that try menâs souls.â.

The scene of officers reading Paine aloud to freezing soldiers before the crossing of the Delaware turns up in biographies, history books, and historical monuments, but the evidence that George Washington ordered it is a lot thinner than its staying power suggests.

The usual version says The American Crisis ran in the Pennsylvania Journal on December 19, 1776, and came out as a pamphlet four days later, an account repeated in David Hackett Fischerâs 2004 history Washingtonâs Crossing. The trouble is that the Journal suspended publication from December 4, 1776, to January 22, 1777, as Philadelphia braced for a British invasion.

Paine, a volunteer aide to Gen. Nathanael Greene on the retreat, went to Philadelphia in early December to finish the essay. He later recalled, âI began it at Newark on the retreat and got it printed in Philadelphia on the 19th of Dec. 1776. But the printer did not choose to put his name to it.â.

The first copies were unsigned pamphlets credited only to âthe Author of Common Sense,â and the first newspaper known to have run the essay, the Pennsylvania Packet, printed its first half on December 27, the day after the battle at Trenton.

Sources indicate that the earliest known version of the reading story comes from James Cheethamâs The Life of Thomas Paine, published soon after Paineâs death in 1809. Cheetham had soured on Paine over his religious writings, and one 19th-century encyclopedia called the book âinspired by enmityâ. He wrote that âthe number was read in the camp, to every corporalâs guard,â and credited it with âmuch of the brilliant little affair which in the same month followed at Trenton.â He named no source and no date for the reading, never said Washington ordered it, and put the pamphletâs publication âearly in December.â.

Industry observers note that later writers kept adding detail. In 1847, George Lippard, the writer who invented the tale of the Liberty Bell ringing for independence, described âthe Crisis read by every Corporal in the army of Washington.â By 1861, a Boston publisher was advertising reprints as essays that were, âby the orders of General Washington, read to each regiment of the army as they were published.â Moncure Conwayâs 1894 edition of Paineâs writings remarked the first Crisis âby order of the Commander was read to groups of his dispirited and suffering soldiers.â Craig Nelsonâs 2007 Paine biography finally gave it a time, âAt dusk on December 23, 1776,â and offered no source. Ron Chernowâs Washington biography then cited Nelson.

When Washington wanted something read to his troops, he put it in writing. His general orders for July 9, 1776, told the brigades to assemble at six that evening to hear the Declaration of Independence âread with an audible voice.â No equivalent order for Paine has turned up. Jett Conner, writing in the Journal of the American Revolution, found no written order in the Library of Congressâs Washington papers, and nothing in the published papers or biographies of Greene, Alexander Hamilton, Henry Knox, John Glover, or James Monroe, who crossed the river hours ahead of Washington. Paineâs name doesnât appear in the volume of Washingtonâs collected writings covering September 1776 to January 1777.

That doesnât mean soldiers never heard it. J. L. Bell, who traced the story on his blog Boston 1775, treats Cheetham as reluctant testimony and thinks âa lot of the Continental Army under Washington read the American Crisis in late 1776,â but he adds, âI know of no documentation for such an order.â.

Recent findings suggest that washington did praise Paine on paper, eight years later. In a June 1784 letter to James Madison, he asked, âCan nothing be done in our Assembly for poor Paine?â and wrote that âhis writings certainly have had a powerful effect on the public mind.â Ten years after that, Monroe got Paine out of a French prison and reported to Madison that Paine believed the president âwinked at his imprisonment.â.

#285. This Huge US Ski Resort Has the World’s Most Reliable Snow, Upcoming Data Claims

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (750 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Matadornetwork ↗ Open Full Page

This Huge US Ski Resort Has the World’s Most Reliable Snow, Upcoming Data Claims

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in early November, the 2026 World Ski Awards handed out its winners, with only a few nods for ski resorts in North America.
  • It has been revealed that the ranking comes from Inghams, a British travel company that has sold packaged ski trips since 1934.
  • In a recent development, sprawling Niseko United in Japan took the second-place spot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in early November, the 2026 World Ski Awards handed out its winners, with only a few nods for ski resorts in North America. But a second ranking just came out, and while it doesn’t rate the best ski resorts, it rates something that may matter more to die-hard skiers: which resorts have the most reliable snowfall.

It has been revealed that the ranking comes from Inghams, a British travel company that has sold packaged ski trips since 1934. It ranked “reliable snow” — not just how much snow it gets, but how dependably lifts and runs stay open from one season to the next — at major ski resorts and regions using historical data rather than reputation. And the resort at the top is decidedly not in the Alps. It’s not even in Colorado or the Rockies. The distinction goes to Mammoth Mountain in California, which scored 93.9 out of 100 on what the company calls its “Reliable Ski Score.”.

In a recent development, sprawling Niseko United in Japan took the second-place spot. Photo: Various images/Shutterstock.

Many “best of” ski lists come down to a basic metric, like how much snow a resort gets on average or how many people vote for it online. But the Inghams process is more involved, scoring 133 resorts and regions on five weighted factors, then averaging them to get a score out of 100. The largest share (35 percent) was based on “mountain running,” or the average percentage of lifts and slopes open during peak season. Snow adequacy, defined as the share of core-season days with at least 30 centimeters (about a foot) at the base, accounted for another 25 percent. The rest of the score rewarded consistency from one season to the next (20 percent); downside protection, or how far a resort’s conditions drop in its worst season compared with a typical one (12 percent); and the average depth of the snowpack on the mountain, where deeper simply scores higher (8 percent).

The researchers pulled seven winters of data, from 2017/18 through 2025/26 (removing the two COVID-affected seasons), and defined peak season as January 5 to March 20. The figures were compiled from public historical listings on skiresort.com and are current as of September 2026.

Mammoth’s win is thanks to its high elevation (the Main Lodge base is about 9,000 feet above sea level) and its long seasons, which can stretch from October into June in strong years. It was the only resort to score well across all five of the reliability measures at once, which is what separated it from the pack.

Photo: Visit Mammoth/Patrick Griley.

Below Mammoth, the rest of the top picks are spread across four countries: Niseko United in Japan (93.3), Pontedilegno-Tonale in Italy (93.1), Obertauern in Austria (92.9), and Jackson Hole in Wyoming (92.5).

Industry observers note that the biggest surprise is how much of the list sits outside the Alps. North American resorts took eight of the top 20 spots. Canada landed five, giving it more than any single European country except France, and the US had three resorts in the top 10. Canada’s Banff Sunshine had one of the most impressive numbers in the study: it hit the “snow-adequacy” bar on every single peak-season day across all seven winters, making it the only resort to get a perfect 100 percent. It’s not a huge minimum, requiring only about a foot at the base, but meeting it every day for seven years is something no other resort managed.

France was the strongest European performer, with five resorts in the top 20, including Les 3 Vallées, the largest linked ski area in the world.

There is a commercial angle here, as there usually is with operator research. Inghams sells packaged trips to many of the resorts it scored, and it backs those bookings with a Snow Guarantee that will move travelers to a nearby resort, free of charge, if fewer than a quarter of the mountain is open due to lack of snow. So in some ways, the ranking doubles as a sales pitch for the idea of booking reliability in the first place.

Industry observers note that nonetheless, the research is data-driven, and the winning mountains are worth a look if you’re deciding where to plan your ski trip this season. The World Ski Awards reward the resorts skiers love, but this list rewards the ones most likely to deliver on conditions, and the two lists aren’t always the same.

Not every great movie moment is planned. Sometimes when budgets are tight, deadlines are looming, and shoots are ongoing, production teams on some of Hollywoodâs most beloved films had to learn to make do. These five examples prove just that.

For John Carpenterâs 1978 horror classic Halloween, production designer Tommy Lee Wallace was given the daunting task of fashioning a mask frightening enough to befit the filmâs murderous antagonist, Michael Myers.Â.

Industry observers note that working with a limited budget, Wallace tried altering a few different commercially available Halloween masks (including one of former president Richard Nixon) before finally landing on a mask modeled after actor William Shatner as his Star Trek character, Capt. James T. Kirk.

Since its design in the late â70s, every Halloween film since has utilized a version of Wallaceâs original hair-raising design.Â.

In the Tom Hanks survival drama Cast Away, Hanksâs character Chuck Noland, a FedEx systems analyst marooned on an island in the South Pacific, befriends a volleyball he affectionately dubs âWilsonâ after the sports brand whoâd manufactured it.

After Noland smears his bloody palm on the ball and draws on a crude face, Wilson becomes the analyst's beloved companion and only tether to sanity throughout the filmâs duration.Â.

Recent findings suggest that producers on the film had originally requested soccer balls from Wilson, but when the fake blood theyâd used wouldnât adhere to the ballâs surface, producers on the film requested volleyballs with the Wilson name printed on just one side be sent instead. Despite most of the filmâs details being kept secret from execs at Wilson, the tech giant obliged, sending Cast Awayâs production team about 150 volleyballs.Â.

After the filmâs release, Wilson benefitted hugely from the unsuspecting partnership, later making replicas of the iconic Cast Away volleyball.

In a recent development, in 1991, basketball player Michael Jordan donned a pair of Nike Air Jordan VIs to carry the Chicago Bulls to their very first NBA Championship win. Sources indicate that while scouting locations for Wes Cravenâs horror film Scream, producer Marianne Maddalena discovered what would become the serial murderer Ghostfaceâs iconic mask. Produced by Fun World, the maskâs design was first sold in Halloween stores in the early 1990s as part of Fun Worldâs âFantastic Facesâ series of Halloween masks.Â.

It has been revealed that craven originally asked special effects make-up artist Howard Berger to design a version of the mask to be used in the film, but the director was eventually able to reach an agreement with Fun World to use their original design in the film. Since Screamâs premiere in 1996, the mask has become one of the most widely purchased Halloween masks in the United States and has remained a mainstay in the franchise since.Â.

According to recent reports, throughout British comedy troupe Monty Pythonâs beloved 1975 comedy Monty Python and the Holy Grail, the cast of the film gallop along while their porters bang coconuts together to simulate riding horses. While this bit later became one of the comedyâs most beloved absurdist qualities, the reasoning behind it was much more pragmatic than comedic.Â.

In a recent development, A make-ahead casserole, like this pumpkin-infused strata scented with nutmeg and herbs and balanced by sharp cheddar, is just what your holiday schedule needs. Assemble it the night before; bake it on Thanksgiving.

Sources indicate that kale, pinto beans, and charred poblanos make these cheesy enchiladas a satisfying holiday main for four to six. Get a head start by making the charred salsa verde up to three days ahead.

Industry observers note that this autumnal risotto works as a standalone dinner or alongside your favorite Thanksgiving sides. Set the table with shallow bowls and pick a fall salad full of color and crunch to balance the buttery rice.

According to recent reports, british beef Wellington meets Cantonese barbecue-style pork in Peter Som’s pastry-wrapped centerpiece. A shiitake mushroom filling and gravy made from the marinade complete the picture; assemble the Wellington a day ahead.

According to recent reports, brisket more your speed? Try our Brisket Bourguignon →.

Turkey skin has competition. Tender pork belly, crisp crackling, and a hard cider pan sauce make a persuasive case for skipping the bird. Pass the chile vinegar to cut through the richness; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

In a recent development, maybe save the brown sugar-glazed ham for Christmas? This whole leg of lamb makes for a centerpiece that’s just as showstopping. And, like ham and turkey, leftover lamb can be deliciously repurposed in sandwiches.

Latest Update: 6 Forgotten Dating Terms From the Early 1900s

💡 Key Takeaways

  • About 100 years ago, people were definitely not calling each other "bae" or "shorty," but they still had their own endearments and words for dating.
  • These words might sound so old to our ears, but they were part of the dating and romance discourse in the early 1900s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we like to think that people in the past only spoke formally, and that modifying language to be more casual is a recent trend. But slang words have been used for millennia. The slang of the past was just different than what we know today.

About 100 years ago, people were definitely not calling each other "bae" or "shorty," but they still had their own endearments and words for dating. Some of the words were even euphemisms for some pretty scandalous activities.

These words might sound so old to our ears, but they were part of the dating and romance discourse in the early 1900s.

Recent findings suggest that the word "woo" actually just means "to court," so wooing and courting mean the same thing: seeking the favor of a person you're interested in. Courting goes back to the royal courts, when people called courtiers attended to the king or queen.

It has been revealed that they helped the royals with daily life and management of the country. Courting someone, or dating with the intent to marry, began to be used in the 1800s, having morphed from this old definition of courtiers.

Recent findings suggest that the word "beau" comes from the French word meaning "handsome or beautiful." Beginning in the 1600s, "beau" was merely a synonym for a dandy, or a man who cared a lot about his presentation and appearance. But it evolved to mean "a male suitor" after 100 years, and remained a popular term well into the 1900s. It was the equivalent of the word "boyfriend.".

Industry observers note that keen, meaning "eager," has been in the English language since the early 1300s. It didn't become a slang word meaning attraction to someone or having a crush until 1900. At the turn of the century, teenagers used keen to describe anything cool or great, i.e., "peachy keen." It easily slid from there to being "keen on" someone, or eager to be with them because of how great you thought they were.

The term "necking" just sounds wrong compared to the modern phrase "making out." Necking was first used in the 1800s to describe kissing and fondling passionately. Maybe it caught on after one too many ladies had hickeys on their necks?

In any case, the term "necking" fell out of favor as the mid-1900s hit, being replaced with "petting" or "heavy petting." In the 1920s, necking or petting parties scandalized conservative America.

Speaking of hickeys, the marks lovers left on each other by sucking on the skin were once called love bites. The term "love bite" dates back to the 1700s, when it was first recorded in John Cleland's novel, Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure.

Industry observers note that the word hickey didn't start to replace "love bite" until 1934 in the U.S. In other countries like the U.K. and Australia, "love bite" is still used and preferred over "hickey.".

In the 1910s and 1920s, a woman who was not interested in necking, or kissing at all, would tell her suitor, "bank's closed." It could also be noted to a highly affectionate couple, with a similar meaning to "get a room.".

The phrase "bank's closed" just meant that kissing at that moment was not appropriate, so there would be no "cashing in.".

The UK's 2025 increases in minimum wage, payroll tax and property tax were meant to fall on major employers. Company filings now landing show they hit hospitality and travel businesses of every size, from Premier Inn's owner to a celebrity chef's seaside restaurants and a regional travel agency.

Recent findings suggest that "The 12 months to 28 December 2025 were exceptionally challenging for the UK hospitality sector," the directors of The Seafood Restaurant (Padstow) Ltd wrote in accounts filed this week with Companies House, the UK's manufacturer register. Rising labor and property costs, which they called "government forced increases," cost the group "in excess of £600,000 [$800,000] in 2025.".

Industry observers note that the group, which runs restaurants, hotel rooms, a cookery school and shops, reported a pre-tax loss of £814,000 ($1.1m). That was almost double the year before, on flat revenue of £18.9 million ($25.1 million). Revenue is down 17% since 2022. It closed its central food production unit in October 2025, with 22 job losses. A sister tech giant with the same owners, Stein's Trading, which runs more of the family's restaurants, noted the same co.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Singer-songwriter Paul Simon has enjoyed so many hits over the years that people still argue over which represents his best work. One song that always enters this conversation, however, is the enduring classic "Bridge Over Troubled Water," which he created when still part of a duo with Art Garfunkel.Â.

Simon penned "Bridge Over Troubled Water" in early 1969, inspired in part by the gospel group the Swan Silvertones, whose song "Oh Mary Donât You Weep" featured the lines: "I'll be your bridge over deep water if you trust in my name." The melody for "Bridgeâ¦" was partly based on Johann Sebastian Bach's "O Sacred Head, Now Wounded" and the finished song served as the title track for Simon's last album with Garfunkel in 1970.Â.

Industry observers note that it proved phenomenally successful, spending six consecutive weeks at number one on the Billboard Hot 100 and performing similar feats in the UK, Canada, and Newly introduced Zealand. At the 13th annual Grammy Awards in 1971, the song scooped up prizes for Record of the Year, Song of the Year, and Best Contemporary Song, and also won the Best Arrangement Accompanying Vocalists category (with Simon co-credited alongside Larry Knechtel) and Best Engineered Recording - Non-Classical (for audio engineer Roy Halee).

Although "Bridge Over Troubled Water" was performed as part of that Grammy Award ceremony, it was not Simon & Garfunkel who sang it that night. That honor went to legendary soul singer Aretha Franklin, whose own recording of the number would be released as a single just three days later, on March 19.Â.

Speaking in an interview in 2018, Simon, when asked for his reflections on Franklin's version, opined: âHer recording is brilliantâmaybe itâs the best cover of any of my songs that anyone ever didâ¦ What Aretha did was, she did explain it to a Black audience and made that song relevant in a way that it was always meant to do."Â.

According to recent reports, the singer remained justifiably proud of his original, however, stressing, "â¦the Simon & Garfunkel recording was really at least as good as Arethaâs. The piano on thatâLarry Knechtelâs pianoâis a beautiful gospel piano, absolutely beautiful. The way [Art Garfunkel] sang it was sort of choirboy, which was very much Artieâthatâs what he was when he grew up.".

2018 was the year in which Aretha Franklin sadly passed, and it is perhaps former President Barack Obama and his wife Michelle Obama who most eloquently summed up the singer's singular talent and importance, writing: "Aretha helped define the American experience. In her voice, we could feel our history, all of it and in every shadeâour power and our pain, our darkness and our light, our quest for redemption and our hard-won respect." Listen to Franklin's recording of "Bridge Over Troubled Water" and you can hear that emotion ring through.Â.

The Best Air Fryers For Faster, Crispier Cooking (2026)
